c.dose: Oral 2-4 g loading, then 2-4 g/day divided (equal parts of each sulfonamide)
ind: Historical treatment of urinary tract infections and other susceptible bacterial infections; largely superseded by co-trimoxazole.
c.doc: Historical alternative when reduced crystalluria risk was needed with older sulfonamides
c.ci: Sulfonamide hypersensitivity, porphyria, pregnancy at term, infants under 2 months
ae: Crystalluria (reduced vs single-agent), rash, nausea, photosensitivity
c.sae: Stevens-Johnson syndrome/toxic epidermal necrolysis, hemolytic anemia (G6PD deficiency)
c.info: Combines three sulfonamides with independent, additive antibacterial (dihydropteroate synthase inhibition) but non-additive urinary solubility, so each remains below its individual saturation point in urine, substantially lowering crystalluria risk compared with an equivalent total dose of any single sulfonamide.
c.caution: Fixed combination of three sulfonamides — confirm the labeled composition and total sulfonamide content before dosing; ensure adequate hydration.
c.preg: Avoid near term (last few weeks of pregnancy) — sulfonamides displace bilirubin from albumin, risking kernicterus in the neonate; also generally avoided in the first trimester given a possible small increase in birth-defect risk with folate-antagonist exposure. Avoid during breastfeeding of newborns, premature infants, or G6PD-deficient infants (kernicterus/hemolysis risk); can be used with more caution in older, healthy infants.
c.renal: Renally eliminated with a risk of crystalluria — ensure adequate hydration and reduce the dose in renal impairment; use with caution in hepatic impairment (rare hepatotoxicity).

ind: Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia, uncomplicated UTIs, community-acquired MRSA skin infections, nocardiosis, and Stenotrophomonas maltophilia infections.
c.doc: Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (treatment and prophylaxis); Nocardiosis; Stenotrophomonas maltophilia bacteremia
c.ci: Severe sulfonamide allergy, documented megaloblastic anemia due to folate deficiency, CrCl <15 mL/min, pregnancy at term, infants <2 months
c.sci: Megaloblastic bone marrow suppression / Severe hyperkalemia
ae: Gastrointestinal upset, hyperkalemia, serum creatinine elevation, morbilliform rash, photosensitivity
c.sae: Hyperkalemia (amiloride-like ENaC blockade by trimethoprim) / Stevens-Johnson syndrome
c.info: Synergistic bactericidal combination in a fixed 5:1 ratio that sequentially blocks microbial folate synthesis (SMX inhibits dihydropteroate synthase, TMP inhibits dihydrofolate reductase).
c.caution: Confirm the trimethoprim:sulfamethoxazole ratio on the product (e.g., 80/400 vs 160/800) before converting a dose to tablets/volume. Encourage good fluid intake; shake the suspension before dosing.
c.preg: Avoid in the first trimester — the trimethoprim component is a folate antagonist linked to a small increase in neural tube defect risk; also avoid near term (sulfamethoxazole displaces bilirubin, risking neonatal kernicterus). Avoid during breastfeeding of premature, jaundiced, or G6PD-deficient infants.
c.renal: Renally eliminated with a risk of crystalluria — ensure adequate hydration and reduce the dose in renal impairment; use with caution in hepatic impairment (rare hepatotoxicity).

ind: Acute bacterial rhinosinusitis, animal/human bite wounds, acute exacerbation of COPD, complicated otitis media, and diabetic foot infections.
c.doc: Mammalian bite wounds (Pasteurella/Eikenella); Amoxicillin-resistant Acute Bacterial Sinusitis
c.ci: History of co-amoxiclav-associated cholestatic jaundice/hepatic impairment, severe penicillin allergy
ae: Diarrhea (clavulanate-induced hypermotility), cholestatic jaundice, nausea, candidiasis
c.sae: Cholestatic hepatitis (clavulanate-mediated) / Diarrhea
c.info: Clavulanic acid is a suicide inhibitor of beta-lactamases (Classes A); clavulanate stimulates GI motility causing secretory diarrhea.
c.caution: Take at the start of a meal to reduce GI upset and improve absorption of the clavulanate component. Shake the oral suspension well; different strength ratios (e.g., 500/125 vs 875/125) are not interchangeable on a per-tablet basis.
c.preg: Considered compatible with pregnancy and generally with breastfeeding, but the clavulanic acid component carries a well-documented, sometimes delayed-onset risk of cholestatic hepatitis/jaundice — higher than with amoxicillin alone; report jaundice or persistent nausea promptly.
c.renal: Predominantly renally eliminated — reduce the dose or extend the interval in renal impairment; no routine hepatic dose adjustment is needed.

ind: Stenotrophomonas maltophilia infections, nosocomial pneumonia, and complicated intra-abdominal infections.
c.doc: Stenotrophomonas maltophilia infections (historical first-line)

ae: Hypokalemia, fluid overload/hypernatremia, bleeding tendency from antiplatelet effect, diarrhea

c.info: High in vitro activity against Stenotrophomonas maltophilia; withdrawn in several countries in favor of piperacillin/tazobactam.
c.caution: Reconstitute and infuse IV per label; monitor sodium load and platelet function with prolonged use.
c.preg: Considered one of the safest antibiotic classes in pregnancy, used at all stages when clinically indicated. Crosses into breast milk in small amounts; compatible with breastfeeding, though watch for infant diarrhea, rash, or oral/diaper thrush from altered gut flora.
c.renal: Renally eliminated, and high IV doses can impair platelet aggregation — reduce the dose in renal impairment and monitor for bleeding, especially in patients with pre-existing renal disease; no routine hepatic adjustment needed.

ind: Intra-abdominal infections, biliary tract infections, complicated skin/soft tissue infections, and febrile neutropenia (widely used in Asia and the Middle East).

c.ci: Penicillin/cephalosporin hypersensitivity
c.sci: Beta-lactam allergy, bleeding disorders (cefoperazone's NMTT side chain impairs vitamin K-dependent clotting)
ae: Diarrhea, disulfiram-like reaction with alcohol, hypoprothrombinemia, injection site pain
c.sae: Bleeding due to hypoprothrombinemia (NMTT side chain), C. difficile colitis
c.info: Sulbactam restores cefoperazone's activity against beta-lactamase-producing Enterobacterales; cefoperazone's high biliary excretion and N-methylthiotetrazole (NMTT) side chain account for both its efficacy in biliary infections and its bleeding/disulfiram-like risks.
c.caution: Reconstitute per label; avoid alcohol during and after treatment due to a possible disulfiram-like reaction.
c.preg: Considered compatible with pregnancy at all stages — one of the best-studied and safest antibiotic classes in pregnancy, with no established teratogenic risk. Crosses into breast milk in small amounts; generally compatible with breastfeeding, though may cause loose stools, diaper rash, or oral thrush from altered infant gut flora.
c.renal: Eliminated mainly via biliary excretion (~70%) rather than the kidney — reduce the dose in significant hepatic impairment or biliary obstruction; renal dose adjustment is usually unnecessary unless renal and hepatic impairment coexist.

c.doc: KPC-producing Carbapenem-Resistant Enterobacterales (CRE)

c.sae: Seizures / C. difficile colitis / Loss of valproate seizure control
c.info: Vaborbactam is a cyclic boronic acid beta-lactamase inhibitor with potent activity against Class A carbapenemases (KPC) and Class C (AmpC) enzymes. It does not inhibit Class B metallo-beta-lactamases (NDM, VIM, IMP) or OXA-48-type (Class D) enzymes, so those producers remain resistant.

c.renal: Cleared by the kidney — reduce the dose when eGFR falls below 50 mL/min.

c.caution: Reconstitute and dilute per the label; infuse IV over 30 minutes. Reduce the dose when CrCl is below 90 mL/min. Avoid with valproate and ganciclovir.
c.preg: Human data are limited but reassuring, and animal studies have not shown teratogenicity; reserve for serious infections where safer beta-lactams are unsuitable. c.renal: Cleared by the kidney — stepwise dose reductions apply when creatinine clearance is below 90 mL/min.

c.preg: Human data are lacking — use in pregnancy only if clearly needed and no better-studied option exists. Breastfeeding data are limited; watch the infant for diarrhea or thrush if used.
c.renal: Not well studied in severe renal impairment — check current labeling before use; probenecid is less effective when GFR is low.

c.mn:
💊 Names: Spelled 'Ceph' (with PH) = the old ones: Cephalothin, Cephaloridine, Cephapirin, Cephradine, Cephalexin. Spelled 'Cef' (with F) = Cefazolin, Cefadroxil. Still used today: Cefazolin, Cephalexin, Cefadroxil.

c.sp:
Gram-positive: MRSA (ceftaroline, ceftobiprole), Streptococcus pneumoniae (including penicillin-resistant strains), Streptococcus pyogenes, Enterococcus faecalis (ceftobiprole)
Gram-negative: Escherichia coli, Klebsiella pneumoniae (including ESBL and KPC producers), Proteus mirabilis, Enterobacter, Pseudomonas aeruginosa (ceftolozane, ceftazidime-avibactam, cefiderocol), Acinetobacter baumannii (cefiderocol, cefoperazone + sulbactam), Stenotrophomonas maltophilia (cefiderocol)
c.mn:
💊 Names: MRSA pair: Ceftaroline, Ceftobiprole (both end in '-role'). Resistant Gram-negative group: Ceftolozane, Ceftazidime-avibactam, Cefiderocol, Cefoperazone + Sulbactam.
🦠 Kills: MRSA (the pair). Multidrug-resistant Gram-negatives including Pseudomonas and Klebsiella (the group).
🎯 Used for: Complicated skin infections, hospital pneumonia, complicated urinary and belly infections.
💡 Tip: 5th generation = last-resort, hospital-only.

ov.moa: Beta-lactam antibiotics that bind penicillin-binding proteins (PBPs) to inhibit bacterial cell wall (peptidoglycan) synthesis, causing bacterial lysis; bactericidal.
ov.ind: Broad-spectrum coverage that shifts toward gram-negative activity with each successive generation; used for skin/soft tissue, respiratory, urinary tract, and surgical prophylaxis, with later generations used for meningitis and serious gram-negative or resistant infections. Covers streptococci and methicillin-susceptible S. aureus, with gram-negative coverage broadening across generations from E. coli, Klebsiella, and Proteus mirabilis (1st gen) to H. influenzae, Neisseria, and Enterobacter (2nd gen) to Serratia, Pseudomonas aeruginosa (select agents), S. pneumoniae, and N. meningitidis (3rd/4th gen); ceftaroline (5th gen) adds MRSA coverage.
ov.ae: GI upset (nausea, diarrhea), rash, and local injection-site reactions with parenteral agents; can cause C. difficile colitis and, rarely, seizures at high doses in renal impairment.
ov.ci: Avoid in patients with a history of severe (anaphylactic) penicillin allergy due to potential cross-reactivity; use with caution and adjust dose in renal impairment.
ov.counsel: Take oral agents as directed (with or without food, per specific drug), complete the full course even if feeling better, and report any rash, swelling, difficulty breathing, or severe/persistent diarrhea immediately.

ind: Neurosyphilis, congenital syphilis, infective endocarditis (Streptococcus viridans), gas gangrene (Clostridium perfringens), meningococcal meningitis.
c.doc: Syphilis (Treponema pallidum); Gas Gangrene (C. perfringens + Clindamycin); Streptococcus pyogenes Necrotizing Fasciitis
c.ci: Penicillin hypersensitivity
ae: Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction in syphilis, hypersensitivity rash, hemolytic anemia, seizures with high-dose IV in renal failure
c.sae: Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction / Penicillin neurotoxicity/seizures
c.info: Acid-labile natural penicillin given IV; binds PBPs inhibiting transpeptidation. Rapidly excreted by tubular secretion (blocked by probenecid).
c.caution: Reconstitute the powder with the diluent volume stated on the label; give by IV injection/infusion or deep IM. Confirm the dose is expressed correctly in units vs grams before drawing up — dosing errors are common.
c.preg: Considered one of the safest antibiotic classes in pregnancy, used at all stages when clinically indicated. Crosses into breast milk in small amounts; compatible with breastfeeding, though watch for infant diarrhea, rash, or oral/diaper thrush from altered gut flora.
c.renal: Predominantly renally eliminated — reduce the dose or extend the interval in renal impairment; no routine hepatic dose adjustment is needed.

ind: Uncomplicated neurosyphilis, moderate streptococcal infections, and anthrax.
c.doc: Syphilis in outpatient regimens
c.ci: Penicillin allergy, ester local anesthetic (procaine) allergy, intravenous administration (MUST BE IM ONLY)
ae: Hoigné syndrome (microembolism causing panic, hallucinations, seizures if given IV), local pain, rash
c.sae: Hoigné syndrome (pseudo-anaphylaxis from accidental vascular injection)
c.info: Equimolar formulation of penicillin G and procaine; creates an IM repository releasing penicillin slowly over 12-24 hours.
c.caution: Deep IM injection only — never give IV or into a vein (risk of procaine toxicity/embolic reaction). Shake the suspension well immediately before drawing up.
c.preg: Considered one of the safest antibiotic classes in pregnancy, used at all stages when clinically indicated. Crosses into breast milk in small amounts; compatible with breastfeeding, though watch for infant diarrhea, rash, or oral/diaper thrush from altered gut flora.
c.renal: Predominantly renally eliminated — reduce the dose or extend the interval in renal impairment; no routine hepatic dose adjustment is needed.

ind: Primary, secondary, and early latent syphilis; rheumatic fever secondary prophylaxis; streptococcal pharyngitis.
c.doc: Primary/Secondary/Early Latent Syphilis (2.4 MU IM single dose); Secondary Rheumatic Fever Prophylaxis
c.ci: Penicillin allergy, INTRAVENOUS ADMINISTRATION CONTRAINDICATED (can cause cardiac arrest and limb ischemia)
c.sci: Accidental IV administration (cardiac arrest / Nicolau syndrome)
ae: Nicolau syndrome (livedoid dermatitis/gangrene from intra-arterial injection), Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction, severe IM pain
c.sae: Nicolau syndrome / Accidental IV cardiac arrest
c.info: Insoluble salt providing sustained low plasma levels of penicillin G over 3-4 weeks from a single deep IM depot.
c.caution: Deep IM injection only — never give IV, SC, or into a small muscle (risk of vascular injury/embolism and tissue necrosis). Shake well and use a large-bore needle due to its thick, viscous suspension.
c.preg: Considered one of the safest antibiotic classes in pregnancy, used at all stages when clinically indicated. Crosses into breast milk in small amounts; compatible with breastfeeding, though watch for infant diarrhea, rash, or oral/diaper thrush from altered gut flora.
c.renal: Predominantly renally eliminated — reduce the dose or extend the interval in renal impairment; no routine hepatic dose adjustment is needed.

ind: Streptococcal pharyngitis, mild erysipelas, prophylaxis against pneumococcal infection in asplenia/sickle cell disease.
c.doc: Group A Streptococcal Pharyngitis (oral first-line)
c.ci: Penicillin hypersensitivity
ae: Nausea, vomiting, epigastric distress, diarrhea, urticaria
c.sae: Hypersensitivity reaction
c.info: Acid-stable analogue of Penicillin G suited for oral administration; food reduces gastric absorption.
c.caution: Best taken on an empty stomach, 1 hour before or 2 hours after food, for optimal absorption. Shake the oral suspension before dosing.
c.preg: Considered one of the safest antibiotic classes in pregnancy, used at all stages when clinically indicated. Crosses into breast milk in small amounts; compatible with breastfeeding, though watch for infant diarrhea, rash, or oral/diaper thrush from altered gut flora.
c.renal: Predominantly renally eliminated — reduce the dose or extend the interval in renal impairment; no routine hepatic dose adjustment is needed.

c.sp:
Gram-positive: Streptococcus pyogenes, Streptococcus pneumoniae (susceptible), viridans streptococci, Staphylococcus aureus (non-penicillinase producing), Bacillus anthracis, Listeria monocytogenes, Corynebacterium diphtheriae
Gram-negative: Neisseria meningitidis, Neisseria gonorrhoeae (susceptible strains), Pasteurella multocida
Anaerobes: Clostridium perfringens, Clostridium tetani, Actinomyces israelii, Peptostreptococcus
Spirochetes: Treponema pallidum
c.mn:
💊 Names: Injections (Penicillin G): Benzyl, Procaine, Benzathine, in order of how long they last: Benzyl (hours), Procaine (a day), Benzathine (weeks). Tablet (Penicillin V): Phenoxymethyl.
🦠 Kills: Streptococci (throat, pneumonia), Neisseria meningitidis, Treponema pallidum (syphilis). Destroyed by penicillinase enzyme, so no good against most Staph.
🎯 Used for: Strep throat, syphilis, rheumatic fever prevention (Benzathine), mild skin and mouth infections.
💡 Tip: G = Get a needle. V = Via mouth.

ind: Historical anti-staphylococcal penicillin; used historically to define MRSA in laboratory testing.
c.doc: Obsolete (reference standard for MRSA definition)
c.ci: Penicillin allergy, pre-existing renal disease
ae: Severe acute interstitial nephritis, hematuria, fever, rash
c.sae: Immune-mediated acute interstitial nephritis
c.info: Discontinued due to high incidence of immune-mediated acute interstitial nephritis; resistance occurs via mecA gene encoding PBP2a.
c.caution: No longer manufactured or used clinically due to interstitial nephritis; retained only as the historical basis for the term MRSA.
c.preg: Considered one of the safest antibiotic classes in pregnancy, used at all stages when clinically indicated. Crosses into breast milk in small amounts; compatible with breastfeeding, though watch for infant diarrhea, rash, or oral/diaper thrush from altered gut flora.
c.renal: Obsolete and no longer clinically used; historically notable for causing acute interstitial nephritis (a hypersensitivity reaction, not simple dose-dependent toxicity) — one of the main reasons it was abandoned in favor of newer isoxazolyl penicillins.

ind: Severe systemic MSSA infections, acute staphylococcal endocarditis, osteomyelitis, and bacteremia.
c.doc: MSSA endocarditis / bacteremia (parenteral standard)
c.ci: Penicillin hypersensitivity
ae: Elevated liver enzymes (transaminitis), hepatitis, interstitial nephritis, phlebitis
c.sae: Hepatotoxicity (transaminitis) / Acute interstitial nephritis
c.info: Does not require renal dose adjustments as it undergoes significant hepatic elimination and biliary excretion.
c.caution: Reconstitute per the vial label; infuse IV over 10–30 minutes. Monitor liver enzymes with prolonged courses.
c.preg: Considered one of the safest antibiotic classes in pregnancy, used at all stages when clinically indicated. Crosses into breast milk in small amounts; compatible with breastfeeding, though watch for infant diarrhea, rash, or oral/diaper thrush from altered gut flora.
c.renal: Eliminated mainly via hepatobiliary excretion rather than the kidney — little or no dose adjustment is usually needed in renal impairment, but use with caution in significant hepatic impairment.

ind: Severe systemic MSSA infections, staphylococcal endocarditis, and osteomyelitis.
c.doc: Serious MSSA bacteremia, endocarditis, and CNS staphylococcal infections
c.ci: Penicillin hypersensitivity
ae: Severe thrombophlebitis, acute interstitial nephritis, neutropenia, hypokalemia
c.sae: Acute interstitial nephritis (AIN) / Severe local tissue necrosis on extravasation
c.info: Mainly eliminated by biliary excretion and hepatic metabolism; no renal dose adjustments needed in renal failure.
c.caution: Highly irritating to veins — give through a large vein or central line where possible and watch closely for extravasation, which can cause tissue necrosis.
c.preg: Considered one of the safest antibiotic classes in pregnancy, used at all stages when clinically indicated. Crosses into breast milk in small amounts; compatible with breastfeeding, though watch for infant diarrhea, rash, or oral/diaper thrush from altered gut flora.
c.renal: Eliminated mainly via hepatobiliary excretion rather than the kidney — little or no dose adjustment is usually needed in renal impairment, but use with caution in significant hepatic impairment.

ind: Skin and soft tissue infections caused by penicillinase-producing staphylococci (MSSA), impetigo, and cellulitis.
c.doc: Methicillin-Sensitive Staphylococcus aureus (MSSA) skin/soft tissue infections
c.ci: Penicillin hypersensitivity
ae: GI upset, phlebitis, rash, cholestatic jaundice, eosinophilia
c.sae: Cholestatic hepatitis
c.info: Isoxazolyl penicillin; bulky isoxazolyl side chain sterically hinders staphylococcal beta-lactamase enzyme.
c.caution: Oral capsules should be taken on an empty stomach. Reconstitute the injection per label and give by slow IV injection or deep IM.
c.preg: Considered one of the safest antibiotic classes in pregnancy, used at all stages when clinically indicated. Crosses into breast milk in small amounts; compatible with breastfeeding, though watch for infant diarrhea, rash, or oral/diaper thrush from altered gut flora.
c.renal: Eliminated mainly via hepatobiliary excretion rather than the kidney — little or no dose adjustment is usually needed in renal impairment, but use with caution in significant hepatic impairment.

ind: Mild-to-moderate MSSA skin and soft tissue infections, folliculitis, and breast abscess / mastitis.
c.doc: Puerperal mastitis (MSSA-suspected outpatient)
c.ci: Penicillin hypersensitivity
ae: Nausea, abdominal pain, diarrhea, pill-induced esophagitis
c.sae: Pill-induced esophagitis
c.info: Highest oral absorption and highest plasma protein binding (>95%) among the isoxazolyl penicillins; take with a full glass of water while upright.
c.caution: Take on an empty stomach, 1 hour before or 2 hours after meals, for reliable absorption.
c.preg: Considered one of the safest antibiotic classes in pregnancy, used at all stages when clinically indicated. Crosses into breast milk in small amounts; compatible with breastfeeding, though watch for infant diarrhea, rash, or oral/diaper thrush from altered gut flora.
c.renal: Eliminated mainly via hepatobiliary excretion rather than the kidney — little or no dose adjustment is usually needed in renal impairment, but use with caution in significant hepatic impairment.

c.st: Cap 250, 500 mg · Inj 250 mg, 500 mg, 1 g · Susp 125, 250 mg/5 mL
c.dose: Cap 250, 500 mg · Inj 250 mg, 500 mg, 1 g · Susp 125, 250 mg/5 mL
ind: Staphylococcal skin/soft tissue infections, wound infections, surgical prophylaxis, and staphylococcal osteomyelitis.
c.doc: MSSA cellulitis and surgical wound infections (first-line in UK/Europe/Australasia)
c.ci: History of flucloxacillin-associated jaundice/hepatic dysfunction
ae: Cholestatic hepatitis, delayed jaundice (up to 2 months post-treatment), diarrhea, rash
c.sae: Delayed cholestatic jaundice & hepatitis (HLA-B*57:01 linked)
c.info: Strong genetic predisposition for idiosyncratic cholestatic jaundice linked to HLA-B*57:01 allele.
c.caution: Oral doses are best taken on an empty stomach. Counsel on the (rare but sometimes delayed) risk of cholestatic hepatitis, more common in older adults and with courses longer than 2 weeks.
c.preg: Considered compatible with pregnancy and breastfeeding, but carries a distinct, well-documented risk (not specific to pregnancy) of delayed-onset cholestatic hepatitis/jaundice, occasionally appearing weeks after the course ends; report jaundice or persistent nausea promptly regardless of when treatment was given.
c.renal: Eliminated mainly via hepatobiliary excretion rather than the kidney — little or no dose adjustment is usually needed in renal impairment, but use with caution in significant hepatic impairment.

c.sp: Gram-positive: Staphylococcus aureus (MSSA, penicillinase-producing), Staphylococcus epidermidis (methicillin-susceptible), Streptococcus pyogenes, Streptococcus pneumoniae (susceptible)
c.mn:
💊 Names: 'Clox' family: Cloxacillin, Dicloxacillin, Flucloxacillin. The other three: Oxacillin, Nafcillin, Methicillin.
🦠 Kills: Staphylococcus aureus (MSSA), even strains that make penicillinase. NOT MRSA.
🎯 Used for: Skin infections, cellulitis, bone infections, Staph heart-valve infections.
💡 Tip: M in MRSA = Methicillin-Resistant, so these do not work on MRSA.

c.st: Cap 250, 500 mg · Inj 250 mg, 500 mg, 1 g, 2 g
c.dose: Cap 250, 500 mg · Inj 250 mg, 500 mg, 1 g, 2 g
ind: Listeria monocytogenes meningitis, Enterococcus faecalis endocarditis, susceptible Gram-negative infections, and neonatal sepsis (+ Gentamicin).
c.doc: Listeria monocytogenes meningitis/sepsis; Enterococcal Endocarditis (+ Gentamicin/Ceftriaxone)
c.ci: Penicillin hypersensitivity, infectious mononucleosis (EBV)
c.sci: Epstein-Barr Virus / Infectious mononucleosis (causes maculopapular rash)
ae: Non-allergic maculopapular rash in viral infections (EBV/CMV), diarrhea, nausea, C. difficile colitis
c.sae: Aminopenicillin-induced viral rash (EBV/infectious mononucleosis)
c.info: Amino side chain enhances passage through Gram-negative porin channels; oral bioavailability is relatively poor (~40%) compared to amoxicillin.
c.caution: Oral doses are best taken on an empty stomach. Reconstituted injection solutions lose potency quickly — use promptly per the label's stated in-use time.
c.preg: Considered one of the safest antibiotic classes in pregnancy, used at all stages when clinically indicated. Crosses into breast milk in small amounts; compatible with breastfeeding, though watch for infant diarrhea, rash, or oral/diaper thrush from altered gut flora.
c.renal: Predominantly renally eliminated — reduce the dose or extend the interval in renal impairment; no routine hepatic dose adjustment is needed.

c.st: Cap 250, 500 mg · Tab 500, 875 mg · Susp 125, 250 mg/5 mL
c.dose: Cap 250, 500 mg · Tab 500, 875 mg · Susp 125, 250 mg/5 mL
ind: Acute otitis media, community-acquired pneumonia, acute streptococcal pharyngitis, Lyme disease (children/pregnancy), and H. pylori eradication.
c.doc: Acute Otitis Media (high-dose 90 mg/kg/day); First-line Community-Acquired Pneumonia in children
c.ci: Penicillin hypersensitivity, infectious mononucleosis
ae: Diarrhea, non-allergic rash in EBV infection, nausea, urticaria
c.sae: Maculopapular rash with concurrent EBV / Diarrhea
c.info: Hydroxyl group increases acid stability and oral bioavailability (>80%), food does not impair its absorption.
c.caution: May be taken with or without food. Shake the oral suspension well before each dose.
c.preg: Considered one of the safest antibiotic classes in pregnancy, used at all stages when clinically indicated. Crosses into breast milk in small amounts; compatible with breastfeeding, though watch for infant diarrhea, rash, or oral/diaper thrush from altered gut flora.
c.renal: Predominantly renally eliminated — reduce the dose or extend the interval in renal impairment; no routine hepatic dose adjustment is needed.

ind: Oral treatment of respiratory and urinary tract infections.
c.doc: Historical oral prodrug of ampicillin
c.ci: Penicillin hypersensitivity
ae: GI upset, diarrhea, rash
c.sae: Hypersensitivity reaction
c.info: Phthalidyl ester prodrug of ampicillin with superior GI absorption; hydrolyzed during absorption.
c.caution: Oral prodrug hydrolyzed to ampicillin after absorption; may be taken with or without food.
c.preg: Considered one of the safest antibiotic classes in pregnancy, used at all stages when clinically indicated. Crosses into breast milk in small amounts; compatible with breastfeeding, though watch for infant diarrhea, rash, or oral/diaper thrush from altered gut flora.
c.renal: Predominantly renally eliminated — reduce the dose or extend the interval in renal impairment; no routine hepatic dose adjustment is needed.

ind: Respiratory tract and urinary tract infections.
c.doc: Oral prodrug for enhanced ampicillin bioavailability
c.ci: Carnitine deficiency, penicillin allergy
ae: Hypocarnitinemia, nausea, vomiting, epigastric distress
c.sae: Carnitine depletion
c.info: Pivaloyloxymethyl ester prodrug of ampicillin; releases pivalic acid that binds carnitine.
c.caution: Oral prodrug hydrolyzed to ampicillin after absorption; take with food to reduce GI upset.
c.preg: Considered one of the safest antibiotic classes in pregnancy, used at all stages when clinically indicated. Crosses into breast milk in small amounts; compatible with breastfeeding, though watch for infant diarrhea, rash, or oral/diaper thrush from altered gut flora.
c.renal: Predominantly renally eliminated — reduce the dose or extend the interval in renal impairment; no routine hepatic dose adjustment is needed.

ind: Upper and lower respiratory tract infections, UTIs, and skin infections.
c.doc: Oral prodrug of ampicillin with reduced diarrhea
c.ci: Penicillin hypersensitivity
ae: Nausea, epigastric pain, rash, mild diarrhea
c.sae: Hypersensitivity reaction
c.info: Ethoxycarbonyloxyethyl ester prodrug with >95% oral absorption; hydrolyzed rapidly to ampicillin in intestinal wall.
c.caution: Oral prodrug hydrolyzed to ampicillin after absorption; better absorbed than ampicillin and may be taken with or without food.
c.preg: Considered one of the safest antibiotic classes in pregnancy, used at all stages when clinically indicated. Crosses into breast milk in small amounts; compatible with breastfeeding, though watch for infant diarrhea, rash, or oral/diaper thrush from altered gut flora.
c.renal: Predominantly renally eliminated — reduce the dose or extend the interval in renal impairment; no routine hepatic dose adjustment is needed.

c.mn:
💊 Names: 'TALL PIVOT BACK': Talampicillin, Pivampicillin, Bacampicillin (Tal-, Piv-, Bac- + ampicillin).
🦠 Kills: Same as Ampicillin, because the body turns them into Ampicillin.
🎯 Used for: Same as Ampicillin, but taken by mouth with better absorption.
💡 Tip: Prodrug = a disguised Ampicillin.

💊 Names: Amoxicillin + Clavulanic acid (Augmentin), Amoxicillin + Sulbactam, Ampicillin + Sulbactam (Unasyn).
🦠 Kills: Everything Ampicillin kills PLUS bacteria that make beta-lactamase (Staph aureus MSSA, Haemophilus, Moraxella, E. coli, Klebsiella) and anaerobes like Bacteroides.
🎯 Used for: Sinus and ear infections, animal bites, skin and belly infections, chest infections.
💡 Tip: Clavulanic and Sulbactam are bodyguards for the penicillin.

c.sp:
Gram-positive: Streptococcus pneumoniae, Streptococcus pyogenes, Enterococcus faecalis, Listeria monocytogenes, Staphylococcus aureus (MSSA, with beta-lactamase inhibitor)
Gram-negative: Haemophilus influenzae, Escherichia coli, Proteus mirabilis, Salmonella, Shigella, Neisseria meningitidis, Helicobacter pylori (amoxicillin), Moraxella catarrhalis and Klebsiella pneumoniae (with beta-lactamase inhibitor)
Anaerobes: Bacteroides fragilis (with beta-lactamase inhibitor)
c.mn:
💊 Names: Two 'AM' drugs: AMPicillin (injection) and AMOXicillin (by mouth, better absorbed).
🦠 Kills: Haemophilus influenzae, E. coli, Listeria, Proteus, Salmonella, Enterococcus, plus streptococci.
🎯 Used for: Ear, sinus, throat and chest infections, urinary infections, baby meningitis (Listeria).
💡 Tip: Remember the bugs as HELPS: Haemophilus, E. coli, Listeria, Proteus, Salmonella.

ind: Pseudomonas aeruginosa and Proteus UTIs and prostatitis.
c.doc: Historical oral anti-pseudomonal UTI therapy
c.ci: Penicillin allergy, severe renal failure
ae: Hypokalemia, high sodium load, platelet dysfunction/bleeding, unpleasant taste
c.sae: Platelet dysfunction & Bleeding diathesis / Sodium overload
c.info: High sodium content in parenteral form; interferes with platelet ADP-mediated aggregation.
c.caution: High sodium content — use caution in patients on a sodium-restricted diet or with heart failure. May impair platelet function; monitor for bleeding with prolonged use or renal impairment.
c.preg: Considered one of the safest antibiotic classes in pregnancy, used at all stages when clinically indicated. Crosses into breast milk in small amounts; compatible with breastfeeding, though watch for infant diarrhea, rash, or oral/diaper thrush from altered gut flora.
c.renal: Renally eliminated, and high IV doses can impair platelet aggregation — reduce the dose in renal impairment and monitor for bleeding, especially in patients with pre-existing renal disease; no routine hepatic adjustment needed.

ind: Severe systemic Pseudomonas aeruginosa infections and septicemia.
c.doc: Historical parenteral anti-pseudomonal therapy
c.ci: Penicillin allergy, bleeding disorders
ae: Platelet dysfunction (bleeding), hypokalemia, fluid retention/congestive failure from sodium load
c.sae: Platelet dysfunction / Hypokalemia
c.info: Carboxypenicillin with greater in vitro anti-pseudomonal activity than carbenicillin.
c.caution: High sodium load — monitor fluid status and serum potassium. Can impair platelet aggregation; watch for bleeding, particularly in renal impairment.
c.preg: Considered one of the safest antibiotic classes in pregnancy, used at all stages when clinically indicated. Crosses into breast milk in small amounts; compatible with breastfeeding, though watch for infant diarrhea, rash, or oral/diaper thrush from altered gut flora.
c.renal: Renally eliminated, and high IV doses can impair platelet aggregation — reduce the dose in renal impairment and monitor for bleeding, especially in patients with pre-existing renal disease; no routine hepatic adjustment needed.

c.mn:
💊 Names: 'CAR-TIC': Carbenicillin, Ticarcillin. Think Car-Ticks.
🦠 Kills: Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Proteus, Enterobacter (Gram-negatives).
🎯 Used for: Older hospital drugs for Pseudomonas infections; now rarely used.

ind: Severe Pseudomonas aeruginosa infections, nosocomial pneumonia, and intra-abdominal sepsis.
c.doc: Severe pseudomonal infections (used with aminoglycoside)
c.ci: Penicillin hypersensitivity
ae: Diarrhea, hypokalemia, phlebitis, reversible neutropenia with prolonged therapy
c.sae: Reversible leukopenia/neutropenia / Hypersensitivity
c.info: Ureidopenicillin derivative modeled on ampicillin with a 4-ethyl-2,3-dioxo-1-piperazinecarbonyl side chain giving high affinity for PBP3.
c.caution: Reconstitute per label and infuse IV; monitor serum potassium (hypokalemia) and full blood count with prolonged courses (reversible neutropenia).
c.preg: Considered one of the safest antibiotic classes in pregnancy, used at all stages when clinically indicated. Crosses into breast milk in small amounts; compatible with breastfeeding, though watch for infant diarrhea, rash, or oral/diaper thrush from altered gut flora.
c.renal: Renally eliminated, and high IV doses can impair platelet aggregation — reduce the dose in renal impairment and monitor for bleeding, especially in patients with pre-existing renal disease; no routine hepatic adjustment needed.

ind: Pseudomonas aeruginosa infections in cystic fibrosis and nosocomial sepsis.
c.doc: Historical anti-pseudomonal therapy in cystic fibrosis
c.ci: Penicillin allergy
ae: Hypokalemia, bleeding tendency, rash, GI disturbance
c.sae: Bleeding diathesis / Hypokalemia
c.info: Acylampicillin with prominent activity against P. aeruginosa.
c.caution: Reconstitute per the vial label; monitor serum potassium and renal function with prolonged use.
c.preg: Considered one of the safest antibiotic classes in pregnancy, used at all stages when clinically indicated. Crosses into breast milk in small amounts; compatible with breastfeeding, though watch for infant diarrhea, rash, or oral/diaper thrush from altered gut flora.
c.renal: Renally eliminated, and high IV doses can impair platelet aggregation — reduce the dose in renal impairment and monitor for bleeding, especially in patients with pre-existing renal disease; no routine hepatic adjustment needed.

ind: Intra-abdominal, biliary, and urinary tract infections caused by Klebsiella and Pseudomonas.
c.doc: Klebsiella and mixed enteric Gram-negative sepsis
c.ci: Penicillin hypersensitivity
ae: Diarrhea, nausea, phlebitis, hypokalemia, transaminitis
c.sae: Hypersensitivity reaction
c.info: High biliary excretion; active against Klebsiella pneumoniae in addition to Pseudomonas.
c.caution: Reconstitute per the vial label; monitor serum sodium/potassium and coagulation status with prolonged high-dose therapy.
c.preg: Considered one of the safest antibiotic classes in pregnancy, used at all stages when clinically indicated. Crosses into breast milk in small amounts; compatible with breastfeeding, though watch for infant diarrhea, rash, or oral/diaper thrush from altered gut flora.
c.renal: Renally eliminated, and high IV doses can impair platelet aggregation — reduce the dose in renal impairment and monitor for bleeding, especially in patients with pre-existing renal disease; no routine hepatic adjustment needed.

c.mn:
💊 Names: 'PAM': Piperacillin, Azlocillin, Mezlocillin.
🦠 Kills: Pseudomonas aeruginosa (stronger than Carbenicillin), Klebsiella, other Gram-negatives, some anaerobes.
🎯 Used for: Serious hospital infections. Only Piperacillin is still common.

💊 Names: Piperacillin + Tazobactam (Zosyn, Tazocin) and Ticarcillin + Clavulanic acid (Timentin). Pip goes with Tazo. Ticar goes with Clav.
🦠 Kills: Very broad: Pseudomonas, most Gram-negatives, Gram-positives and anaerobes.
🎯 Used for: Hospital pneumonia, belly infections, sepsis, fever in low-white-cell patients.
💡 Tip: Pip-Taz = the go-to broad hospital antibiotic.

c.sp:
Gram-positive: Streptococcus pyogenes, Enterococcus faecalis (piperacillin, mezlocillin), Staphylococcus aureus (MSSA, with beta-lactamase inhibitor)
Gram-negative: Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Escherichia coli, Proteus mirabilis, indole-positive Proteus, Enterobacter, Klebsiella pneumoniae, Serratia marcescens, Haemophilus influenzae
Anaerobes: Bacteroides fragilis (with beta-lactamase inhibitor)
c.mn:
💊 Names: 'CAR-TIC' (Carbenicillin, Ticarcillin) and 'PAM' (Piperacillin, Azlocillin, Mezlocillin), each with or without a beta-lactamase inhibitor.
🦠 Kills: Pseudomonas aeruginosa plus other Gram-negatives; the inhibitor combinations add Staph aureus (MSSA) and anaerobes.
🎯 Used for: Hospital infections such as pneumonia, sepsis, belly infections and fever in low-white-cell patients.
💡 Tip: Anti-Pseudo = 'Pseudo-killers'. Only Piperacillin-Tazobactam is in common use today.

c.sp:
Gram-positive: Staphylococcus aureus (MSSA, penicillinase-producing), Streptococcus pneumoniae, Streptococcus pyogenes, Enterococcus faecalis
Gram-negative: Escherichia coli, Proteus mirabilis, Haemophilus influenzae
c.mn:
💊 Names: Ampiclox = Ampicillin + Cloxacillin. Amoxiclox = Amoxicillin + Cloxacillin.
🦠 Kills: Staph aureus (from the Clox part) plus streptococci and many Gram-negatives (from the Amp/Amox part).
🎯 Used for: Mixed skin and wound infections, respiratory infections.
💡 Tip: Two drugs in one pill: broad + Staph.

ov.moa: Beta-lactam antibiotics that inhibit bacterial cell wall synthesis by binding penicillin-binding proteins, leading to bacterial lysis; bactericidal.
ov.ind: Used for a range of gram-positive infections (streptococcal and some staphylococcal), and, when combined with beta-lactamase inhibitors or as extended-spectrum agents, for gram-negative and mixed infections including respiratory, skin, dental, and urinary infections. Natural penicillins cover Streptococcus pyogenes, Neisseria, Treponema pallidum, and Clostridium; aminopenicillins (ampicillin, amoxicillin) extend to H. influenzae, E. coli, Listeria monocytogenes, and Enterococcus; antistaphylococcal penicillins (nafcillin, oxacillin, dicloxacillin) target methicillin-susceptible S. aureus; and extended-spectrum agents combined with beta-lactamase inhibitors add Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Klebsiella, and anaerobes such as Bacteroides.
ov.ae: GI upset (nausea, diarrhea), rash, and hypersensitivity reactions ranging from mild rash to anaphylaxis; can cause C. difficile colitis.
ov.ci: Contraindicated in patients with a history of anaphylactic penicillin allergy; use caution in renal impairment (dose adjustment needed) and in patients with infectious mononucleosis due to increased rash risk with aminopenicillins.
ov.counsel: Take as prescribed, often on an empty stomach for better absorption unless told otherwise, complete the full course, and seek immediate medical attention for signs of an allergic reaction.

ind: Toxoplasmosis (in combination with pyrimethamine), secondary prophylaxis of rheumatic fever, and nocardiosis.
c.doc: Acute toxoplasmic encephalitis in HIV/immunocompromised patients (with Pyrimethamine and Leucovorin)
c.ci: Sulfonamide hypersensitivity, severe renal or hepatic failure, porphyria, pregnancy at term, infants under 2 months
c.sci: Term pregnancy and neonates under 2 months (kernicterus risk)
ae: Crystalluria, rash, nausea, vomiting, leukopenia, drug fever
c.sae: Crystalluria and nephrolithiasis / Stevens-Johnson syndrome
c.info: Competitive inhibitor of bacterial dihydropteroate synthase; relatively low urinary solubility necessitates high fluid intake and urinary alkalinization to prevent renal tubular crystallization.
c.caution: Ensure adequate fluid intake during treatment to reduce the risk of crystalluria; urine alkalinization may be advised for high-dose therapy.
c.preg: Avoid near term (last few weeks of pregnancy) — sulfonamides displace bilirubin from albumin, risking kernicterus in the neonate; also generally avoided in the first trimester given a possible small increase in birth-defect risk with folate-antagonist exposure. Avoid during breastfeeding of newborns, premature infants, or G6PD-deficient infants (kernicterus/hemolysis risk); can be used with more caution in older, healthy infants.
c.renal: Renally eliminated with a risk of crystalluria — ensure adequate hydration and reduce the dose in renal impairment; use with caution in hepatic impairment (rare hepatotoxicity).

ind: Uncomplicated urinary tract infections and pediatric acute otitis media (combined with erythromycin).
c.doc: Acute otitis media in penicillin-allergic pediatric patients (as erythromycin-sulfisoxazole combination)
c.ci: Sulfonamide hypersensitivity, porphyria, pregnancy at term, infants under 2 months
c.sci: Neonates under 2 months (bilirubin displacement from albumin leading to kernicterus)
ae: GI upset, headache, pruritus, mild crystalluria, urticaria
c.sae: Neonatal kernicterus / Stevens-Johnson syndrome
c.info: Rapidly absorbed short-acting sulfonamide with high solubility at physiological urinary pH, significantly minimizing the risk of renal crystalluria compared to older sulfonamides.
c.caution: Maintain good hydration to reduce crystalluria risk; shake any liquid formulation before dosing.
c.preg: Avoid near term (last few weeks of pregnancy) — sulfonamides displace bilirubin from albumin, risking kernicterus in the neonate; also generally avoided in the first trimester given a possible small increase in birth-defect risk with folate-antagonist exposure. Avoid during breastfeeding of newborns, premature infants, or G6PD-deficient infants (kernicterus/hemolysis risk); can be used with more caution in older, healthy infants.
c.renal: Renally eliminated with a risk of crystalluria — ensure adequate hydration and reduce the dose in renal impairment; use with caution in hepatic impairment (rare hepatotoxicity).

c.sp:
Gram-positive: Streptococcus pyogenes, Streptococcus pneumoniae, Staphylococcus aureus (variable), Nocardia asteroides
Gram-negative: Escherichia coli, Klebsiella pneumoniae, Proteus mirabilis, Haemophilus influenzae, Haemophilus ducreyi, Shigella, Vibrio cholerae
Atypicals: Chlamydia trachomatis
c.mn:
💊 Names: Two drugs: SulfaDIazine and SulfIsoxazole (say 'DI' and 'ISO').
🦠 Kills: Urinary bacteria (E. coli) and Toxoplasma (Sulfadiazine, with pyrimethamine). Also Nocardia.
🎯 Used for: Urinary tract infections, toxoplasmosis, rheumatic fever prevention.
💡 Tip: Short-acting = taken several times a day.

ind: Urinary tract infections and systemic bacterial infections; almost exclusively utilized in combination with trimethoprim.
c.doc: Co-administered with trimethoprim as Co-trimoxazole for Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia and uncomplicated UTIs
c.ci: Sulfonamide allergy, G6PD deficiency, severe renal impairment (CrCl <15 mL/min), pregnancy at term
c.sci: G6PD deficiency (precipitates severe acute hemolytic anemia)
ae: Nausea, vomiting, morbilliform rash, photosensitivity, anorexia, crystalluria
c.sae: Acute hemolytic anemia in G6PD deficiency / Stevens-Johnson syndrome
c.info: Intermediate-acting sulfonamide that competitively inhibits dihydropteroate synthase; its elimination kinetics closely match trimethoprim to maintain synergistic synergy.
c.caution: Usually dispensed only in combination (with trimethoprim, as co-trimoxazole) — confirm the formulation before dispensing as a single agent. Encourage adequate fluid intake.
c.preg: Avoid near term (last few weeks of pregnancy) — sulfonamides displace bilirubin from albumin, risking kernicterus in the neonate; also generally avoided in the first trimester given a possible small increase in birth-defect risk with folate-antagonist exposure. Avoid during breastfeeding of newborns, premature infants, or G6PD-deficient infants (kernicterus/hemolysis risk); can be used with more caution in older, healthy infants.
c.renal: Renally eliminated with a risk of crystalluria — ensure adequate hydration and reduce the dose in renal impairment; use with caution in hepatic impairment (rare hepatotoxicity).

c.sp:
Gram-positive: Streptococcus pyogenes, Streptococcus pneumoniae, Staphylococcus aureus (variable), Nocardia asteroides
Gram-negative: Escherichia coli, Klebsiella pneumoniae, Proteus mirabilis, Haemophilus influenzae, Haemophilus ducreyi, Shigella, Vibrio cholerae
Atypicals: Chlamydia trachomatis
c.mn:
💊 Names: One drug: Sulfamethoxazole (the 'SMX' in Co-trimoxazole).
🦠 Kills: E. coli, Klebsiella and other urinary bacteria; Nocardia. With Trimethoprim it also kills Pneumocystis.
🎯 Used for: Urinary infections; mostly used inside Co-trimoxazole.
💡 Tip: M for sulfaMethoxazole = Middle-acting.

ind: Historical long-acting sulfonamide for urinary tract and respiratory infections; largely withdrawn due to unacceptable cutaneous toxicity.
c.doc: Historical use only (obsolete / withdrawn)
c.ci: Sulfonamide hypersensitivity, severe renal failure, hepatic dysfunction, term pregnancy
c.sci: High incidence of fatal Stevens-Johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis
ae: Severe erythema multiforme, crystalluria, hematuria, leukopenia
c.sae: Life-threatening Stevens-Johnson syndrome / TEN
c.info: Long-acting sulfonamide with an elimination half-life exceeding 36 hours; high rates of immune-complex mediated cutaneous toxicities led to its clinical abandonment.
c.caution: Long half-life — confirm the intended once-daily/less-frequent dosing schedule before dispensing to avoid inadvertent overdosing.
c.preg: Avoid near term (last few weeks of pregnancy) — sulfonamides displace bilirubin from albumin, risking kernicterus in the neonate; also generally avoided in the first trimester given a possible small increase in birth-defect risk with folate-antagonist exposure. Avoid during breastfeeding of newborns, premature infants, or G6PD-deficient infants (kernicterus/hemolysis risk); can be used with more caution in older, healthy infants.
c.renal: Renally eliminated with a risk of crystalluria — ensure adequate hydration and reduce the dose in renal impairment; use with caution in hepatic impairment (rare hepatotoxicity).

c.dose: Tab 500 mg (fixed combination with pyrimethamine 25 mg)
ind: Intermittent preventive treatment of malaria in pregnancy (IPTp) and treatment of uncomplicated Plasmodium falciparum malaria.
c.doc: Intermittent Preventive Treatment in Pregnancy (IPTp-SP) for malaria in endemic zones
c.ci: Severe sulfonamide hypersensitivity, megaloblastic anemia, severe hepatic impairment, pregnancy near term
c.sci: Severe cutaneous adverse reactions (Stevens-Johnson syndrome / Toxic Epidermal Necrolysis)
ae: Severe rash, erythema multiforme, nausea, vomiting, agranulocytosis
c.sae: Toxic epidermal necrolysis (TEN) / Stevens-Johnson syndrome
c.info: Features an ultra-long elimination half-life (~7 to 9 days) due to extensive plasma protein binding (>90%) and slow tubular clearance; acts as a plasmodial dihydropteroate synthase inhibitor.
c.caution: Fixed-ratio combination with pyrimethamine — confirm the labeled ratio before dosing; usually given as a single supervised dose.
c.preg: Avoid near term (last few weeks of pregnancy) — sulfonamides displace bilirubin from albumin, risking kernicterus in the neonate; also generally avoided in the first trimester given a possible small increase in birth-defect risk with folate-antagonist exposure. Avoid during breastfeeding of newborns, premature infants, or G6PD-deficient infants (kernicterus/hemolysis risk); can be used with more caution in older, healthy infants.
c.renal: Renally eliminated with a risk of crystalluria — ensure adequate hydration and reduce the dose in renal impairment; use with caution in hepatic impairment (rare hepatotoxicity).

c.sp:
Gram-positive: Streptococcus pyogenes, Streptococcus pneumoniae, Staphylococcus aureus (variable), Nocardia asteroides
Gram-negative: Escherichia coli, Klebsiella pneumoniae, Proteus mirabilis, Haemophilus influenzae, Haemophilus ducreyi, Shigella, Vibrio cholerae
Atypicals: Chlamydia trachomatis
c.mn:
💊 Names: Two drugs: Sulfadoxine and Sulfamethoxypyridazine ('DOX' and 'PYRIDAZINE').
🦠 Kills: Weak against bacteria. Sulfadoxine + pyrimethamine kills malaria parasites (Plasmodium falciparum).
🎯 Used for: Malaria (Sulfadoxine, brand Fansidar). One dose lasts days.
💡 Tip: Long-acting = weekly-type dosing.

c.dose: Ophth Soln 10%, 15% · Ophth Oint 10% · Topical lotion/wash 10%
ind: Topical management of superficial bacterial conjunctivitis, corneal ulcers, acne vulgaris, and seborrheic dermatitis.
c.doc: Superficial bacterial conjunctivitis and adjunctive topical management of acne rosacea
c.ci: Known sulfonamide hypersensitivity, viral or fungal ocular infections
c.sci: Severe sulfonamide allergy (risk of ocular and systemic hypersensitivity)
ae: Transient ocular stinging, localized burning, conjunctival hyperemia, periorbital dermatitis
c.sae: Severe ocular hypersensitivity / Conjunctival Stevens-Johnson syndrome
c.info: Highly water-soluble sodium salt that yields neutral pH (7.4) formulations, providing effective local antimicrobial activity without causing caustic ocular irritation.
c.caution: For ophthalmic use, avoid touching the dropper/tube tip to the eye to prevent contamination; discard per the in-use period stated on the label.
c.preg: Minimal systemic absorption with standard ophthalmic/topical use — generally considered compatible with pregnancy and breastfeeding at recommended doses, unlike systemic sulfonamides.
c.renal: Minimal systemic absorption with standard ophthalmic/topical use — no renal or hepatic dose adjustment is generally needed.

ind: Adjunctive topical therapy for controlling burn wound sepsis in deep full-thickness burns and suppurative chondritis of the ear.
c.doc: Deep eschar-penetrating burn infections and suppurative chondritis (auricular burns)
c.ci: Known mafenide hypersensitivity, acute renal failure, pre-existing metabolic acidosis
c.sci: Systemic carbonic anhydrase inhibition causing severe metabolic acidosis
ae: Intense burning pain upon application, hyperventilation, metabolic acidosis, rash
c.sae: Systemic metabolic acidosis with compensatory hyperventilation
c.info: Diffuses through non-vascularized thick burn eschars and avascular cartilage far more efficiently than silver sulfadiazine; systemic absorption of its metabolite causes potent carbonic anhydrase inhibition.
c.caution: Apply to clean, debrided burn wounds; can cause a stinging/burning sensation on application — warn patients in advance.
c.preg: Avoid near term (last few weeks of pregnancy) — sulfonamides displace bilirubin from albumin, risking kernicterus in the neonate; also generally avoided in the first trimester given a possible small increase in birth-defect risk with folate-antagonist exposure. Avoid during breastfeeding of newborns, premature infants, or G6PD-deficient infants (kernicterus/hemolysis risk); can be used with more caution in older, healthy infants.
c.renal: A carbonic anhydrase inhibitor that can cause metabolic acidosis, especially with extensive burn-surface application or in renal impairment — monitor acid-base status closely; use with caution in patients with pre-existing renal or respiratory compromise (reduced compensation for the acidosis).

ind: Topical antimicrobial prophylaxis and management of wound sepsis in second- and third-degree thermal burns.
c.doc: Topical antimicrobial burn wound prophylaxis for partial and full-thickness burns
c.ci: Sulfonamide hypersensitivity, pregnancy at term, premature infants / neonates under 2 months
c.sci: Use in neonates and near-term pregnancy (kernicterus risk via systemic silver sulfadiazine absorption)
ae: Transient leukopenia, localized skin burning/irritation, skin discoloration (argyria), rash
c.sae: Transient reversible leukopenia / Local argyria
c.info: Slowly releases silver ions that disrupt microbial DNA and cell walls, alongside sulfadiazine which inhibits bacterial folic acid synthesis; does not cause systemic metabolic acidosis.
c.caution: Apply with a sterile gloved hand to a clean wound; reapply if cream is wiped off. Avoid in term neonates and pregnant women near term (kernicterus risk from the sulfa component).
c.preg: Avoid in the third trimester and in infants under 2 months — systemic absorption from burn wounds can be clinically significant and carries the same kernicterus risk as oral sulfonamides. Avoid applying to the breast/nipple area during breastfeeding.
c.renal: Systemic absorption from large burn surfaces can reach levels seen with oral sulfonamides — monitor renal function and serum sulfonamide levels with extensive burn use; use with caution in hepatic impairment.

c.sp:
Gram-positive: Staphylococcus aureus, Streptococcus pyogenes, Streptococcus pneumoniae
Gram-negative: Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Escherichia coli, Klebsiella pneumoniae, Enterobacter, Proteus, Haemophilus influenzae
Anaerobes: Clostridium species (mafenide)
Atypicals: Chlamydia trachomatis (sulfacetamide, trachoma)
c.mn:
💊 Names: Burns pair: Silver sulfadiazine, Mafenide. Eye drop: Sulfacetamide.
🦠 Kills: Burn-wound bacteria (Pseudomonas, Staph aureus, E. coli) and eye bacteria that cause conjunctivitis.
🎯 Used for: Burn creams (Silver sulfadiazine, Mafenide) and eye infection drops (Sulfacetamide).
💡 Tip: SulfaCETamide = 'see-tamide' = eyes.

ind: Induction and maintenance of remission in mild-to-moderate ulcerative colitis, Crohn disease, and DMARD therapy for rheumatoid arthritis.
c.doc: First-line conventional 5-ASA therapy for mild-to-moderate Ulcerative Colitis maintenance
c.ci: Sulfonamide or salicylate hypersensitivity, intestinal or urinary tract obstruction, porphyria
c.sci: Severe hypersensitivity to sulfonamide or salicylate moieties
ae: Nausea, dyspepsia, headache, reversible oligospermia, orange-yellow urine/skin discoloration
c.sae: Reversible male oligospermia / Agranulocytosis / Hemolytic anemia
c.info: Azo-linked conjugate of sulfapyridine and 5-aminosalicylic acid (5-ASA); cleaved by colonic bacterial azoreductases to deliver anti-inflammatory 5-ASA locally while the absorbed sulfapyridine drives adverse effects.
c.caution: Enteric-coated tablets should be swallowed whole, not crushed or chewed. May cause harmless orange-yellow discoloration of urine, skin, or contact lenses.
c.preg: Considered relatively safe throughout pregnancy and breastfeeding at standard doses, since only a minority is absorbed systemically as sulfapyridine — widely used in pregnant patients with inflammatory bowel disease or rheumatoid arthritis; ensure adequate folate supplementation given its antifolate activity.
c.renal: Mostly acts locally in the gut with limited systemic absorption — dose adjustment for renal impairment is not usually required at standard doses, though the sulfapyridine metabolite is renally cleared and can accumulate in significant impairment; use with caution in hepatic impairment (rare hepatotoxicity).

c.sp: Not used for its antibacterial spectrum. Split in the colon by gut bacteria into sulfapyridine and 5-aminosalicylic acid; used mainly as an anti-inflammatory.
c.mn:
💊 Names: One drug: SulfaSALazine = Sulfa + SALicylate.
🦠 Kills: Not used as an antibiotic. It stays in the gut and calms inflammation.
🎯 Used for: Ulcerative colitis, Crohn's colitis, rheumatoid arthritis.

c.sp:
Gram-positive: Staphylococcus aureus (including some MRSA), Streptococcus pyogenes, Streptococcus pneumoniae, Listeria monocytogenes, Nocardia asteroides
Gram-negative: Escherichia coli, Klebsiella pneumoniae, Proteus mirabilis, Enterobacter, Serratia marcescens, Salmonella (including Salmonella typhi), Shigella, Vibrio cholerae, Yersinia enterocolitica, Haemophilus influenzae, Moraxella catarrhalis, Stenotrophomonas maltophilia
Atypicals: Chlamydia trachomatis, Mycoplasma pneumoniae, Legionella pneumophila (erythromycin component)
c.mn:
💊 Names: Co-trimoxazole = Trimethoprim + Sulfamethoxazole. Triple sulfonamides = three sulfa drugs together. Erythromycin + Sulfisoxazole = child ear-infection mix.
🦠 Kills: Co-trimoxazole: E. coli, Shigella, Pneumocystis jirovecii, Nocardia, Stenotrophomonas. Erythromycin + Sulfisoxazole: Haemophilus influenzae.
🎯 Used for: Urinary infections, Pneumocystis pneumonia (often in HIV), traveller's diarrhea, child ear infections.
💡 Tip: Co-trimoxazole = two hits on one pathway (folate).

ov.moa: Inhibit bacterial folate synthesis by competitively blocking dihydropteroate synthase, preventing production of folic acid needed for nucleic acid synthesis; often paired with trimethoprim for a synergistic, bactericidal effect.
ov.ind: Used for urinary tract infections, some respiratory and gastrointestinal infections, Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia treatment/prophylaxis (with trimethoprim), and certain protozoal or other opportunistic infections. Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole covers E. coli, Proteus, Klebsiella, and other urinary gram-negatives, Pneumocystis jirovecii, Stenotrophomonas maltophilia, Nocardia, and some MRSA and Listeria strains; also used with pyrimethamine for Toxoplasma gondii.
ov.ae: GI upset, photosensitivity, rash including risk of severe reactions such as Stevens-Johnson syndrome, hyperkalemia, and hematologic effects such as hemolysis in G6PD deficiency.
ov.ci: Avoid in sulfa allergy, G6PD deficiency, pregnancy near term and in breastfeeding of newborns due to kernicterus risk, and severe renal or hepatic impairment.
ov.counsel: Take with plenty of water to reduce the risk of crystalluria, avoid excessive sun exposure, and report any rash, fever, sore throat, or unusual bruising or bleeding right away.

ind: Superficial ocular and localized skin infections caused by susceptible organisms.
c.doc: Historical prototype tetracycline; now restricted to topical ophthalmic/dermatological use
c.ci: Known tetracycline hypersensitivity, application to deep puncture wounds
c.sci: Children under 8 years and pregnancy (if systemic absorption occurs)
ae: Local skin stinging, erythema, contact dermatitis, yellow skin staining
c.sae: Severe allergic contact dermatitis
c.info: First discovered tetracycline (isolated from Streptomyces aureofaciens); binds reversibly to the 30S ribosomal subunit. Oral forms are obsolete due to poor bioavailability and GI intolerance.
c.caution: Mainly used topically/ophthalmically now — confirm the route before dispensing an oral formulation. Avoid administering with milk, antacids, or mineral supplements, which impair absorption.
c.preg: Contraindicated throughout pregnancy — deposits in developing fetal bone and teeth, causing permanent tooth discoloration and enamel hypoplasia, and can cause maternal hepatotoxicity (especially with high-dose IV use). Contraindicated during breastfeeding for the same reasons, despite the calcium in milk limiting infant absorption somewhat.
c.renal: Can accumulate in renal impairment and worsen azotemia — avoid or use with caution and reduced dosing; no significant hepatic dose adjustment needed at usual oral doses, though high-dose IV use should be avoided in hepatic impairment.

c.dose: Cap 250 mg · Inj 50, 125 mg/mL · Ophth/Topical Ointment
ind: Superficial ocular/skin infections, chlamydial infections, and historically for rickettsial diseases.
c.doc: Ophthalmic prophylaxis/infections and veterinary medicine
c.ci: Pregnancy, nursing mothers, children <8 years, severe renal failure
c.sci: Pregnancy and children <8 years (permanent teeth discoloration & bone growth restriction)
ae: GI distress, nausea, photosensitivity, epigastric burning
c.sae: Permanent dental discoloration / Enamel hypoplasia in children
c.info: Natural fermentation product of Streptomyces rimosus; hydrophilic short-acting tetracycline requiring QID dosing. Readily forms insoluble chelates with polyvalent cations (Ca2+, Mg2+, Fe2+, Al3+).
c.caution: Take on an empty stomach with a full glass of water, and avoid dairy products, antacids, or iron/calcium/magnesium supplements within 2 hours of dosing.
c.preg: Contraindicated throughout pregnancy — deposits in developing fetal bone and teeth, causing permanent tooth discoloration and enamel hypoplasia, and can cause maternal hepatotoxicity (especially with high-dose IV use). Contraindicated during breastfeeding for the same reasons, despite the calcium in milk limiting infant absorption somewhat.
c.renal: Can accumulate in renal impairment and worsen azotemia — avoid or use with caution and reduced dosing; no significant hepatic dose adjustment needed at usual oral doses, though high-dose IV use should be avoided in hepatic impairment.

ind: Helicobacter pylori quadruple eradication therapy, moderate-to-severe acne vulgaris, and chlamydial urethritis.
c.doc: Second-line component of Bismuth Quadruple Therapy for H. pylori eradication
c.ci: Pregnancy, breastfeeding, children <8 years, renal impairment (CrCl <50 mL/min)
c.sci: Use of expired capsules (causes Fanconi-type renal tubular acidosis)
ae: Nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, epigastric distress, photosensitivity, esophageal ulceration
c.sae: Fanconi syndrome (from toxic degradation products of expired drug) / Hepatotoxicity in pregnancy
c.info: Prototype 30S ribosomal inhibitor blocking aminoacyl-tRNA attachment. Must be taken on an empty stomach with a full glass of water while remaining upright to prevent pill-induced esophagitis.
c.caution: Take on an empty stomach with plenty of water; avoid lying down for 30 minutes after dosing to reduce oesophageal irritation. Separate from dairy, antacids, and mineral supplements by at least 2 hours.
c.preg: Contraindicated throughout pregnancy — deposits in developing fetal bone and teeth, causing permanent tooth discoloration and enamel hypoplasia, and can cause maternal hepatotoxicity (especially with high-dose IV use). Contraindicated during breastfeeding for the same reasons, despite the calcium in milk limiting infant absorption somewhat.
c.renal: Can accumulate in renal impairment and worsen azotemia — avoid or use with caution and reduced dosing; no significant hepatic dose adjustment needed at usual oral doses, though high-dose IV use should be avoided in hepatic impairment.

ind: Historical parenteral management of severe systemic infections when oral tetracycline administration was impossible.
c.doc: Historical parenteral tetracycline (largely superseded by IV doxycycline and tigecycline)
c.ci: Tetracycline hypersensitivity, severe renal failure, pregnancy
c.sci: Rapid IV infusion (causes severe thrombophlebitis and hypotension)
ae: Pain at injection site, thrombophlebitis, flushing, dizziness
c.sae: Severe acute renal failure / Hepatotoxicity with high IV doses
c.info: Mannich base prodrug synthesized by condensing tetracycline, formaldehyde, and pyrrolidine to enhance water solubility for intramuscular and intravenous injection.
c.caution: Parenteral prodrug of tetracycline — reconstitute per the vial label and give by slow IV injection.
c.preg: Contraindicated throughout pregnancy — deposits in developing fetal bone and teeth, causing permanent tooth discoloration and enamel hypoplasia, and can cause maternal hepatotoxicity (especially with high-dose IV use). Contraindicated during breastfeeding for the same reasons, despite the calcium in milk limiting infant absorption somewhat.
c.renal: Can accumulate in renal impairment and worsen azotemia — avoid or use with caution and reduced dosing; no significant hepatic dose adjustment needed at usual oral doses, though high-dose IV use should be avoided in hepatic impairment.

c.sp:
Gram-positive: Streptococcus pneumoniae, Staphylococcus aureus (resistance common), Bacillus anthracis, Cutibacterium acnes
Gram-negative: Haemophilus influenzae, Vibrio cholerae, Brucella, Francisella tularensis, Yersinia pestis, Helicobacter pylori (in combination), Neisseria gonorrhoeae (resistance common)
Atypicals: Chlamydia trachomatis, Chlamydophila pneumoniae, Mycoplasma pneumoniae, Rickettsia, Coxiella burnetii, Ureaplasma urealyticum
Spirochetes: Treponema pallidum, Borrelia burgdorferi, Leptospira
c.mn:
💊 Names: 'Cute Owls Take Rest' = Chlortetracycline, Oxytetracycline, Tetracycline, Rolitetracycline.
🦠 Kills: Rickettsia (typhus, spotted fever), Chlamydia, Mycoplasma, Vibrio cholerae, Borrelia (Lyme), Brucella, H. pylori, acne bacteria.
🎯 Used for: Chest infections, cholera, acne, Chlamydia eye and genital infections, rickettsial diseases.
💡 Tip: TETRA = 4: taken 4 times a day.

ind: Syndrome of Inappropriate Antidiuretic Hormone (SIADH) secretion and resistant bacterial infections.
c.doc: Historical second-line non-aquaretic agent for chronic euvolemic hyponatremia due to SIADH
c.ci: Pregnancy, children <8 years, pre-existing renal impairment
c.sci: Severe phototoxic cutaneous reactions / Drug-induced nephrogenic diabetes insipidus
ae: Exaggerated sunburn photosensitivity, polyuria, polydipsia, azotemia
c.sae: Nephrogenic diabetes insipidus / Severe phototoxicity with onycholysis
c.info: Unique tetracycline that blocks cyclic AMP generation in renal medullary collecting tubule cells, antagonizing ADH (vasopressin) action on V2 receptors.
c.caution: Take on an empty stomach with a full glass of water; strongly photosensitizing — advise sun/UV protection during treatment.
c.preg: Contraindicated throughout pregnancy — deposits in developing fetal bone and teeth, causing permanent tooth discoloration and enamel hypoplasia, and can cause maternal hepatotoxicity (especially with high-dose IV use). Contraindicated during breastfeeding for the same reasons, despite the calcium in milk limiting infant absorption somewhat.
c.renal: Can accumulate in renal impairment and worsen azotemia — avoid or use with caution. Also used deliberately (off-label) to induce nephrogenic diabetes insipidus in SIADH — be alert for excess free-water loss and hypernatremia if used for that purpose in a patient with normal renal function.

c.dose: Cap 300, 408 mg (equivalent to 300 mg tetracycline base)
ind: Moderate-to-severe inflammatory acne vulgaris and acne rosacea.
c.doc: First-line systemic tetracycline for inflammatory acne vulgaris in dermatological practice
c.ci: Pregnancy, breastfeeding, children under 8 years, concurrent systemic retinoids
c.sci: Concurrent use with oral Isotretinoin (high risk of Pseudotumor Cerebri)
ae: Epigastric discomfort, nausea, headache, diarrhea
c.sae: Pseudotumor cerebri (benign intracranial hypertension)
c.info: Water-soluble prodrug formed by linking tetracycline with the amino acid L-lysine; absorbed by active transport mechanisms and less dependent on stomach acid, minimizing food interactions.
c.caution: Capsules should be swallowed whole with plenty of water while sitting or standing, to reduce oesophageal irritation.
c.preg: Contraindicated throughout pregnancy — deposits in developing fetal bone and teeth, causing permanent tooth discoloration and enamel hypoplasia, and can cause maternal hepatotoxicity (especially with high-dose IV use). Contraindicated during breastfeeding for the same reasons, despite the calcium in milk limiting infant absorption somewhat.
c.renal: Can accumulate in renal impairment and worsen azotemia — avoid or use with caution and reduced dosing; no significant hepatic dose adjustment needed at usual oral doses, though high-dose IV use should be avoided in hepatic impairment.

ind: Respiratory tract infections, urinary tract infections, and acne vulgaris.
c.doc: Historical intermediate-acting tetracycline (largely obsolete)
c.ci: Pregnancy, lactation, children under 8 years, severe renal failure
c.sci: Pregnancy and early childhood (permanent tooth staining)
ae: GI irritation, nausea, photosensitivity, rash
c.sae: Hepatotoxicity / Benign intracranial hypertension
c.info: Semi-synthetic tetracycline obtained by chemical modification of oxytetracycline; intermediate lipophilicity providing pharmacokinetic properties between tetracycline and doxycycline.
c.caution: Take with a full glass of water; separate from dairy, antacids, and mineral supplements by at least 2 hours.
c.preg: Contraindicated throughout pregnancy — deposits in developing fetal bone and teeth, causing permanent tooth discoloration and enamel hypoplasia, and can cause maternal hepatotoxicity (especially with high-dose IV use). Contraindicated during breastfeeding for the same reasons, despite the calcium in milk limiting infant absorption somewhat.
c.renal: Can accumulate in renal impairment and worsen azotemia — avoid or use with caution and reduced dosing; no significant hepatic dose adjustment needed at usual oral doses, though high-dose IV use should be avoided in hepatic impairment.

c.sp:
Gram-positive: Streptococcus pneumoniae, Staphylococcus aureus (resistance common), Bacillus anthracis, Cutibacterium acnes
Gram-negative: Haemophilus influenzae, Vibrio cholerae, Brucella, Francisella tularensis, Yersinia pestis, Helicobacter pylori (in combination), Neisseria gonorrhoeae (resistance common)
Atypicals: Chlamydia trachomatis, Chlamydophila pneumoniae, Mycoplasma pneumoniae, Rickettsia, Coxiella burnetii, Ureaplasma urealyticum
Spirochetes: Treponema pallidum, Borrelia burgdorferi, Leptospira
c.mn:
💊 Names: 'Dogs Munch Lemons' = Demeclocycline, Methacycline, Lymecycline.
🦠 Kills: Same bugs as Tetracycline: Rickettsia, Chlamydia, Mycoplasma, acne bacteria.
🎯 Used for: Acne (Lymecycline), chest infections; Demeclocycline is also used for SIADH (low blood sodium).
💡 Tip: Taken twice a day.

c.dose: Cap/Tab 100 mg · Inj 100 mg (100 mg BID on Day 1, then 100 mg OD-BID)
ind: Scrub typhus, rickettsial diseases, cholera, chlamydial urethritis/cervicitis, Lyme disease, community-acquired atypical pneumonia, malaria prophylaxis, and inflammatory acne.
c.doc: Scrub Typhus, Cholera (single 300 mg dose), Early Lyme Disease, Rickettsial Spotted Fevers, and Chlamydia trachomatis (7-day regimen)
c.ci: Hypersensitivity to tetracyclines, third trimester of pregnancy (unless life-threatening rickettsia), concurrent oral retinoids
c.sci: Co-administration with Isotretinoin (precipitates idiopathic intracranial hypertension / pseudotumor cerebri)
ae: Pill-induced esophageal ulceration, epigastric burning, nausea, cutaneous photosensitivity
c.sae: Pill-induced severe esophagitis / Pseudotumor cerebri / Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction in spirochetal treatment
c.info: Highly lipophilic; virtually completely absorbed from the upper GI tract. Excreted mainly via feces as inactive chelates without renal elimination; requires NO dose adjustment in renal impairment.
c.caution: Take with a full glass of water and remain upright for at least 30 minutes afterward to prevent oesophageal irritation/ulceration; may be taken with food (unlike older tetracyclines) to reduce GI upset.
c.preg: Contraindicated throughout pregnancy — deposits in developing fetal bone and teeth, causing permanent tooth discoloration and enamel hypoplasia, and can cause maternal hepatotoxicity (especially with high-dose IV use). Contraindicated during breastfeeding for the same reasons, despite the calcium in milk limiting infant absorption somewhat.
c.renal: Unlike older tetracyclines, eliminated mainly via non-renal (fecal/biliary) routes and does not significantly accumulate in renal impairment — no dose adjustment is usually needed, making it the preferred tetracycline if one must be used with reduced renal function.

c.dose: Cap/Tab 50, 100 mg (100 mg BID or 50 mg TID)
ind: Recalcitrant acne vulgaris, hidradenitis suppurativa, MRSA skin/soft tissue infections, and meningococcal carrier eradication.
c.doc: Moderate-to-severe papulopustular acne vulgaris and multidrug-resistant Acinetobacter/Stenotrophomonas salvage
c.ci: Tetracycline hypersensitivity, pregnancy, nursing mothers, children <8 years, severe hepatic dysfunction
c.sci: Development of drug-induced systemic lupus erythematosus (DILE) or autoimmune hepatitis
ae: Vestibular toxicity (vertigo, ataxia, dizziness, nausea), blue-gray hyperpigmentation of skin/gums/sclera, photosensitivity
c.sae: Drug-induced lupus erythematosus (positive ANA/anti-histone) / Autoimmune hepatitis / Vestibular toxicity
c.info: Most lipophilic tetracycline with extensive blood-brain barrier and inner ear endolymph penetration. Undergoes hepatic metabolism; causes dose-dependent vestibular disturbances, especially in women.
c.caution: May be taken with food to reduce GI upset. Advise on the small risk of vestibular side effects (dizziness) and, with long-term use, skin/mucosal pigmentation.
c.preg: Contraindicated throughout pregnancy — deposits in developing fetal bone and teeth, causing permanent tooth discoloration and enamel hypoplasia, and can cause maternal hepatotoxicity (especially with high-dose IV use). Contraindicated during breastfeeding for the same reasons, despite the calcium in milk limiting infant absorption somewhat.
c.renal: Unlike older tetracyclines, eliminated mainly via non-renal routes and does not significantly accumulate in renal impairment — no dose adjustment is usually needed. However, long-term use carries a distinct, well-documented risk of drug-induced autoimmune hepatitis and a lupus-like syndrome — avoid in significant hepatic impairment and monitor liver function with prolonged courses.

c.sp:
Gram-positive: Streptococcus pneumoniae, Staphylococcus aureus (including some MRSA), Bacillus anthracis, Cutibacterium acnes, Actinomyces
Gram-negative: Haemophilus influenzae, Moraxella catarrhalis, Vibrio cholerae, Brucella, Francisella tularensis, Yersinia pestis, Neisseria meningitidis (minocycline), Acinetobacter (minocycline), Stenotrophomonas maltophilia (minocycline)
