ind: Pain and fever; antiplatelet prevention after MI, stroke or TIA; acute coronary syndrome; inflammatory arthritis and Kawasaki disease.
ae: Dyspepsia, heartburn, nausea, easy bruising, GI blood loss, tinnitus, bronchospasm in aspirin-sensitive asthma
c.doc: Low-dose (75–100 mg) secondary prevention after MI/stroke; 300 mg chewed at once in suspected acute MI; Kawasaki disease
c.ci: Active peptic ulcer or GI bleeding, hemophilia or other bleeding disorders, NSAID-induced asthma, children and teenagers under 16 with viral illness (Reye syndrome), severe renal or hepatic failure, third trimester (analgesic doses)
c.sci: Children and teenagers with fever or viral illness (Reye syndrome)
c.sae: GI hemorrhage / Reye syndrome / Salicylate toxicity (tinnitus, hyperventilation, metabolic acidosis)
c.info: Irreversibly acetylates COX-1 in platelets, blocking thromboxane A2 for the platelet's 7–10 day lifespan, so the antiplatelet effect lasts about a week after a dose. At analgesic doses it also inhibits COX-2. Elimination becomes saturable at high doses, so toxicity rises steeply.
c.caution: Take with or after food and a full glass of water; use enteric-coated tablets for long-term low-dose therapy. Do not give to children under 16 unless prescribed. Stop before surgery as advised (usually 5–7 days) unless taken for secondary prevention. Avoid other NSAIDs at the same time.
c.preg: Avoid analgesic doses, especially from 20 weeks and in the third trimester (fetal kidney dysfunction, ductus closure, bleeding, prolonged labor). Low-dose aspirin (75–150 mg) is used deliberately from about 12 weeks to reduce pre-eclampsia risk in high-risk women. Low-dose exposure through breast milk is small and generally acceptable; avoid regular analgesic doses while breastfeeding.
c.renal: Avoid analgesic doses in severe renal impairment (CrCl below 10–30 mL/min) because of fluid retention, AKI and hyperkalemia; low-dose antiplatelet use is generally tolerated. Avoid in severe hepatic impairment (bleeding risk).

ind: Osteoarthritis, rheumatoid arthritis and other rheumatic conditions where a gentler salicylate is preferred.
ae: Nausea, dyspepsia, tinnitus, dizziness, headache, rash
c.doc: Chronic arthritis when a non-acetylated salicylate is preferred (less GI irritation and little platelet effect)
c.ci: Salicylate or NSAID hypersensitivity, active peptic ulcer or GI bleeding, severe renal impairment, children with viral illness (Reye syndrome), third trimester
c.sae: Salicylate toxicity (tinnitus, hearing loss) / GI bleeding
c.info: Ester of two salicylic acid molecules that is hydrolysed after absorption; a non-acetylated salicylate with little effect on platelet aggregation or bleeding time. Salicylate blood levels can be monitored.
c.caution: Take with food and water and swallow tablets whole; usual dose 1.5–3 g/day in divided doses. Watch for tinnitus with high doses; monitor salicylate levels in the elderly and in renal impairment.
c.preg: Avoid from 20 weeks (risk of fetal kidney dysfunction and low amniotic fluid) and in the third trimester (premature closure of the ductus arteriosus, bleeding, prolonged labor); earlier in pregnancy use only if clearly needed, at the lowest dose for the shortest time. Salicylate passes into breast milk in small amounts; use with caution and prefer ibuprofen while breastfeeding.
c.renal: Avoid in severe renal impairment; use lower doses and monitor salicylate levels in mild–moderate impairment. Use caution in liver disease.

ind: Mild-to-moderate pain, osteoarthritis and rheumatoid arthritis.
ae: Nausea, dyspepsia, diarrhea, headache, rash, dizziness
c.doc: Longer-acting analgesic for musculoskeletal pain and arthritis, dosed twice daily
c.ci: Aspirin/NSAID hypersensitivity, active peptic ulcer or GI bleeding, severe renal failure, third trimester
c.sae: GI bleeding / Hypersensitivity (anaphylaxis, Stevens-Johnson syndrome)
c.info: Difluorophenyl derivative of salicylic acid that is not broken down to salicylate; long half-life (8–12 h) allows twice-daily dosing. Weak antiplatelet effect and little antipyretic action.
c.caution: Swallow whole with food; do not crush. Avoid taking with aspirin. Rare hypersensitivity syndrome (fever, rash, liver and kidney injury) — stop and seek review.
c.preg: Avoid from 20 weeks (risk of fetal kidney dysfunction and low amniotic fluid) and in the third trimester (premature closure of the ductus arteriosus, bleeding, prolonged labor); earlier in pregnancy use only if clearly needed, at the lowest dose for the shortest time. Small amounts pass into breast milk; use with caution, and prefer ibuprofen while breastfeeding.
c.renal: Cleared by the kidneys — reduce the dose in renal impairment and avoid in severe renal failure. Use caution in liver disease.

c.mn:
💊 Names: 'SAD': Salsalate, Aspirin, Diflunisal (all salicylic-acid based).
🎯 Used for: Pain, fever and inflammation. Low-dose aspirin prevents clots after MI and stroke.
💡 Tip: Only aspirin blocks platelets irreversibly. Never give aspirin to children under 16 with a viral illness (Reye syndrome).

ind: Severe acute pain, colic, cancer pain and high fever that does not respond to other measures.
ae: Hypotension after rapid IV injection, rash, allergic reactions, red discoloration of urine (harmless)
c.doc: Severe pain and colic (antispasmodic effect) and fever unresponsive to other antipyretics, where it is licensed; banned in several countries
c.ci: Pyrazolone hypersensitivity, history of agranulocytosis or bone-marrow disease, acute intermittent porphyria, G6PD deficiency, third trimester, infants under 3 months or under 5 kg, unstable circulation (IV)
c.sci: History of agranulocytosis or other bone-marrow disorder
c.sae: Agranulocytosis / Anaphylaxis / Severe hypotension / Stevens-Johnson syndrome
c.info: Pyrazolone prodrug hydrolysed to the active 4-methylaminoantipyrine. Analgesic, antipyretic and antispasmodic with weak anti-inflammatory action and little GI or platelet toxicity. Agranulocytosis risk is rare but unpredictable and sudden; it is banned in the US, UK and several other countries but widely used elsewhere.
c.caution: Give IV very slowly (no more than 1 mL/minute) with the patient lying down to avoid hypotension. Stop and seek review immediately for fever, sore throat or mouth ulcers (possible agranulocytosis). May turn urine red. Avoid alcohol.
c.preg: Avoid in the first trimester unless there is no alternative; contraindicated in the third trimester (ductus arteriosus closure). Passes into breast milk — avoid breastfeeding during and for 48 hours after a dose.
c.renal: Metabolites accumulate in renal or hepatic impairment — avoid repeated high doses; reduce the dose and lengthen the interval, and avoid in severe impairment.

ind: Historical: ankylosing spondylitis, gout and rheumatoid arthritis. Now mainly veterinary (horses).
ae: Nausea, dyspepsia, sodium and water retention, edema, rash, dizziness
c.doc: Obsolete in humans / Veterinary use only
c.ci: Blood disorders, active peptic ulcer, heart, renal or hepatic disease, hypertension, history of drug-induced blood dyscrasia, pregnancy
c.sae: Aplastic anemia / Agranulocytosis / Stevens-Johnson syndrome / Fluid overload
c.info: Pyrazolidinedione NSAID with strong anti-inflammatory action but a very long, variable half-life (50–100 h). Withdrawn from or severely restricted in human medicine in most countries because of aplastic anemia and agranulocytosis; still used in horses and banned in food-producing animals.
c.caution: Not for routine human use — retained for historical reference. Obtain a blood count before and regularly during any use, and limit to the shortest course.
c.preg: Contraindicated in pregnancy and breastfeeding (bone-marrow toxicity risk; class effects on the fetal kidney and ductus arteriosus).
c.renal: Contraindicated in renal impairment — causes sodium and water retention and can worsen renal function. Also avoid in hepatic impairment.

ind: Historical: rheumatoid arthritis, ankylosing spondylitis, gout and other inflammatory joint disease.
ae: Nausea, dyspepsia, edema, rash, dizziness
c.doc: Obsolete / Withdrawn
c.ci: Blood disorders, active peptic ulcer, heart, renal or hepatic disease, pregnancy
c.sae: Aplastic anemia / Agranulocytosis / Stevens-Johnson syndrome
c.info: Active hydroxylated metabolite of phenylbutazone with similar potency and toxicity, including a long half-life. Withdrawn from the market in the 1980s after reports of fatal aplastic anemia.
c.caution: Withdrawn from clinical use — do not dispense; retained for historical reference only.
c.preg: Contraindicated in pregnancy and breastfeeding (bone-marrow toxicity risk; class effects on the fetal kidney and ductus arteriosus).
c.renal: Contraindicated in renal impairment (sodium and water retention); also avoid in hepatic impairment.

c.mn:
💊 Names: 'MOP': Metamizole, Oxyphenbutazone, Phenylbutazone.
🎯 Used for: Metamizole for severe pain, colic and stubborn fever; the two -butazones are obsolete in humans.
💡 Tip: Danger is bone marrow: agranulocytosis with metamizole, aplastic anemia with the butazones.

ind: Mild-to-moderate pain, fever, headache and migraine, dysmenorrhea, dental pain, osteoarthritis, rheumatoid arthritis, and IV use to close a patent ductus arteriosus in preterm infants.
ae: Dyspepsia, nausea, abdominal pain, headache, dizziness, fluid retention, rash
c.doc: First-line NSAID for fever and pain in children; dysmenorrhea; closure of patent ductus arteriosus in premature infants
c.ci: Active peptic ulcer or GI bleeding, NSAID/aspirin-induced asthma or urticaria, severe heart failure, severe renal or hepatic failure, third trimester, peri-operative CABG surgery
c.sae: GI bleeding / Cardiovascular thrombotic events / Acute kidney injury
c.info: Reversible non-selective COX inhibitor with a short half-life (~2 h). Usual analgesic dose 200–400 mg every 4–6 h (OTC maximum 1.2 g/day; prescription up to 2.4–3.2 g/day). Lowest GI and cardiovascular risk of the traditional NSAIDs at low doses. It can block aspirin's antiplatelet effect.
c.caution: Take with food or milk. Take low-dose aspirin at least 30 minutes before, or 8 hours after, ibuprofen. Children: 5–10 mg/kg every 6–8 h (maximum 40 mg/kg/day); give under 3 months only on medical advice. Avoid when dehydrated or during chickenpox.
c.preg: Avoid from 20 weeks (risk of fetal kidney dysfunction and low amniotic fluid) and in the third trimester (premature closure of the ductus arteriosus, bleeding, prolonged labor); earlier in pregnancy use only if clearly needed, at the lowest dose for the shortest time. Ibuprofen is the preferred NSAID during breastfeeding — very low milk levels, compatible with nursing.
c.renal: NSAIDs lower renal prostaglandins and can cause acute kidney injury, fluid retention and hyperkalemia — avoid in severe renal impairment (CrCl below 30 mL/min), and be careful with dehydration, diuretics and ACE inhibitors/ARBs. Avoid in severe hepatic impairment; caution in cirrhosis (fluid retention and renal failure).

ind: Rheumatoid arthritis, osteoarthritis, ankylosing spondylitis, acute gout, dysmenorrhea, musculoskeletal and postoperative pain; topical gel for localized pain.
ae: Dyspepsia, nausea, abdominal pain, headache, dizziness, rash; topical: skin irritation and photosensitivity
c.doc: Musculoskeletal pain and inflammation (oral and topical gel)
c.ci: Active peptic ulcer or GI bleeding, NSAID/aspirin-induced asthma or urticaria, severe heart failure, severe renal or hepatic failure, third trimester, peri-operative CABG surgery; topical form: known photoallergy to ketoprofen, fenofibrate or benzophenone-containing sunscreens
c.sae: Photoallergic dermatitis (topical) / GI bleeding / Hypersensitivity reaction
c.info: Propionic acid NSAID with COX inhibition and weak leukotriene inhibition; half-life about 2 h unless in a modified-release form. Racemic — dexketoprofen is its active S-enantiomer. Topical use is linked to photoallergic reactions.
c.caution: Take with food; swallow modified-release capsules whole. Topical: protect treated skin from sunlight and tanning beds during treatment and for at least 2 weeks after; do not use under occlusive dressings.
c.preg: Avoid from 20 weeks (risk of fetal kidney dysfunction and low amniotic fluid) and in the third trimester (premature closure of the ductus arteriosus, bleeding, prolonged labor); earlier in pregnancy use only if clearly needed, at the lowest dose for the shortest time. Small amounts pass into breast milk; short oral use is acceptable, but prefer ibuprofen. Topical gel has lower systemic exposure but is still avoided in the third trimester.
c.renal: NSAIDs lower renal prostaglandins and can cause acute kidney injury, fluid retention and hyperkalemia — avoid in severe renal impairment (CrCl below 30 mL/min), and be careful with dehydration, diuretics and ACE inhibitors/ARBs. Reduce the dose in mild–moderate renal or hepatic impairment.

ind: Rheumatoid arthritis, osteoarthritis, ankylosing spondylitis, mild-to-moderate pain, dysmenorrhea, sore throat (lozenge/spray), and ophthalmic use to prevent surgical miosis.
ae: Dyspepsia, nausea, diarrhea, headache, dizziness, rash; lozenge: mouth irritation
c.doc: Arthritis pain; local sore-throat relief with lozenges; eye drops to prevent miosis during cataract surgery
c.ci: Active peptic ulcer or GI bleeding, NSAID/aspirin-induced asthma or urticaria, severe heart failure, severe renal or hepatic failure, third trimester, peri-operative CABG surgery
c.sae: GI bleeding / Cardiovascular thrombotic events / Acute kidney injury
c.info: Potent reversible COX inhibitor with a half-life of about 4–6 h, allowing 2–3 times daily dosing. Available as tablets, throat lozenge/spray and ophthalmic drops.
c.caution: Take tablets with food. Lozenges: dissolve slowly in the mouth and limit to 3 days for a sore throat unless advised. Ophthalmic drops: remove contact lenses.
c.preg: Avoid from 20 weeks (risk of fetal kidney dysfunction and low amniotic fluid) and in the third trimester (premature closure of the ductus arteriosus, bleeding, prolonged labor); earlier in pregnancy use only if clearly needed, at the lowest dose for the shortest time. Very small amounts pass into breast milk and short-term use is considered acceptable, but ibuprofen has more data.
c.renal: NSAIDs lower renal prostaglandins and can cause acute kidney injury, fluid retention and hyperkalemia — avoid in severe renal impairment (CrCl below 30 mL/min), and be careful with dehydration, diuretics and ACE inhibitors/ARBs. Reduce the dose in mild–moderate hepatic impairment and avoid in severe impairment.

ind: Rheumatoid arthritis, osteoarthritis and mild-to-moderate pain.
ae: Dyspepsia, constipation, nausea, headache, dizziness, tinnitus, rash
c.doc: Arthritis pain (largely replaced by ibuprofen and naproxen)
c.ci: Active peptic ulcer or GI bleeding, NSAID/aspirin-induced asthma or urticaria, severe heart failure, severe renal or hepatic failure, third trimester, peri-operative CABG surgery; significant renal impairment
c.sci: Renal impairment (risk of interstitial nephritis and nephrotic syndrome)
c.sae: Interstitial nephritis / Nephrotic syndrome / GI bleeding
c.info: Propionic acid NSAID with a short half-life (~3 h) and very high protein binding; uniquely linked to interstitial nephritis with nephrotic syndrome. Phenobarbital shortens its half-life.
c.caution: Take with food if it upsets the stomach (food slows absorption). Check renal function and urine protein with long-term use. Report swelling, reduced urine, or foamy urine.
c.preg: Avoid from 20 weeks (risk of fetal kidney dysfunction and low amniotic fluid) and in the third trimester (premature closure of the ductus arteriosus, bleeding, prolonged labor); earlier in pregnancy use only if clearly needed, at the lowest dose for the shortest time. Fenoprofen is rarely used and there is little breast-milk data; prefer ibuprofen while breastfeeding.
c.renal: Avoid in significant renal impairment — linked to interstitial nephritis and nephrotic syndrome; monitor renal function and urine protein in others. Use caution in liver disease.

c.st: Tab 250, 375, 500 mg · Na salt 275, 550 mg · Susp 125 mg/5 mL
ind: Rheumatoid arthritis, osteoarthritis, ankylosing spondylitis, juvenile arthritis, acute gout, tendinitis, bursitis, dysmenorrhea, migraine and mild-to-moderate pain.
ae: Dyspepsia, heartburn, nausea, abdominal pain, headache, dizziness, edema, bruising
c.dose: Tab 250, 375, 500 mg · Na salt 275, 550 mg · Susp 125 mg/5 mL
c.doc: Acute gout; dysmenorrhea; long-acting twice-daily choice for arthritis with the lowest cardiovascular risk among traditional NSAIDs
c.ci: Active peptic ulcer or GI bleeding, NSAID/aspirin-induced asthma or urticaria, severe heart failure, severe renal or hepatic failure, third trimester, peri-operative CABG surgery
c.sae: GI bleeding / Cardiovascular thrombotic events / Acute kidney injury
c.info: Reversible COX inhibitor with a long half-life (12–17 h), allowing twice-daily dosing. The sodium salt has faster onset. Appears to have lower cardiovascular thrombotic risk than diclofenac or the coxibs, but similar GI risk.
c.caution: Take with food or milk. Do not take naproxen and naproxen sodium products together. OTC naproxen sodium: 220 mg every 8–12 h, maximum 660 mg/day. Report black stools or vomiting blood.
c.preg: Avoid from 20 weeks (risk of fetal kidney dysfunction and low amniotic fluid) and in the third trimester (premature closure of the ductus arteriosus, bleeding, prolonged labor); earlier in pregnancy use only if clearly needed, at the lowest dose for the shortest time. Present in breast milk and its long half-life may cause accumulation in the infant; prefer ibuprofen, especially for newborns.
c.renal: NSAIDs lower renal prostaglandins and can cause acute kidney injury, fluid retention and hyperkalemia — avoid in severe renal impairment (CrCl below 30 mL/min), and be careful with dehydration, diuretics and ACE inhibitors/ARBs. Avoid in severe hepatic impairment.

ind: Osteoarthritis, rheumatoid arthritis and juvenile rheumatoid arthritis.
ae: Dyspepsia, nausea, constipation, diarrhea, rash, photosensitivity
c.doc: Once-daily NSAID for chronic arthritis
c.ci: Active peptic ulcer or GI bleeding, NSAID/aspirin-induced asthma or urticaria, severe heart failure, severe renal or hepatic failure, third trimester, peri-operative CABG surgery
c.sae: GI bleeding / Cardiovascular thrombotic events / Photosensitivity reactions
c.info: Propionic acid NSAID with a very long half-life (about 55 h), allowing once-daily dosing; steady state takes several days. Reversible non-selective COX inhibitor.
c.caution: Take once daily with food. Avoid strong sun exposure and use sun protection because of photosensitivity. Usual dose 600–1200 mg/day.
c.preg: Avoid from 20 weeks (risk of fetal kidney dysfunction and low amniotic fluid) and in the third trimester (premature closure of the ductus arteriosus, bleeding, prolonged labor); earlier in pregnancy use only if clearly needed, at the lowest dose for the shortest time. Limited breast-milk data; prefer ibuprofen while breastfeeding.
c.renal: NSAIDs lower renal prostaglandins and can cause acute kidney injury, fluid retention and hyperkalemia — avoid in severe renal impairment (CrCl below 30 mL/min), and be careful with dehydration, diuretics and ACE inhibitors/ARBs. In severe renal impairment or on dialysis, start at 600 mg once daily. Use caution in liver disease.

ind: Short-term relief of mild-to-moderate pain: musculoskeletal, dental and postoperative pain, and dysmenorrhea.
ae: Nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, diarrhea, dyspepsia, dizziness, headache
c.doc: Rapid short-term analgesia (as the trometamol salt); active S-enantiomer of ketoprofen at half the dose
c.ci: Active peptic ulcer or GI bleeding, NSAID/aspirin-induced asthma or urticaria, severe heart failure, severe renal or hepatic failure, third trimester, peri-operative CABG surgery; moderate–severe renal impairment (CrCl below about 60 mL/min); coagulation disorders
c.sae: GI bleeding / Acute kidney injury / Hypersensitivity reaction
c.info: The active S-(+)-enantiomer of ketoprofen. The trometamol salt is absorbed quickly, with onset in about 30 minutes; half-life 1.5–2 h. Not available in the US.
c.caution: Usual dose 12.5 mg every 4–6 h or 25 mg every 8 h; maximum 75 mg/day. Use for the shortest time, generally a few days. Take with food if stomach upset occurs; food delays onset.
c.preg: Avoid from 20 weeks (risk of fetal kidney dysfunction and low amniotic fluid) and in the third trimester (premature closure of the ductus arteriosus, bleeding, prolonged labor); earlier in pregnancy use only if clearly needed, at the lowest dose for the shortest time. Limited breast-milk data; not recommended while breastfeeding — prefer ibuprofen.
c.renal: Contraindicated in moderate–severe renal impairment (CrCl below about 60 mL/min); in mild impairment limit to 50 mg/day. Contraindicated in severe hepatic impairment; reduce the dose in mild–moderate impairment.

c.mn:
💊 Names: Most end in '-profen': Ibuprofen, Ketoprofen, Flurbiprofen, Fenoprofen, Oxaprozin, Dexketoprofen. The odd one out is Naproxen.
🎯 Used for: Pain, fever, arthritis, period pain, gout.
💡 Tip: Ibuprofen = safest for kids and breastfeeding. Naproxen = long-acting with the lowest heart risk. Oxaprozin = once a day.

ind: Mild-to-moderate pain, primary dysmenorrhea, heavy menstrual bleeding, dental and postoperative pain, and short-term arthritis pain.
ae: Diarrhea, nausea, dyspepsia, abdominal pain, headache, dizziness, rash
c.doc: Dysmenorrhea and heavy menstrual bleeding (short courses of up to 7 days)
c.ci: Active peptic ulcer or GI bleeding, NSAID/aspirin-induced asthma or urticaria, severe heart failure, severe renal or hepatic failure, third trimester, peri-operative CABG surgery; inflammatory bowel disease
c.sae: Severe diarrhea / Hemolytic anemia / Seizures in overdose / GI bleeding
c.info: Fenamate NSAID that inhibits COX and antagonises some prostaglandin receptors; short half-life (~2 h). Unlike other NSAIDs, overdose commonly causes seizures. It can also give a positive direct Coombs test.
c.caution: Take with food. Usual adult dose 500 mg once, then 250 mg every 6 h, for no more than 7 days. Stop if diarrhea or rash develops. Keep away from children — overdose can cause seizures.
c.preg: Avoid from 20 weeks (risk of fetal kidney dysfunction and low amniotic fluid) and in the third trimester (premature closure of the ductus arteriosus, bleeding, prolonged labor); earlier in pregnancy use only if clearly needed, at the lowest dose for the shortest time. Passes into breast milk in small amounts; short-term use is acceptable, though prefer ibuprofen.
c.renal: NSAIDs lower renal prostaglandins and can cause acute kidney injury, fluid retention and hyperkalemia — avoid in severe renal impairment (CrCl below 30 mL/min), and be careful with dehydration, diuretics and ACE inhibitors/ARBs. Contraindicated in severe hepatic impairment; monitor renal function during longer use.

ind: Musculoskeletal and joint pain and inflammation (mainly topical); oral use in arthritis is historical.
ae: Diarrhea, nausea, dyspepsia, headache, rash; topical: skin irritation and photosensitivity
c.doc: Mostly topical relief of muscle and joint pain; oral use largely abandoned
c.ci: Active peptic ulcer or GI bleeding, NSAID/aspirin-induced asthma or urticaria, severe heart failure, severe renal or hepatic failure, third trimester, peri-operative CABG surgery; inflammatory bowel disease
c.sae: Severe diarrhea / GI bleeding / Photoallergic dermatitis (topical)
c.info: Original fenamate NSAID (1963) with COX inhibition and effects on prostaglandin receptors and chloride channels. It has been largely replaced by other agents; still found in some topical products and used as a research tool.
c.caution: Topical: apply a thin layer to intact skin only, wash hands afterwards and protect treated areas from sunlight. Oral use should be with food and for the shortest time.
c.preg: Avoid from 20 weeks (risk of fetal kidney dysfunction and low amniotic fluid) and in the third trimester (premature closure of the ductus arteriosus, bleeding, prolonged labor); earlier in pregnancy use only if clearly needed, at the lowest dose for the shortest time. Limited breast-milk data; topical use has low systemic exposure but avoid in the third trimester.
c.renal: NSAIDs lower renal prostaglandins and can cause acute kidney injury, fluid retention and hyperkalemia — avoid in severe renal impairment (CrCl below 30 mL/min), and be careful with dehydration, diuretics and ACE inhibitors/ARBs. Avoid in severe hepatic impairment.

ind: Rheumatoid arthritis, osteoarthritis, mild-to-moderate pain, primary dysmenorrhea and heavy menstrual bleeding.
ae: Diarrhea (common), nausea, dyspepsia, abdominal pain, headache, dizziness, rash
c.doc: Arthritis and dysmenorrhea (diarrhea is a frequent limiting effect); largely superseded
c.ci: Active peptic ulcer or GI bleeding, NSAID/aspirin-induced asthma or urticaria, severe heart failure, severe renal or hepatic failure, third trimester, peri-operative CABG surgery; inflammatory bowel disease
c.sae: Severe diarrhea / GI bleeding / Hemolytic anemia / Cardiovascular thrombotic events
c.info: Fenamate NSAID that inhibits COX and antagonises prostaglandin receptors; also inhibits lipoxygenase. Half-life about 2 h. Diarrhea is common and often dose-limiting; the US brand was discontinued.
c.caution: Take with food or milk. Swallow capsules whole. Stop and seek review for persistent diarrhea or black stools. Usual dose 200–400 mg/day in divided doses.
c.preg: Avoid from 20 weeks (risk of fetal kidney dysfunction and low amniotic fluid) and in the third trimester (premature closure of the ductus arteriosus, bleeding, prolonged labor); earlier in pregnancy use only if clearly needed, at the lowest dose for the shortest time. Passes into breast milk in small amounts; prefer ibuprofen while breastfeeding.
c.renal: NSAIDs lower renal prostaglandins and can cause acute kidney injury, fluid retention and hyperkalemia — avoid in severe renal impairment (CrCl below 30 mL/min), and be careful with dehydration, diuretics and ACE inhibitors/ARBs. Avoid in severe hepatic impairment.

c.mn:
💊 Names: Mefenamic acid, Flufenamic acid, Meclofenamate (all 'fenam-' names).
🎯 Used for: Period pain, heavy periods and mild pain; flufenamic acid mostly topical.
💡 Tip: Diarrhea is common, and overdose can cause seizures. Mefenamic acid: limit to 7 days.

c.st: Tab 25, 50, 75, 100 mg · Inj 75 mg/3 mL · Gel 1%
ind: Osteoarthritis, rheumatoid arthritis, ankylosing spondylitis, acute gout, musculoskeletal and postoperative pain, dysmenorrhea, renal and biliary colic; topical gel for localized pain.
ae: Dyspepsia, abdominal pain, nausea, headache, dizziness, raised liver enzymes, fluid retention; injection-site pain
c.dose: Tab 25, 50, 75, 100 mg · Inj 75 mg/3 mL · Gel 1%
c.doc: Postoperative and musculoskeletal pain; acute gout; topical 1% gel for local osteoarthritis with lower systemic exposure
c.ci: Established ischemic heart disease, stroke, peripheral arterial disease or heart failure (NYHA II–IV); active peptic ulcer or GI bleeding; peri-operative CABG surgery; severe renal or hepatic failure; third trimester; NSAID-induced asthma
c.sae: Cardiovascular thrombotic events (MI, stroke) / Hepatotoxicity / GI bleeding
c.info: Phenylacetic acid NSAID with some COX-2 preference (similar to celecoxib) and a cardiovascular risk close to the coxibs. Extensive first-pass metabolism (~50% bioavailability); short plasma half-life (~2 h) but it concentrates in synovial fluid. Potassium salt acts fast; enteric-coated sodium salt is delayed.
c.caution: Take with or after food; swallow enteric-coated and modified-release tablets whole. Use the lowest dose for the shortest time and check liver enzymes with long-term use. IM injection can damage tissue — use only when needed. Topical gel: thin layer on intact skin, wash hands.
c.preg: Avoid from 20 weeks (risk of fetal kidney dysfunction and low amniotic fluid) and in the third trimester (premature closure of the ductus arteriosus, bleeding, prolonged labor); earlier in pregnancy use only if clearly needed, at the lowest dose for the shortest time. Very low levels in breast milk; generally acceptable while breastfeeding at usual doses.
c.renal: NSAIDs lower renal prostaglandins and can cause acute kidney injury, fluid retention and hyperkalemia — avoid in severe renal impairment (CrCl below 30 mL/min), and be careful with dehydration, diuretics and ACE inhibitors/ARBs. Hepatotoxic — monitor liver enzymes and avoid in severe hepatic impairment.

ind: Short-term (up to 5 days) treatment of moderately severe acute pain, including postoperative pain and renal colic; ophthalmic use for post-cataract inflammation and allergic conjunctivitis.
ae: Nausea, dyspepsia, abdominal pain, headache, dizziness, edema, injection-site pain; eye drops: stinging
c.doc: Short-course postoperative pain and renal colic when opioids are undesirable; eye drops after cataract surgery
c.ci: Active or recent GI bleeding or ulcer; cerebrovascular bleeding or high bleeding risk; moderate–severe renal impairment or volume depletion; peri-operative CABG surgery; labor and delivery; breastfeeding; concurrent aspirin, other NSAIDs, probenecid or pentoxifylline
c.sci: Renal impairment / Bleeding risk / Labor and delivery
c.sae: GI bleeding and perforation / Acute kidney injury / Hemorrhage
c.info: Potent NSAID with analgesic effect comparable to modest-dose opioids but no sedation or respiratory depression. High GI and renal toxicity, so total systemic therapy (IV, IM and oral) is limited to 5 days. Racemic; the S-enantiomer is active. Ophthalmic 0.4–0.5% solutions available.
c.caution: Maximum 5 days for all systemic routes combined; oral tablets only as continuation after IV/IM. Reduce dose if over 65, under 50 kg, or with mild renal impairment. Correct dehydration first. Eye drops: remove contact lenses and wait 5 minutes between different drops.
c.preg: Contraindicated in labor and delivery (may affect fetal circulation and inhibit uterine contractions); avoid in pregnancy, especially from 20 weeks and in the third trimester. Low milk levels, but labels advise against use in nursing mothers; ibuprofen is preferred.
c.renal: Contraindicated in moderate–severe renal impairment and volume depletion; reduce the dose in mild impairment and in patients over 65. Avoid in patients at risk of bleeding and in severe hepatic impairment.

ind: Osteoarthritis, rheumatoid arthritis, ankylosing spondylitis, acute musculoskeletal and dental pain, dysmenorrhea.
ae: Dyspepsia, abdominal pain, nausea, diarrhea, dizziness, raised liver enzymes, pruritus
c.doc: Chronic osteoarthritis and rheumatoid pain with twice-daily dosing and slightly better GI tolerability
c.ci: Active peptic ulcer or GI bleeding, NSAID/aspirin-induced asthma or urticaria, severe heart failure, severe renal or hepatic failure, third trimester, peri-operative CABG surgery
c.sae: GI bleeding / Hepatotoxicity / Cardiovascular thrombotic events
c.info: Glycolic acid ester of diclofenac, partly converted to diclofenac in the body. Preferentially inhibits COX-2 and reduces IL-1β and TNF-α while sparing cartilage proteoglycan synthesis. Not approved in the US.
c.caution: Take with food and swallow whole; usual dose 100 mg twice daily. Check liver function and blood pressure with long-term use. Use the lowest effective dose.
c.preg: Avoid from 20 weeks (risk of fetal kidney dysfunction and low amniotic fluid) and in the third trimester (premature closure of the ductus arteriosus, bleeding, prolonged labor); earlier in pregnancy use only if clearly needed, at the lowest dose for the shortest time. Limited breast-milk data; prefer ibuprofen while breastfeeding.
c.renal: NSAIDs lower renal prostaglandins and can cause acute kidney injury, fluid retention and hyperkalemia — avoid in severe renal impairment (CrCl below 30 mL/min), and be careful with dehydration, diuretics and ACE inhibitors/ARBs. In mild–moderate hepatic impairment start with 100 mg once daily; avoid in severe impairment.

c.mn:
💊 Names: 'DAK': Diclofenac, Aceclofenac, Ketorolac (all acetic-acid based).
🎯 Used for: Post-operative pain, arthritis, colic (Diclofenac); strong short-term pain relief (Ketorolac).
💡 Tip: Diclofenac carries a heart risk close to the coxibs. Ketorolac is limited to 5 days because of stomach and kidney risk.

c.st: Cap 25, 50 mg · SR cap 75 mg · Supp 100 mg
ind: Acute gout, ankylosing spondylitis, rheumatoid arthritis and osteoarthritis, bursitis and tendinitis, and IV closure of a patent ductus arteriosus in preterm infants.
ae: Frontal headache, dizziness, dyspepsia, nausea, abdominal pain, fluid retention, confusion in the elderly
c.dose: Cap 25, 50 mg · SR cap 75 mg · Supp 100 mg
c.doc: Acute gout; ankylosing spondylitis; patent ductus arteriosus closure in premature infants; indomethacin-responsive headaches (paroxysmal hemicrania, hemicrania continua)
c.ci: Active peptic ulcer or GI bleeding, NSAID/aspirin-induced asthma or urticaria, severe heart failure, severe renal or hepatic failure, third trimester, peri-operative CABG surgery; nasal polyps with angioedema
c.sci: Neonates: necrotizing enterocolitis, renal impairment, active bleeding (IV use)
c.sae: GI bleeding and perforation / CNS effects (depression, psychosis, seizures) / Acute kidney injury / Neonatal necrotizing enterocolitis
c.info: Indole acetic acid derivative and one of the most potent COX inhibitors, with a half-life of about 4.5 h and enterohepatic recycling. Frequent CNS side effects (headache, dizziness) and reduced renal blood flow. Historically also used briefly as a tocolytic.
c.caution: Take with food, milk or an antacid. Start with a low dose and increase gradually, since headache is common early on. Avoid driving if drowsy or dizzy. Suppository can irritate the rectum. Use the lowest dose for the shortest time.
c.preg: Avoid in the third trimester and after 20 weeks (oligohydramnios, ductus closure); short tocolytic courses before 32 weeks need close fetal monitoring. Passes into breast milk in small amounts, but rare infant CNS effects have been reported; prefer ibuprofen while breastfeeding.
c.renal: NSAIDs lower renal prostaglandins and can cause acute kidney injury, fluid retention and hyperkalemia — avoid in severe renal impairment (CrCl below 30 mL/min), and be careful with dehydration, diuretics and ACE inhibitors/ARBs. Avoid in severe hepatic impairment; the elderly are particularly sensitive to CNS effects.

ind: Osteoarthritis, rheumatoid arthritis, ankylosing spondylitis, acute gout and acute painful shoulder.
ae: Dyspepsia, nausea, abdominal pain, diarrhea, headache, dizziness, rash, tinnitus
c.doc: Arthritis pain in patients at risk for renal effects, because the prodrug is largely spared in the kidney
c.ci: Active peptic ulcer or GI bleeding, NSAID/aspirin-induced asthma or urticaria, severe heart failure, severe renal or hepatic failure, third trimester, peri-operative CABG surgery
c.sae: Hepatotoxicity / Pancreatitis / GI bleeding / Stevens-Johnson syndrome
c.info: Prodrug (sulfoxide) converted in the liver to the active sulfide, then reoxidised to inactive sulfoxide in the kidney — so it has less effect on renal prostaglandins than most NSAIDs. Enterohepatic recycling gives a long effective half-life (~18 h for the active metabolite). Twice-daily dosing.
c.caution: Take with food or milk; usual dose 150–200 mg twice daily. Report yellow skin, dark urine or severe abdominal pain. Drink plenty of fluids to reduce risk of kidney stones.
c.preg: Avoid from 20 weeks (risk of fetal kidney dysfunction and low amniotic fluid) and in the third trimester (premature closure of the ductus arteriosus, bleeding, prolonged labor); earlier in pregnancy use only if clearly needed, at the lowest dose for the shortest time. Limited breast-milk data; prefer ibuprofen while breastfeeding.
c.renal: NSAIDs lower renal prostaglandins and can cause acute kidney injury, fluid retention and hyperkalemia — avoid in severe renal impairment (CrCl below 30 mL/min), and be careful with dehydration, diuretics and ACE inhibitors/ARBs. Less renal prostaglandin inhibition than others, but still avoid in advanced renal disease; reduce the dose in hepatic impairment.

c.mn:
💊 Names: Indomethacin, Sulindac ('Indo' + 'Sul' = indole).
🎯 Used for: Gout, ankylosing spondylitis, arthritis; indomethacin also closes a patent ductus arteriosus in premature infants.
💡 Tip: Indomethacin = strongest, but headache and confusion. Sulindac = prodrug, gentler on the kidney.

ind: Osteoarthritis, rheumatoid arthritis, ankylosing spondylitis, acute gout and acute musculoskeletal disorders.
ae: Dyspepsia, nausea, abdominal pain, edema, headache, dizziness, rash, tinnitus
c.doc: Once-daily arthritis therapy; use restricted to second-line in some regions because of GI and skin risk
c.ci: Active peptic ulcer or GI bleeding, NSAID/aspirin-induced asthma or urticaria, severe heart failure, severe renal or hepatic failure, third trimester, peri-operative CABG surgery; history of serious skin reactions
c.sci: History of serious skin reactions / Peptic ulcer
c.sae: GI bleeding and perforation / Serious skin reactions (SJS/TEN) / Photosensitivity
c.info: Oxicam (enolic acid) with a very long half-life (about 50 h) allowing once-daily dosing; steady state takes 7–12 days. It has one of the highest GI-bleeding risks among NSAIDs.
c.caution: Take once daily with food; maximum 20 mg/day. Avoid in the elderly where possible, or use PPI cover. Stop at the first skin rash. Avoid strong sun exposure.
c.preg: Avoid from 20 weeks (risk of fetal kidney dysfunction and low amniotic fluid) and in the third trimester (premature closure of the ductus arteriosus, bleeding, prolonged labor); earlier in pregnancy use only if clearly needed, at the lowest dose for the shortest time. Small amounts pass into breast milk; prefer ibuprofen while breastfeeding.
c.renal: NSAIDs lower renal prostaglandins and can cause acute kidney injury, fluid retention and hyperkalemia — avoid in severe renal impairment (CrCl below 30 mL/min), and be careful with dehydration, diuretics and ACE inhibitors/ARBs. Avoid in severe hepatic impairment.

ind: Osteoarthritis, rheumatoid arthritis, ankylosing spondylitis, acute musculoskeletal disorders and gout.
ae: Dyspepsia, nausea, abdominal pain, headache, dizziness, edema, rash
c.doc: Once-daily arthritis and musculoskeletal pain therapy; not available in the US
c.ci: Active peptic ulcer or GI bleeding, NSAID/aspirin-induced asthma or urticaria, severe heart failure, severe renal or hepatic failure, third trimester, peri-operative CABG surgery
c.sae: GI bleeding / Cardiovascular thrombotic events / Acute kidney injury / Serious skin reactions
c.info: Oxicam with the longest half-life of its class (about 72 h), allowing once-daily dosing; steady state takes several days. Also given IV or IM in some markets.
c.caution: Take once daily with food; usual dose 20 mg. Use short courses for acute conditions. Avoid strong sun exposure. Use PPI cover in high-risk patients.
c.preg: Avoid from 20 weeks (risk of fetal kidney dysfunction and low amniotic fluid) and in the third trimester (premature closure of the ductus arteriosus, bleeding, prolonged labor); earlier in pregnancy use only if clearly needed, at the lowest dose for the shortest time. Small amounts pass into breast milk; prefer ibuprofen while breastfeeding.
c.renal: NSAIDs lower renal prostaglandins and can cause acute kidney injury, fluid retention and hyperkalemia — avoid in severe renal impairment (CrCl below 30 mL/min), and be careful with dehydration, diuretics and ACE inhibitors/ARBs. Avoid in severe hepatic impairment.

ind: Acute mild-to-moderate pain, postoperative pain, sciatica, osteoarthritis and rheumatoid arthritis.
ae: Nausea, dyspepsia, abdominal pain, diarrhea, dizziness, headache
c.doc: Short-acting oxicam for acute pain and postoperative analgesia (oral and injection); marketed in Europe and Asia
c.ci: Active peptic ulcer or GI bleeding, NSAID/aspirin-induced asthma or urticaria, severe heart failure, severe renal or hepatic failure, third trimester, peri-operative CABG surgery; bleeding disorders
c.sae: GI bleeding / Cardiovascular thrombotic events / Acute kidney injury
c.info: Oxicam with a short half-life (3–5 h), unlike other oxicams, and potent, balanced COX-1/COX-2 inhibition. Metabolised by CYP2C9, so exposure is higher in poor metabolisers. Not approved in the US.
c.caution: Tablets: 8–16 mg/day for acute pain in 2–3 divided doses, with food. Injection: 8 mg IV/IM, may repeat once after 12 h; maximum 16 mg/day. Reconstitute with 2 mL water for injection. Reduce the dose in known CYP2C9 poor metabolisers.
c.preg: Avoid from 20 weeks (risk of fetal kidney dysfunction and low amniotic fluid) and in the third trimester (premature closure of the ductus arteriosus, bleeding, prolonged labor); earlier in pregnancy use only if clearly needed, at the lowest dose for the shortest time. Limited breast-milk data; avoid while breastfeeding and prefer ibuprofen.
c.renal: NSAIDs lower renal prostaglandins and can cause acute kidney injury, fluid retention and hyperkalemia — avoid in severe renal impairment (CrCl below 30 mL/min), and be careful with dehydration, diuretics and ACE inhibitors/ARBs. Avoid in severe hepatic impairment; reduce the dose in mild–moderate impairment.

c.mn:
💊 Names: All end in '-oxicam': Piroxicam, Tenoxicam, Lornoxicam (Meloxicam sits in the COX-2 group).
🎯 Used for: Arthritis and musculoskeletal pain with once-daily dosing.
💡 Tip: Long half-life means once a day, except Lornoxicam (short-acting). Piroxicam carries the highest stomach-bleeding risk.

ind: Acute pain, painful osteoarthritis, primary dysmenorrhea and fever, in countries where it is approved.
ae: Nausea, diarrhea, dyspepsia, dizziness, rash, raised transaminases
c.doc: Short-course (up to 15 days) second-line acute pain where marketed; restricted or withdrawn in several countries
c.ci: Prior liver reaction to nimesulide, active liver disease, GI ulcer or bleeding, alcohol or drug abuse, severe renal or cardiac failure, children under 12, third trimester
c.sae: Hepatotoxicity (acute liver failure)
c.info: Sulfonanilide NSAID with preferential COX-2 inhibition and rapid onset. Restricted or withdrawn in several countries for liver injury; the EU limits it to short-term second-line use (100 mg twice daily for up to 15 days). Not available in the US.
c.caution: Use for the shortest time, up to 15 days at 100 mg twice daily. Stop and seek review for nausea, dark urine, yellow skin or abdominal pain. Avoid alcohol and other hepatotoxic drugs.
c.preg: Contraindicated in the third trimester and best avoided throughout pregnancy. Avoid while breastfeeding (limited data; safer NSAIDs are available).
c.renal: Contraindicated in severe renal impairment (CrCl below 30 mL/min) and in hepatic impairment; use caution in mild–moderate renal impairment.

ind: Osteoarthritis, rheumatoid arthritis, juvenile arthritis (ER form) and acute pain.
ae: Dyspepsia, nausea, abdominal pain, headache, dizziness, edema, rash
c.doc: Arthritis pain with somewhat better GI tolerability than non-selective NSAIDs
c.ci: Active peptic ulcer or GI bleeding, NSAID/aspirin-induced asthma or urticaria, severe heart failure, severe renal or hepatic failure, third trimester, peri-operative CABG surgery
c.sae: GI bleeding / Cardiovascular thrombotic events / Acute kidney injury
c.info: Pyranocarboxylic acid NSAID with preferential COX-2 inhibition (about 10-fold); half-life about 7 h. Racemic, S-enantiomer active. Can cause false-positive urine bilirubin and ketone tests.
c.caution: Take with food or milk; swallow extended-release tablets whole. Tell the lab about use if urine tests are unexpectedly positive for bilirubin or ketones.
c.preg: Avoid from 20 weeks (risk of fetal kidney dysfunction and low amniotic fluid) and in the third trimester (premature closure of the ductus arteriosus, bleeding, prolonged labor); earlier in pregnancy use only if clearly needed, at the lowest dose for the shortest time. Limited breast-milk data; prefer ibuprofen while breastfeeding.
c.renal: NSAIDs lower renal prostaglandins and can cause acute kidney injury, fluid retention and hyperkalemia — avoid in severe renal impairment (CrCl below 30 mL/min), and be careful with dehydration, diuretics and ACE inhibitors/ARBs. Use caution in hepatic impairment.

ind: Osteoarthritis and rheumatoid arthritis.
ae: Diarrhea, dyspepsia, abdominal pain, nausea, headache, edema, rash
c.doc: Once-daily arthritis therapy with lower direct GI irritation because it is a non-acidic prodrug
c.ci: Active peptic ulcer or GI bleeding, NSAID/aspirin-induced asthma or urticaria, severe heart failure, severe renal or hepatic failure, third trimester, peri-operative CABG surgery
c.sae: GI bleeding / Cardiovascular thrombotic events / Photosensitivity
c.info: Non-acidic prodrug converted in the liver to 6-methoxy-2-naphthylacetic acid (6-MNA), which preferentially inhibits COX-2. The 6-MNA half-life of about 24 h allows once-daily dosing.
c.caution: Take with food (increases absorption) once daily; usual dose 1000 mg/day, up to 2000 mg. Avoid strong sun exposure.
c.preg: Avoid from 20 weeks (risk of fetal kidney dysfunction and low amniotic fluid) and in the third trimester (premature closure of the ductus arteriosus, bleeding, prolonged labor); earlier in pregnancy use only if clearly needed, at the lowest dose for the shortest time. Limited breast-milk data; prefer ibuprofen while breastfeeding.
c.renal: NSAIDs lower renal prostaglandins and can cause acute kidney injury, fluid retention and hyperkalemia — avoid in severe renal impairment (CrCl below 30 mL/min), and be careful with dehydration, diuretics and ACE inhibitors/ARBs. In moderate impairment (CrCl 30–49 mL/min) start at 750 mg/day; in severe impairment (CrCl below 30) start at 500 mg/day. Use caution in hepatic impairment.

ind: Osteoarthritis, rheumatoid arthritis, juvenile arthritis and ankylosing spondylitis.
ae: Dyspepsia, nausea, diarrhea, abdominal pain, headache, edema, anemia
c.doc: Once-daily arthritis therapy; lower GI toxicity than non-selective NSAIDs at the 7.5 mg dose
c.ci: Active peptic ulcer or GI bleeding, NSAID/aspirin-induced asthma or urticaria, severe heart failure, severe renal or hepatic failure, third trimester, peri-operative CABG surgery
c.sae: GI bleeding / Cardiovascular thrombotic events / Acute kidney injury
c.info: Oxicam with preferential COX-2 inhibition at 7.5 mg that fades at 15 mg; long half-life (about 20 h) allows once-daily dosing.
c.caution: Take once daily with food; maximum 15 mg/day. Shake the oral suspension well. Use the lowest effective dose.
c.preg: Avoid from 20 weeks (risk of fetal kidney dysfunction and low amniotic fluid) and in the third trimester (premature closure of the ductus arteriosus, bleeding, prolonged labor); earlier in pregnancy use only if clearly needed, at the lowest dose for the shortest time. Limited breast-milk data; prefer ibuprofen while breastfeeding.
c.renal: NSAIDs lower renal prostaglandins and can cause acute kidney injury, fluid retention and hyperkalemia — avoid in severe renal impairment (CrCl below 30 mL/min), and be careful with dehydration, diuretics and ACE inhibitors/ARBs. Maximum 7.5 mg/day in hemodialysis patients. Use caution in mild–moderate hepatic impairment.

c.mn:
💊 Names: 'NEMN': Nimesulide, Etodolac, Meloxicam, Nabumetone.
🎯 Used for: Arthritis and pain with somewhat less stomach irritation than non-selective NSAIDs.
💡 Tip: 'Preferential' means COX-2 is favoured at low doses but not exclusively. Nimesulide can injure the liver; Nabumetone is a prodrug.

ind: Osteoarthritis, rheumatoid arthritis, ankylosing spondylitis, juvenile arthritis, acute pain and primary dysmenorrhea.
ae: Dyspepsia, abdominal pain, diarrhea, headache, peripheral edema, hypertension, upper respiratory tract infection
c.doc: Arthritis in patients at high GI-bleeding risk (with a PPI when the risk is high); no antiplatelet effect
c.ci: Sulfonamide allergy; Established ischemic heart disease, stroke, peripheral arterial disease or heart failure (NYHA II–IV); active peptic ulcer or GI bleeding; peri-operative CABG surgery; severe renal or hepatic failure; third trimester
c.sae: Cardiovascular thrombotic events (MI, stroke) / Serious skin reactions (SJS/TEN, DRESS) / GI bleeding
c.info: Diaryl-substituted pyrazole with a sulfonamide group that selectively inhibits COX-2 (about 10–20-fold). It spares platelet thromboxane, so it gives no cardiac protection and aspirin is still needed if indicated. Metabolised by CYP2C9.
c.caution: Take with food; capsule contents can be sprinkled on applesauce. Avoid in sulfonamide allergy. Halve the dose in known CYP2C9 poor metabolisers. Use the lowest effective dose for the shortest time.
c.preg: Avoid from 20 weeks (risk of fetal kidney dysfunction and low amniotic fluid) and in the third trimester (premature closure of the ductus arteriosus, bleeding, prolonged labor); earlier in pregnancy use only if clearly needed, at the lowest dose for the shortest time. Very low levels in breast milk; considered acceptable while breastfeeding.
c.renal: NSAIDs lower renal prostaglandins and can cause acute kidney injury, fluid retention and hyperkalemia — avoid in severe renal impairment (CrCl below 30 mL/min), and be careful with dehydration, diuretics and ACE inhibitors/ARBs. Reduce the dose by about 50% in moderate hepatic impairment (Child-Pugh B); avoid in severe impairment.

ind: Historical: osteoarthritis, rheumatoid arthritis, acute pain and dysmenorrhea; withdrawn worldwide in 2004.
ae: Dyspepsia, edema, hypertension, diarrhea, nausea
c.doc: Obsolete / Withdrawn
c.ci: Withdrawn — do not use; any cardiovascular disease
c.sae: Myocardial infarction and stroke
c.info: Highly selective COX-2 inhibitor withdrawn by Merck in September 2004 after the APPROVe trial showed about double the risk of MI and stroke with long-term use. It suppressed vascular prostacyclin while sparing platelet thromboxane, tipping the balance toward clotting.
c.caution: Withdrawn from clinical use worldwide — do not dispense; retained for historical reference only.
c.preg: Withdrawn; no current use. NSAIDs as a class are avoided from 20 weeks of pregnancy and in the third trimester.
c.renal: Withdrawn; no current use. As a class, coxibs cause fluid retention, hypertension and reduced renal function, so they are avoided in advanced renal disease.

ind: Historical: osteoarthritis, rheumatoid arthritis and dysmenorrhea; withdrawn in 2005.
ae: Dyspepsia, abdominal pain, nausea, headache, edema, hypertension
c.doc: Obsolete / Withdrawn
c.ci: Withdrawn — do not use; sulfonamide allergy, cardiovascular disease
c.sae: Stevens-Johnson syndrome / Toxic epidermal necrolysis / Myocardial infarction
c.info: Selective COX-2 inhibitor with a sulfonamide group, withdrawn in April 2005 at the FDA's request because of serious skin reactions and increased cardiovascular events, particularly after CABG surgery. It is the active metabolite of parecoxib.
c.caution: Withdrawn from clinical use — do not dispense; retained for historical reference only.
c.preg: Withdrawn; no current use. NSAIDs as a class are avoided from 20 weeks of pregnancy and in the third trimester.
c.renal: Withdrawn; no current use. As a class, coxibs cause fluid retention and hypertension and are avoided in advanced renal disease.

ind: Osteoarthritis, rheumatoid arthritis, ankylosing spondylitis, acute gout, acute dental and postoperative pain, dysmenorrhea.
ae: Dyspepsia, edema, hypertension, dizziness, headache, raised ALT/AST
c.doc: Acute gout (120 mg once daily for at most 8 days); ankylosing spondylitis; not FDA-approved
c.ci: Uncontrolled hypertension; Established ischemic heart disease, stroke, peripheral arterial disease or heart failure (NYHA II–IV); active peptic ulcer or GI bleeding; peri-operative CABG surgery; severe renal or hepatic failure; third trimester; breastfeeding
c.sae: Cardiovascular thrombotic events / Hypertensive crisis / GI bleeding
c.info: Highly selective COX-2 inhibitor (about 100-fold) with a long half-life (~22 h) allowing once-daily dosing; metabolised by CYP3A4. Widely used in Europe and Asia but not approved by the US FDA. Monitor blood pressure.
c.caution: Once daily with or without food (food delays onset). Maximum 60 mg for osteoarthritis, 90 mg for rheumatoid arthritis and ankylosing spondylitis, 120 mg for acute gout (up to 8 days). Check blood pressure before and during treatment.
c.preg: Avoid from 20 weeks (risk of fetal kidney dysfunction and low amniotic fluid) and in the third trimester (premature closure of the ductus arteriosus, bleeding, prolonged labor); earlier in pregnancy use only if clearly needed, at the lowest dose for the shortest time. Present in breast milk in animal studies; breastfeeding is not recommended.
c.renal: NSAIDs lower renal prostaglandins and can cause acute kidney injury, fluid retention and hyperkalemia — avoid in severe renal impairment (CrCl below 30 mL/min), and be careful with dehydration, diuretics and ACE inhibitors/ARBs. Contraindicated with CrCl below 30 mL/min. Limit to 60 mg every other day in mild hepatic impairment and 30 mg daily in moderate impairment; avoid in severe impairment.

ind: Short-term perioperative pain management when oral medication is not possible.
ae: Nausea, hypertension or hypotension, back pain, peripheral edema, postoperative anemia, dizziness
c.doc: Postoperative analgesia by IV or IM injection (not after CABG surgery)
c.ci: Sulfonamide allergy; Established ischemic heart disease, stroke, peripheral arterial disease or heart failure (NYHA II–IV); active peptic ulcer or GI bleeding; peri-operative CABG surgery; severe renal or hepatic failure; third trimester
c.sae: Serious skin reactions (SJS/TEN) / Cardiovascular thrombotic events / GI bleeding
c.info: Water-soluble prodrug rapidly hydrolysed in the liver to valdecoxib; the only injectable selective COX-2 inhibitor, with onset in 7–14 minutes. Approved in Europe, Asia and Australia but not by the US FDA.
c.caution: Reconstitute with 0.9% saline, 5% dextrose or sterile water — not with lactated Ringer's or dextrose-saline. Give as an IV bolus over at least 15 seconds or a deep IM injection. Usual dose 40 mg then 20–40 mg every 6–12 h, maximum 80 mg/day; limit to about 3 days. Stop at the first skin rash.
c.preg: Avoid from 20 weeks (risk of fetal kidney dysfunction and low amniotic fluid) and in the third trimester (premature closure of the ductus arteriosus, bleeding, prolonged labor); earlier in pregnancy use only if clearly needed, at the lowest dose for the shortest time. Its active metabolite valdecoxib passes into breast milk; avoid while breastfeeding.
c.renal: NSAIDs lower renal prostaglandins and can cause acute kidney injury, fluid retention and hyperkalemia — avoid in severe renal impairment (CrCl below 30 mL/min), and be careful with dehydration, diuretics and ACE inhibitors/ARBs. Reduce the dose (maximum 40 mg/day) in severe renal impairment; do not use in severe hepatic impairment.

c.mn:
💊 Names: All end in '-coxib': Celecoxib, Rofecoxib, Valdecoxib, Etoricoxib, Parecoxib.
🎯 Used for: Arthritis and pain in patients who need less stomach bleeding; Parecoxib is the injection.
💡 Tip: They spare platelets, so no heart protection and higher clot risk. Rofecoxib (heart attacks) and Valdecoxib (severe skin reactions) were withdrawn. Celecoxib, valdecoxib and parecoxib contain a sulfonamide group.

c.t: 4. Analgesic-Antipyretics with Weak Anti-Inflammatory Action (formerly called "COX-3 inhibitors")

c.st: Tab 500, 650 mg, 1 g · Susp 120, 250 mg/5 mL · Supp 80–1000 mg · Inj 10 mg/mL
ind: Mild-to-moderate pain, fever and headache, including post-vaccination fever; IV for postoperative pain and fever.
ae: Well tolerated at recommended doses; occasional nausea, rash; raised liver enzymes with prolonged high dosing
c.dose: Tab 500, 650 mg, 1 g · Susp 120, 250 mg/5 mL · Supp 80–1000 mg · Inj 10 mg/mL
c.doc: First-line analgesic and antipyretic, including in pregnancy, children and patients who cannot take NSAIDs; IV for perioperative use
c.ci: Severe hepatic impairment or decompensated liver disease, paracetamol hypersensitivity
c.sci: Chronic alcohol use, malnutrition or low body weight (higher liver-toxicity risk)
c.sae: Acute liver failure (overdose) / Rare severe skin reactions (SJS/TEN)
c.info: Analgesic-antipyretic with only weak anti-inflammatory action; acts mainly centrally (COX inhibition in low-peroxide environments, plus serotonergic and endocannabinoid pathways). Metabolised by glucuronidation and sulfation; a minor CYP2E1 pathway forms toxic NAPQI, normally detoxified by glutathione. In overdose glutathione is depleted and liver failure follows. Antidote is N-acetylcysteine, best started within 8–10 h.
c.caution: Adults 500 mg–1 g every 4–6 h, maximum 4 g/day (3 g/day or less with chronic alcohol use, malnutrition or low weight). Children 10–15 mg/kg every 4–6 h, maximum 60 mg/kg/day. Check combination cold and flu products to avoid double dosing. Overdose is an emergency even if the person feels well — seek urgent care.

ind: Major depression, generalized anxiety disorder, social anxiety disorder, panic disorder.

ind: Depression, especially with anxiety, agitation or insomnia.
ae: Drowsiness, dizziness, weight gain, dry mouth, dizziness on standing

ind: Major depression; insomnia and anxiety (off-label, low dose).
ae: Drowsiness, dizziness on standing, dry mouth, headache, blurred vision, nausea
c.doc: Sedating antidepressant; widely used at low doses (25–100 mg) for sleep

c.sci: Priapism history / QT prolongation / Bipolar disorder
c.sae: Priapism (seek emergency care for erection over 4 hours) / QT prolongation and arrhythmia / Serotonin syndrome / Suicidal thoughts in young people
c.info: Serotonin antagonist and reuptake inhibitor (SARI) that blocks 5-HT2A, H1 and alpha-1 receptors, giving a sedating profile with little anticholinergic effect. Metabolised by CYP3A4 to mCPP.
c.caution: Take after food, with the main dose at night. Rise slowly (orthostatic hypotension). Stop and seek emergency care for an erection lasting more than 4 hours. Avoid alcohol.
c.preg: Limited data; use only if needed. Small amounts pass into breast milk; usually compatible at usual doses.
c.renal: No adjustment for mild renal impairment; use caution and lower doses in severe renal or hepatic impairment.

ind: Major depression, seasonal affective disorder prevention, smoking cessation.

c.doc: Activating antidepressant without sexual dysfunction or weight gain; also used for smoking cessation

c.info: Norepinephrine and dopamine reuptake inhibitor (and nicotinic antagonist). Strong CYP2D6 inhibitor. Seizure risk rises above 450 mg/day (IR 150 mg per dose, SR 200 mg, XL 450 mg).
c.caution: Take in the morning (insomnia). Do not crush or chew SR/XL tablets. Do not exceed the maximum single and daily doses. Avoid heavy alcohol use. Smoking cessation: start 1–2 weeks before the quit date.

c.renal: Reduce the dose or frequency in renal impairment (metabolites accumulate); in severe hepatic impairment (Child-Pugh C) maximum 150 mg every other day.

ind: Major depression, especially with insomnia, anxiety or reduced appetite.
ae: Drowsiness, increased appetite, weight gain, dry mouth, dizziness, constipation
c.doc: Sedating antidepressant with appetite stimulation; minimal sexual side effects
c.ci: MAO inhibitors, or within 14 days of stopping one (5 weeks after fluoxetine); hypersensitivity
c.sae: Agranulocytosis (rare) / Serotonin syndrome / Suicidal thoughts in young people / Raised cholesterol
c.info: Noradrenergic and specific serotonergic antidepressant (NaSSA): blocks alpha-2, 5-HT2, 5-HT3 and H1 receptors. Sedation is greater at lower doses (7.5–15 mg) and lessens at higher doses.

c.preg: Limited data; may be used when needed. Small amounts pass into breast milk; generally compatible with monitoring of infant sedation.
c.renal: Clearance falls about 30% in moderate and 50% in severe renal impairment, and in hepatic impairment — use lower doses.

ind: Major depression (Europe and elsewhere).
ae: Insomnia, sweating, dry mouth, constipation, fast heartbeat, dizziness, urinary hesitancy
c.doc: Selective noradrenaline reuptake inhibitor; not available in the US

c.preg: Limited data; avoid unless essential. Passes into breast milk; avoid.

ind: Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (children, adolescents and adults).

ind: Major depression.

ind: Glaucoma, acute mountain sickness, epilepsy (adjunct), periodic paralysis, idiopathic intracranial hypertension, edema of heart failure, metabolic alkalosis.
ae: Tingling of fingers and toes, taste changes (carbonated drinks taste flat), increased urination, fatigue, drowsiness, nausea, metabolic acidosis
c.dose: Tab 125, 250 mg · ER cap 500 mg · Inj 500 mg
c.doc: Prevention and treatment of altitude sickness (125–250 mg twice daily, start the day before ascent); glaucoma; idiopathic intracranial hypertension; metabolic alkalosis
c.ci: Sulfonamide allergy, hyponatremia or hypokalemia, hyperchloremic acidosis, severe renal or hepatic impairment (risk of hepatic coma), adrenal failure
c.sae: Severe metabolic acidosis / Stevens-Johnson syndrome or TEN / Aplastic anemia or agranulocytosis / Kidney stones
c.info: Carbonic anhydrase inhibitor (non-antibacterial sulfonamide) that blocks bicarbonate reabsorption in the proximal tubule, causing a mild self-limiting diuresis and metabolic acidosis; also lowers aqueous humor and CSF production.
c.caution: Drink plenty of fluids to reduce kidney stone risk; swallow ER capsules whole. Stop at the first rash. Monitor electrolytes and bicarbonate on longer use. High-dose aspirin can cause toxicity (lower clearance, acidosis).
c.preg: Avoid in the first trimester (limb defects in animal studies); use later only if clearly needed. Small amounts pass into breast milk; usually compatible.
c.renal: Avoid when CrCl is below 10 mL/min; lengthen the interval (for example every 12 h) when CrCl is 10–50 mL/min. Avoid in severe hepatic impairment (hepatic coma).

ind: Primary hyperkalemic and hypokalemic periodic paralysis; glaucoma (historical).
ae: Tingling, cognitive slowing, taste changes, fatigue, metabolic acidosis, hypokalemia
c.doc: Treatment of primary periodic paralysis (reduces attacks of weakness); glaucoma use is historical
c.ci: Hepatic insufficiency, severe pulmonary obstruction with respiratory acidosis, sulfonamide allergy, hypokalemia
c.sae: Severe metabolic acidosis / Stevens-Johnson syndrome or TEN / Aplastic anemia or agranulocytosis / Kidney stones / Hypokalemia
c.info: Carbonic anhydrase inhibitor with stronger potassium-wasting action than acetazolamide; it lowers attack frequency in periodic paralysis. Dosing is individualized; check availability, as brands and indications vary.
c.caution: Titrate with periodic checks of potassium and bicarbonate. Tell doctors if cognitive symptoms or tingling occur. Avoid high-dose aspirin.
c.preg: Limited data; use only if clearly needed (animal studies suggest fetal harm). Breastfeeding data are lacking.
c.renal: Use caution in renal impairment (dose reduction may be needed); avoid in hepatic insufficiency.

ind: Chronic open-angle glaucoma; secondary glaucoma; pre-operative lowering of intraocular pressure.
ae: Tingling, fatigue, drowsiness, taste changes, nausea, increased urination
c.doc: Oral glaucoma therapy with fewer renal and electrolyte effects than acetazolamide
c.ci: Sulfonamide allergy, hyponatremia or hypokalemia, hyperchloremic acidosis, severe renal or hepatic impairment (risk of hepatic coma), adrenal failure
c.sae: Severe metabolic acidosis / Stevens-Johnson syndrome or TEN / Aplastic anemia or agranulocytosis / Kidney stones
c.info: Lipophilic carbonic anhydrase inhibitor with a longer half-life (about 14 h) and better tissue penetration than acetazolamide, so it is dosed less often and causes less systemic acidosis and diuresis.
c.caution: Usual dose 50–100 mg two to three times daily. Stop at the first rash. Drink fluids to reduce stone risk. Monitor electrolytes and blood counts on longer use.
c.preg: Avoid in pregnancy unless essential (animal teratogenicity); limited breastfeeding data.
c.renal: Use caution and lower doses in renal impairment; avoid in severe renal or hepatic impairment.

ind: Open-angle glaucoma and ocular hypertension (topical).
ae: Stinging or burning on instillation, bitter taste, blurred vision, eye redness and itching
c.doc: Topical glaucoma therapy alone (three times daily) or with timolol (twice daily, fixed combination)
c.ci: Sulfonamide allergy, severe renal impairment (CrCl below 30 mL/min), hyperchloremic acidosis
c.sae: Corneal edema in patients with endothelial disease / Stevens-Johnson syndrome (rare) / Systemic carbonic anhydrase inhibitor effects
c.info: Topical carbonic anhydrase II inhibitor that reduces aqueous humor secretion. It is not a diuretic in practice because systemic absorption is low, but it belongs to the class.
c.caution: Remove soft contact lenses before use (contains benzalkonium chloride) and wait 15 minutes before reinserting. Space other eye drops by 10 minutes. Keep the bottle from touching the eye.

c.renal: Lose effect as eGFR falls below about 30 mL/min (chlorthalidone, indapamide and metolazone keep some effect). Use caution in hepatic impairment — electrolyte shifts can trigger encephalopathy.

ind: Hypertension, edema, nephrolithiasis prevention; also used in chronic kidney disease.
ae: Hypokalemia, hyponatremia, hyperuricemia, dizziness, hyperglycemia, raised cholesterol, photosensitivity, erectile dysfunction
c.doc: Preferred thiazide-like agent for hypertension (ALLHAT); long-acting; effective in advanced CKD (CLICK trial)
c.ci: Anuria, severe renal impairment, sulfonamide allergy, uncorrected hypokalemia, hyponatremia or hypercalcemia, symptomatic gout, severe hepatic impairment
c.sae: Severe hyponatremia / Hypokalemia and arrhythmias / Acute angle-closure glaucoma or myopia / Pancreatitis
c.info: Thiazide-like diuretic (not a true thiazide) with a long half-life (40–60 h), so it gives smoother 24-hour blood-pressure control and retains effect at lower GFR than hydrochlorothiazide. More potent per milligram, with more hypokalemia.
c.caution: Take in the morning to avoid night-time urination. Check potassium, sodium, glucose and uric acid at the start and periodically; protect skin from sun. Stop during vomiting or diarrhea (dehydration, kidney injury). Usual 12.5–25 mg once daily; monitor potassium closely.
c.preg: Not first-line in pregnancy; avoid for hypertension or ankle swelling unless essential (volume contraction, neonatal electrolyte disturbances, thrombocytopenia, jaundice). Passes into breast milk in small amounts and high doses may suppress lactation; low doses are usually acceptable.
c.renal: Retains effect in CKD stage 4 (shown in CLICK trial) but monitor electrolytes and creatinine closely; use caution in hepatic impairment.

c.ci: Anuria, severe renal impairment, sulfonamide allergy, uncorrected hypokalemia, hyponatremia or hypercalcemia, symptomatic gout, severe hepatic impairment
c.sae: Severe hyponatremia / Hypokalemia and arrhythmias / Acute angle-closure glaucoma or myopia / Pancreatitis
c.info: Sulfonamide thiazide-like diuretic with a loop-like effect at higher doses (about 40 mg) and a duration of 12–24 h. Often effective when GFR is reduced.
c.caution: Take in the morning to avoid night-time urination. Check potassium, sodium, glucose and uric acid at the start and periodically; protect skin from sun. Stop during vomiting or diarrhea (dehydration, kidney injury).

ind: Edema of heart failure and renal disease (including CKD); hypertension; synergy with loop diuretics in resistant edema.

c.ci: Anuria, severe renal impairment, sulfonamide allergy, uncorrected hypokalemia, hyponatremia or hypercalcemia, symptomatic gout, severe hepatic impairment; hepatic coma
c.sae: Severe hyponatremia / Hypokalemia and arrhythmias / Acute angle-closure glaucoma or myopia / Pancreatitis / Severe hypokalemia and hyponatremia with loop combinations
c.info: Thiazide-like diuretic (quinazoline) that keeps working at low GFR and synergizes with loop diuretics. Its different formulations (slow-release versus rapid-acting) are not interchangeable.
c.caution: Start at 2.5–5 mg once daily, often 30 minutes before the loop dose. Check potassium, sodium and creatinine within 2–3 days and frequently after. Do not interchange brands.

c.st: Tab 20, 40, 80 mg · Inj 10 mg/mL · Oral soln 10 mg/mL
ind: Edema (heart failure, cirrhosis, renal disease), acute pulmonary edema, hypertension, hypercalcemia.
ae: Hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia, hyponatremia, dehydration, low blood pressure, dizziness, hyperuricemia, muscle cramps
c.dose: Tab 20, 40, 80 mg · Inj 10 mg/mL · Oral soln 10 mg/mL
c.doc: Pulmonary edema (IV 20–40 mg); heart failure and ascites; hypercalcemia; resistant hypertension with CKD
c.ci: Anuria, severe hypovolemia or electrolyte depletion (hypokalemia, hyponatremia), hepatic coma, hypersensitivity to the drug or sulfonamides
c.sae: Profound volume depletion and hypotension / Arrhythmia from hypokalemia / Ototoxicity (high-dose rapid IV) / Acute kidney injury
c.info: Prototype loop diuretic that blocks the Na-K-2Cl cotransporter in the thick ascending limb; onset 30–60 min orally (5–10 min IV), duration 6–8 h. Oral bioavailability is variable (about 50%).
c.caution: Take in the morning (second dose early afternoon). Weigh daily and check potassium, magnesium and creatinine. Give IV doses slowly (furosemide no faster than 4 mg/min) to avoid ototoxicity. Avoid with aminoglycosides and NSAIDs. Switch to torsemide or IV when gut edema limits absorption.
c.preg: Use only for clear indications such as heart failure or pulmonary edema; do not use routinely for pregnancy swelling or hypertension (fetal diuresis, reduced placental perfusion). May suppress lactation; small amounts in milk.
c.renal: Higher doses are needed as GFR falls (tubular secretion is reduced); effective even in severe renal impairment. Use caution in cirrhosis — rapid diuresis can precipitate encephalopathy and hepatorenal syndrome.

ind: Heart failure with reduced ejection fraction, resistant hypertension, primary hyperaldosteronism, ascites in cirrhosis, nephrotic edema; acne and hirsutism in women (off-label).
ae: Gynecomastia and breast tenderness, menstrual irregularity, hyperkalemia, dizziness, nausea
c.doc: Mortality benefit in heart failure (RALES); resistant hypertension; ascites with cirrhosis; primary aldosteronism
c.ci: Hyperkalemia (potassium above about 5.0–5.5 mmol/L), severe renal impairment or anuria, Addison disease, concurrent potassium supplements or other potassium-sparing agents
c.sae: Life-threatening hyperkalemia / Hyponatremia / Acute kidney injury (with NSAIDs, ACE inhibitors, ARBs)
c.info: Competitive aldosterone receptor antagonist (prodrug with active metabolites including canrenone); onset is slow (days) and half-life of the active metabolites is long. Its antiandrogen and progestogen effects explain gynecomastia and menstrual changes.
c.caution: Check potassium and creatinine within the first week, at 4 weeks, then regularly. Avoid potassium supplements, salt substitutes and NSAIDs. Hold during dehydration or vomiting. Gynecomastia is dose-related; switch to eplerenone if troublesome.
c.preg: Avoid in pregnancy (antiandrogenic effects, risk of feminization of a male fetus in animals). Canrenone passes into breast milk in small amounts; usually acceptable.
c.renal: Avoid when eGFR is below 30 mL/min or potassium above 5.0; monitor potassium and creatinine closely in CKD; use caution in cirrhosis.

ind: Edema and ascites, heart failure and primary hyperaldosteronism when oral therapy is not possible.
ae: Hyperkalemia, gynecomastia, menstrual irregularity, injection-site irritation, dizziness
c.doc: IV aldosterone antagonist used in parts of Europe when oral spironolactone is not feasible
c.ci: Hyperkalemia (potassium above about 5.0–5.5 mmol/L), severe renal impairment or anuria, Addison disease, concurrent potassium supplements or other potassium-sparing agents
c.sae: Life-threatening hyperkalemia / Hyponatremia / Acute kidney injury (with NSAIDs, ACE inhibitors, ARBs)
c.info: Prodrug that is converted to canrenone, the active metabolite of spironolactone. Available mainly in some European countries as an IV formulation.
c.caution: Check potassium and creatinine within the first week, at 4 weeks, then regularly. Avoid potassium supplements, salt substitutes and NSAIDs. Hold during dehydration or vomiting. Infuse slowly and avoid extravasation.
c.preg: Avoid in pregnancy (antiandrogenic effects). Canrenone passes into breast milk; use caution.
c.renal: Avoid when eGFR is below 30 mL/min or potassium is high; monitor closely.

ind: Heart failure after myocardial infarction (LVEF 40% or lower), heart failure with reduced ejection fraction, hypertension.
ae: Hyperkalemia, dizziness, diarrhea, raised cholesterol or triglycerides, fatigue
c.doc: Selective aldosterone antagonist with fewer hormonal side effects than spironolactone; survival benefit post-MI (EPHESUS)
c.ci: Hyperkalemia (potassium above about 5.0–5.5 mmol/L), severe renal impairment or anuria, Addison disease, concurrent potassium supplements or other potassium-sparing agents; strong CYP3A4 inhibitors (ketoconazole, itraconazole, clarithromycin)
c.sae: Life-threatening hyperkalemia / Hyponatremia / Acute kidney injury (with NSAIDs, ACE inhibitors, ARBs)
c.info: Selective mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist with little antiandrogen or progestogen effect, so gynecomastia is rare. Metabolised by CYP3A4; half-life 4–6 h.
c.caution: Check potassium and creatinine within the first week, at 4 weeks, then regularly. Avoid potassium supplements, salt substitutes and NSAIDs. Hold during dehydration or vomiting. Typical 25 mg daily, rising to 50 mg. Avoid strong CYP3A4 inhibitors; reduce dose with moderate inhibitors.
c.preg: Limited human data; avoid in pregnancy unless essential. Excretion into breast milk unknown; use caution.
c.renal: Contraindicated for hypertension when CrCl is below 50 mL/min and for all uses when CrCl is below 30 mL/min or potassium above 5.5; use caution in hepatic impairment.

ind: Chronic kidney disease with type 2 diabetes (reduces kidney function decline, cardiovascular death and heart-failure hospitalization); heart failure with LVEF 40% or higher in some regions.
ae: Hyperkalemia, low blood pressure, hyponatremia, drop in eGFR initially
c.doc: Nonsteroidal mineralocorticoid antagonist for diabetic kidney disease (FIDELIO-DKD, FIGARO-DKD); added to ACE inhibitor or ARB therapy
c.ci: Addison disease, concurrent strong CYP3A4 inhibitors, hyperkalemia (potassium above 5.0 at start), eGFR below 25 mL/min/1.73 m² (do not start)
c.sae: Life-threatening hyperkalemia / Acute kidney injury
c.info: Nonsteroidal, selective mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist with balanced distribution in heart and kidney, causing less hyperkalemia and fewer hormonal effects than steroidal agents. Not a strong diuretic; its benefit is organ protection.
c.caution: Start 10 mg daily (eGFR 25–<60) or 20 mg (eGFR 60 or above); check potassium and eGFR at 4 weeks and adjust. Avoid grapefruit and strong CYP3A4 inhibitors. Avoid potassium supplements and salt substitutes.
c.preg: Not recommended in pregnancy (animal toxicity); contraception advised. Excreted in animal milk; avoid while breastfeeding.
c.renal: Do not start when eGFR is below 25; pause if potassium exceeds 5.5 and resume at a lower dose when below 5.0. Avoid in severe hepatic impairment (Child-Pugh C); reduce in moderate impairment.
