ind: Edema and hypertension (usually with a thiazide to prevent potassium loss).
ae: Hyperkalemia, nausea, leg cramps, dizziness, blue fluorescent urine, folate deficiency
c.doc: Potassium-sparing diuretic usually combined with hydrochlorothiazide
c.ci: Hyperkalemia (potassium above about 5.0–5.5 mmol/L), severe renal impairment or anuria, Addison disease, concurrent potassium supplements or other potassium-sparing agents
c.sae: Life-threatening hyperkalemia / Hyponatremia / Acute kidney injury (with NSAIDs, ACE inhibitors, ARBs) / Kidney stones / Megaloblastic anemia (folate antagonism)
c.info: Directly blocks the epithelial sodium channel (ENaC) in the collecting duct; not an aldosterone antagonist. Short half-life (2–4 h) with active sulfate metabolite; can cause crystalluria.
c.caution: Check potassium and creatinine within the first week, at 4 weeks, then regularly. Avoid potassium supplements, salt substitutes and NSAIDs. Hold during dehydration or vomiting. Urine may turn blue. Take with food. Avoid NSAIDs (acute kidney injury).
c.preg: Folate antagonist; avoid in pregnancy unless essential. Small amounts in breast milk; use caution.
c.renal: Contraindicated in severe renal impairment, anuria and hyperkalemia; use caution in hepatic impairment (folate).

ind: Adjunct to thiazide or loop diuretics in heart failure and hypertension to prevent hypokalemia; lithium-induced nephrogenic diabetes insipidus; hypokalemia.
ae: Hyperkalemia, nausea, loss of appetite, headache, muscle cramps, weakness
c.doc: Potassium-sparing diuretic used with thiazides or loops; lithium-induced nephrogenic DI
c.ci: Hyperkalemia (potassium above about 5.0–5.5 mmol/L), severe renal impairment or anuria, Addison disease, concurrent potassium supplements or other potassium-sparing agents
c.sae: Life-threatening hyperkalemia / Hyponatremia / Acute kidney injury (with NSAIDs, ACE inhibitors, ARBs)
c.info: Blocks ENaC in the collecting duct, reducing sodium reabsorption and potassium secretion; weak diuretic by itself. Half-life 6–9 h; excreted unchanged by the kidney.
c.caution: Check potassium and creatinine within the first week, at 4 weeks, then regularly. Avoid potassium supplements, salt substitutes and NSAIDs. Hold during dehydration or vomiting. Take with food. Hold during acute illness.
c.preg: Limited data; use only if clearly needed. Excretion into breast milk is unknown; avoid.
c.renal: Contraindicated in renal failure and when potassium is above 5.5; reduce dose in mild–moderate impairment; use caution in hepatic impairment.

c.mn:
💊 Names: Triamterene and Amiloride ('TA' — block ENaC channels).
🎯 Used for: Adding to thiazides or loops to prevent low potassium.
💡 Tip: Both can cause hyperkalemia; triamterene turns urine blue and lowers folate.

ind: Oral: hyponatremia of SIADH; IV (historical): reduction of raised intracranial or intraocular pressure.
ae: Nausea, vomiting, headache, unpleasant taste, thirst, hypernatremia
c.st: Oral powder (15–30 g sachets) · Inj 40 g (historical)
c.dose: Oral powder (15–30 g sachets) · Inj 40 g (historical)
c.doc: Oral osmotic agent for SIADH-related hyponatremia; IV use for brain or eye pressure is largely replaced by mannitol
c.ci: Severe renal impairment (oliguria), severe liver failure, active intracranial bleeding (IV)
c.sae: Pulmonary edema from fluid shift / Hyperosmolar state / Hypernatremia / Acute kidney injury / Tissue necrosis with extravasation (IV)
c.info: Osmotic diuretic filtered by the glomerulus and poorly reabsorbed, so it holds water in the tubule. Oral urea increases free-water excretion and raises serum sodium in SIADH.
c.caution: Oral: dissolve in water, juice or flavored drink to mask the taste; monitor sodium. IV: avoid extravasation. Not for severe renal impairment.
c.preg: Limited data; use only if clearly needed. Safety in breastfeeding is not established.
c.renal: Avoid in severe renal impairment (accumulation, azotemia); use caution in liver failure (ammonia handling).

ind: Reduction of raised intraocular pressure (acute glaucoma, pre-operative) and raised intracranial pressure.
ae: Nausea, vomiting, headache, thirst, dizziness
c.doc: Short-term oral osmotic agent to lower eye pressure before surgery or in acute glaucoma
c.ci: Anuria, severe dehydration, severe cardiac decompensation, hypersensitivity
c.sae: Severe dehydration and hyperosmolar state / Hyperglycemia in diabetes / Confusion
c.info: Oral osmotic agent (glycerol) absorbed and metabolised to glucose, which draws fluid from the eye and brain; effect within 30–90 minutes and lasting about 5–6 hours.
c.caution: Chill and serve over ice to reduce nausea; do not give with a large amount of fluid in cardiac patients. Monitor blood glucose in diabetes (about 4 kcal/g).
c.preg: Limited data; avoid unless essential. Breastfeeding data are limited.
c.renal: Use caution in renal impairment; avoid in anuria.

ind: Raised intracranial pressure, raised intraocular pressure, oliguria in acute renal failure (limited role), promotion of urinary excretion of toxins.
ae: Fluid and electrolyte disturbance, headache, nausea, vomiting, thirst, rebound increase in intracranial pressure
c.doc: Rapid reduction of raised intracranial pressure or acute glaucoma pressure (0.25–1 g/kg IV over 30–60 minutes)
c.ci: Anuria, severe pulmonary congestion or edema, severe heart failure, severe dehydration, active intracranial bleeding (except craniotomy), progressive renal failure after starting
c.sae: Pulmonary edema from fluid shift / Hyperosmolar state / Hypernatremia / Acute kidney injury / Osmotic nephrosis / Tissue necrosis on extravasation
c.info: Osmotic diuretic (sugar alcohol) that is freely filtered and not reabsorbed; it expands plasma volume before diuresis, then pulls water into the urine. Must not be crystallized — warm to dissolve and use a filter for high concentrations.
c.caution: Use an in-line filter for 20–25% solutions and check for crystals. Give via a large vein; avoid extravasation. Monitor osmolality, electrolytes, urine output and fluid balance. A test dose may be used when renal function is uncertain.
c.preg: Use only if clearly needed; limited data. Breastfeeding data are limited.
c.renal: Contraindicated in anuria and progressive renal failure after starting; use with caution in renal impairment (accumulation, volume overload).

ind: Short-term reduction of intraocular pressure (pre-operative or acute glaucoma); raised intracranial pressure.
ae: Nausea, vomiting, headache, thirst, dizziness
c.doc: Oral osmotic agent for acute glaucoma and pre-operative eye pressure control; not metabolised, so it can be used in diabetes
c.ci: Anuria, severe dehydration, severe cardiac decompensation, hypersensitivity
c.sae: Severe dehydration and hyperosmolar state / Confusion
c.info: Oral osmotic agent that is not metabolised to glucose, so it is suitable in diabetic patients; distinct from isosorbide dinitrate and mononitrate used in angina.
c.caution: Serve over ice to reduce nausea; do not confuse with the nitrate isosorbide mononitrate or dinitrate. Avoid large fluid loads in cardiac disease.
c.preg: Limited data; use only if clearly needed. Breastfeeding data are limited.
c.renal: Use caution in renal impairment; avoid in anuria.

c.mn:
💊 Names: Urea, Glycerine, Mannitol, Isosorbide.
🎯 Used for: Raised intracranial or eye pressure; SIADH (oral urea).
💡 Tip: They pull water by osmosis; avoid in pulmonary edema and heart failure because they first expand blood volume.

c.t: E. Drugs Increasing GFR / Secondary Diuretics

ind: Apnea of prematurity (caffeine citrate), headache with analgesics, fatigue; weak diuretic effect.
ae: Insomnia, jitteriness, palpitations, tachycardia, nausea, headache, increased urination
c.doc: Mild diuretic effect only; mainly used for apnea of prematurity and as an analgesic adjunct
c.ci: Hypersensitivity, uncontrolled arrhythmia, severe anxiety or seizure disorder (caution)
c.sae: Arrhythmia / Seizures in overdose / Neonatal necrotizing enterocolitis (infants)
c.info: Methylxanthine that blocks adenosine receptors and inhibits phosphodiesterase, producing CNS stimulation and a mild increase in urine output and GFR. Tolerance to the diuretic effect develops with regular use.
c.caution: Limit total intake from drinks and medicines (generally under 400 mg/day for adults). Infant dosing (caffeine citrate) is weight-based with level monitoring. Avoid close to bedtime.
c.preg: Limit intake to under 200 mg/day in pregnancy (miscarriage and low birth weight risk at higher intakes). Moderate maternal intake is acceptable while breastfeeding; infants may become irritable.
c.renal: No adjustment in renal impairment; reduce the dose in significant hepatic impairment (clearance falls).

ind: Asthma and COPD (bronchodilator); apnea of prematurity; weak diuretic effect.
ae: Nausea, vomiting, headache, tremor, insomnia, palpitations, increased urination
c.doc: Mainly a bronchodilator with a minor diuretic effect; narrow therapeutic range (5–15 mcg/mL)
c.ci: Uncontrolled arrhythmia, active peptic ulcer, seizure disorder (caution), hypersensitivity
c.sae: Arrhythmia / Seizures / Toxicity at levels above 20 mcg/mL
c.info: Methylxanthine bronchodilator that inhibits phosphodiesterase and blocks adenosine receptors. Metabolised by CYP1A2 (levels fall with smoking and rise with ciprofloxacin, fluvoxamine, cimetidine, macrolides), which makes level monitoring important.
c.caution: Swallow SR products whole. Monitor serum levels and avoid sudden dose changes. Smoking, fever, heart failure and liver disease alter clearance. Do not combine with high caffeine intake.
c.preg: Crosses the placenta; use the lowest effective dose and monitor levels, since clearance changes in pregnancy. Passes into breast milk; irritability may occur in the infant.
c.renal: No adjustment for mild renal impairment; reduce the dose in heart failure, cirrhosis, and the elderly; monitor levels.

ind: Severe asthma and COPD exacerbations (IV); weak diuretic effect.
ae: Nausea, vomiting, headache, tremor, palpitations, insomnia
c.doc: IV bronchodilator for severe asthma; minor diuretic effect; narrow therapeutic range
c.ci: Uncontrolled arrhythmia, active peptic ulcer, porphyria, hypersensitivity to ethylenediamine
c.sae: Arrhythmia / Seizures / Toxicity at levels above 20 mcg/mL
c.info: Theophylline-ethylenediamine salt (about 80% theophylline) that is soluble for IV use. The same interactions and level monitoring as theophylline apply.
c.caution: Give IV loading doses slowly (no faster than 25 mg/min); omit the loading dose if the patient has had theophylline. Monitor levels, heart rate and rhythm. Do not mix with other drugs in the same bag.
c.preg: Use the lowest effective dose and monitor levels; passes into breast milk and may irritate the infant.
c.renal: No adjustment for mild renal impairment; reduce the dose in heart failure, cirrhosis and the elderly; monitor levels.

c.mn:
💊 Names: Caffeine, Theophylline, Aminophylline.
🎯 Used for: Mild diuretics, but mainly for apnea of prematurity (caffeine) and asthma (theophylline).
💡 Tip: Theophylline has a narrow therapeutic range; levels rise with ciprofloxacin and fall with smoking.

ind: Cardiogenic and septic shock, hypotension, and acute heart failure (IV infusion).
ae: Nausea, vomiting, headache, palpitations, tachycardia, chest pain, extravasation tissue injury
c.st: Inj 40 mg/mL concentrate · premixed in dextrose
c.dose: Inj 40 mg/mL concentrate · premixed in dextrose
c.doc: Vasopressor and inotrope; low-dose “renal-dose” dopamine does not prevent kidney injury
c.ci: Pheochromocytoma, uncorrected tachyarrhythmias or ventricular fibrillation, hypersensitivity to sulfites
c.sae: Arrhythmias / Severe hypertension at high doses / Tissue necrosis on extravasation / Peripheral ischemia
c.info: Catecholamine precursor of norepinephrine whose effects depend on dose: low (renal and mesenteric dilation), moderate (beta-1 inotropy), high (alpha vasoconstriction). The renal vasodilator effect has not been shown to improve outcomes.
c.caution: Give through a central line if possible, titrated by blood pressure and rate. Correct hypovolemia first. In extravasation infiltrate phentolamine promptly. Avoid with MAO inhibitors.
c.preg: Use only if clearly needed (uterine vasoconstriction at high doses). Breastfeeding data are limited; it is used in critical care.
c.renal: No renal dose adjustment; monitor urine output. Avoid reliance on low-dose dopamine to protect the kidneys.

ind: Euvolemic and hypervolemic hyponatremia in hospitalized patients.
ae: Infusion-site reactions (phlebitis), headache, thirst, hypokalemia, fever
c.doc: IV vasopressin (V1a/V2) antagonist for hospitalized patients with hyponatremia, including SIADH and heart failure
c.ci: Hypovolemic hyponatremia, concurrent strong CYP3A4 inhibitors (ketoconazole, itraconazole, clarithromycin), anuria
c.sae: Osmotic demyelination syndrome with overly rapid sodium correction / Infusion-site phlebitis
c.info: Dual V1a/V2 vasopressin receptor antagonist given IV as a 20 mg loading dose over 30 minutes then 20 mg/day by continuous infusion for 2–4 days. Causes aquaresis (water loss without sodium). Inhibits CYP3A4.
c.caution: Use only in hospital with frequent sodium checks; do not raise serum sodium by more than 12 mEq/L in 24 hours (risk of osmotic demyelination). Rotate infusion sites every 24 hours.
c.preg: Avoid in pregnancy unless essential (animal data); excretion into breast milk is unknown.
c.renal: Not effective when CrCl is below 30 mL/min; avoid in anuria; use caution in hepatic impairment.

ind: Clinically significant hypervolemic and euvolemic hyponatremia (SIADH, heart failure, cirrhosis); a separate product slows kidney function decline in ADPKD.
ae: Thirst, dry mouth, increased urination, constipation, hyperglycemia, nausea
c.doc: Oral V2 antagonist for hyponatremia, started in hospital with careful sodium monitoring
c.ci: Urgent need to raise sodium, hypovolemia, anuria, concurrent strong CYP3A4 inhibitors; for the hyponatremia product, autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease; liver injury
c.sae: Osmotic demyelination syndrome with overly rapid sodium correction / Serious liver injury / Hypernatremia
c.info: Selective V2 vasopressin receptor antagonist that blocks water reabsorption in the collecting duct (aquaresis) and raises serum sodium. CYP3A4 substrate. Limited to 30 days for hyponatremia because of liver injury.
c.caution: Start in hospital; check sodium at 6 and 24 hours; do not restrict fluids at the start and do not exceed an increase of 12 mEq/L in 24 hours. Do not use for more than 30 days for hyponatremia. Avoid grapefruit and strong CYP3A4 inhibitors. Monitor liver tests.
c.preg: Avoid in pregnancy (animal toxicity); contraindicated in some regions. Avoid while breastfeeding (unknown excretion).
c.renal: Not effective when CrCl is below 10 mL/min; no adjustment above that. Avoid in significant hepatic impairment; stop for liver injury.

c.mn:
💊 Names: Conivaptan, Tolvaptan (both '-vaptan').
🎯 Used for: Low sodium (hyponatremia) in SIADH, heart failure and cirrhosis.
💡 Tip: Remove water without sodium; correct sodium slowly to avoid osmotic demyelination. Tolvaptan can injure the liver.

c.st: Tab 0.1, 0.2 mg · Nasal 10 mcg/spray · Inj 4 mcg/mL

Tab 5, 10, 20, 25 mg · Oral soln 5 mg/5 mL

ind: Type 1 and type 2 diabetes; diabetic ketoacidosis and perioperative glucose control (IV); hyperkalemia with glucose.
ae: Hypoglycemia, weight gain, injection-site reactions or lipodystrophy, mild edema when starting, hypokalemia
c.doc: The only insulin given IV (DKA, critical illness, perioperative); mealtime insulin given about 30 min before eating; used in pregnancy
c.ci: Hypoglycemia; hypersensitivity to the insulin or its excipients
c.sae: Severe hypoglycemia / Hypokalemia / Anaphylaxis (rare)
c.info: Human insulin (recombinant) that forms hexamers at the injection site, delaying absorption: onset about 30 min, peak 2–4 h, duration 6–8 h. U-500 concentrated insulin is a different product with different dosing.
c.caution: Inject subcutaneously 30 minutes before meals; rotate sites and never share pens. Check the concentration (U-100 vs U-500) before drawing up. Hypoglycemia risk rises with exercise, alcohol and missed meals. Keep unopened insulin in the refrigerator; in-use pens or vials are kept at room temperature for the time on the label (usually 28 days).
c.preg: Insulin is the treatment of choice in pregnancy; needs usually fall in the first trimester, rise in the second and third, and drop sharply after delivery. Compatible with breastfeeding (needs may fall).
c.renal: Insulin clearance falls in renal impairment, so requirements drop — reduce doses and monitor glucose closely. Hypoglycemia risk is also higher in liver disease.

ind: Type 1 and type 2 diabetes for mealtime glucose control; insulin pump (CSII).
ae: Hypoglycemia, weight gain, injection-site reactions or lipodystrophy, mild edema when starting, hypokalemia
c.doc: Mealtime insulin injected up to 15 min before or right after a meal; pump therapy; used in pregnancy
c.ci: Hypoglycemia; hypersensitivity to the insulin or its excipients
c.sae: Severe hypoglycemia / Hypokalemia / Anaphylaxis (rare)
c.info: Rapid-acting insulin analogue (lysine and proline swapped in the B chain) that does not form hexamers, so it absorbs faster: onset 10–15 min, peak 1–2 h, duration 3–5 h. A faster formulation with added excipients also exists.
c.caution: Inject 0–15 minutes before a meal (or just after). The 200 units/mL pen must not be drawn into a syringe or diluted. Can be used in pumps; check for pump failure and ketones. Do not mix with other insulins unless the label allows (NPH only). Keep unopened insulin in the refrigerator; in-use pens or vials are kept at room temperature for the time on the label (usually 28 days).
c.preg: Insulin is the treatment of choice in pregnancy; needs usually fall in the first trimester, rise in the second and third, and drop sharply after delivery. Compatible with breastfeeding (needs may fall).
c.renal: Insulin clearance falls in renal impairment, so requirements drop — reduce doses and monitor glucose closely. Hypoglycemia risk is also higher in liver disease.

ind: Type 1 and type 2 diabetes for mealtime glucose control; insulin pump; IV use under supervision.
ae: Hypoglycemia, weight gain, injection-site reactions or lipodystrophy, mild edema when starting, hypokalemia
c.doc: Mealtime insulin analogue with good pregnancy data; pump therapy; faster-acting formulation available
c.ci: Hypoglycemia; hypersensitivity to the insulin or its excipients
c.sae: Severe hypoglycemia / Hypokalemia / Anaphylaxis (rare)
c.info: Rapid-acting analogue (aspartic acid at B28) with onset 10–20 min, peak 1–3 h, duration 3–5 h. A faster-acting formulation adds niacinamide for quicker absorption.
c.caution: Inject 0–10 minutes before a meal (or just after). Can be given via pump. Rotate sites. Do not mix with other insulins unless the label allows (NPH only). Keep unopened insulin in the refrigerator; in-use pens or vials are kept at room temperature for the time on the label (usually 28 days).
c.preg: Insulin is the treatment of choice in pregnancy; needs usually fall in the first trimester, rise in the second and third, and drop sharply after delivery. Compatible with breastfeeding (needs may fall).
c.renal: Insulin clearance falls in renal impairment, so requirements drop — reduce doses and monitor glucose closely. Hypoglycemia risk is also higher in liver disease.

ind: Type 1 and type 2 diabetes for mealtime glucose control; insulin pump.
ae: Hypoglycemia, weight gain, injection-site reactions or lipodystrophy, mild edema when starting, hypokalemia
c.doc: Rapid-acting mealtime insulin; can be given shortly before or after meals
c.ci: Hypoglycemia; hypersensitivity to the insulin or its excipients
c.sae: Severe hypoglycemia / Hypokalemia / Anaphylaxis (rare)
c.info: Rapid-acting analogue (lysine at B29, glutamic acid at B3) with onset 10–20 min, peak about 1 h, duration 3–5 h. Formulated without zinc, so it is less stable and may not be available in all markets.
c.caution: Inject within 15 minutes before or 20 minutes after starting a meal. Do not mix with any insulin other than NPH. Use a fresh reservoir and infusion set in pumps. Keep unopened insulin in the refrigerator; in-use pens or vials are kept at room temperature for the time on the label (usually 28 days).
c.preg: Limited pregnancy data compared with lispro and aspart; use only if clearly needed, since insulin needs shift across pregnancy. Compatible with breastfeeding (needs may fall).
c.renal: Insulin clearance falls in renal impairment, so requirements drop — reduce doses and monitor glucose closely. Hypoglycemia risk is also higher in liver disease.

c.mn:
💊 Names: Regular (soluble), Lispro, Aspart, Glulisine.
🎯 Used for: Mealtime glucose control; regular insulin is the only one given IV.
💡 Tip: Analogues (lispro, aspart, glulisine) work in 10–15 min — inject just before eating. Regular needs 30 min.

ind: Type 1 and type 2 diabetes for basal glucose control; steroid-induced hyperglycemia; pregnancy.
ae: Hypoglycemia, weight gain, injection-site reactions or lipodystrophy, mild edema when starting, hypokalemia
c.doc: Basal insulin twice daily or at bedtime; used in pregnancy and with corticosteroids; premixed with regular or rapid insulin
c.ci: Hypoglycemia; hypersensitivity to the insulin or its excipients
c.sci: During hypoglycemia (treat first); nocturnal hypoglycemia risk
c.sae: Severe hypoglycemia / Hypokalemia / Anaphylaxis (rare)
c.info: NPH insulin (human insulin bound to protamine and zinc), a cloudy suspension: onset 1–2 h, peak 4–8 h, duration 12–18 h. Its pronounced peak gives a higher risk of nocturnal hypoglycemia than long-acting analogues.
c.caution: Roll the vial or pen gently 10 times to resuspend (do not shake); the suspension should be uniformly cloudy. Never give IV. Can be mixed in one syringe with regular or rapid insulin (draw the clear one first). Keep unopened insulin in the refrigerator; in-use pens or vials are kept at room temperature for the time on the label (usually 28 days).
c.preg: Insulin is the treatment of choice in pregnancy; needs usually fall in the first trimester, rise in the second and third, and drop sharply after delivery. Compatible with breastfeeding (needs may fall).
c.renal: Insulin clearance falls in renal impairment, so requirements drop — reduce doses and monitor glucose closely. Hypoglycemia risk is also higher in liver disease.

ind: Type 1 and type 2 diabetes for basal glucose control (historical Lente-type insulin).
ae: Hypoglycemia, weight gain, injection-site reactions or lipodystrophy, mild edema when starting, hypokalemia
c.doc: Historical intermediate insulin, largely withdrawn in favor of NPH and analogues
c.ci: Hypoglycemia; hypersensitivity to the insulin or its excipients
c.sci: During hypoglycemia (treat first); nocturnal hypoglycemia risk
c.sae: Severe hypoglycemia / Hypokalemia / Anaphylaxis (rare)
c.info: Lente-type insulin zinc suspension (mixture of amorphous and crystalline zinc insulin): onset 1–3 h, peak 6–12 h, duration 18–24 h. Discontinued in many markets, so check local availability.
c.caution: Roll gently to resuspend before use; never give IV. Do not mix with other insulins unless the label allows. Check availability, as many products have been withdrawn. Keep unopened insulin in the refrigerator; in-use pens or vials are kept at room temperature for the time on the label (usually 28 days).
c.preg: Insulin is the treatment of choice in pregnancy; needs usually fall in the first trimester, rise in the second and third, and drop sharply after delivery. Compatible with breastfeeding (needs may fall).
c.renal: Insulin clearance falls in renal impairment, so requirements drop — reduce doses and monitor glucose closely. Hypoglycemia risk is also higher in liver disease.

c.mn:
💊 Names: Isophane (NPH) and Insulin zinc suspension (Lente).
🎯 Used for: Basal cover, usually twice daily or at bedtime.
💡 Tip: Cloudy insulins — roll gently, never shake. Peak at 4–8 h, so watch for night-time lows.

ind: Type 1 and type 2 diabetes for once-daily basal glucose control.
ae: Hypoglycemia, weight gain, injection-site reactions or lipodystrophy, mild edema when starting, hypokalemia
c.doc: Once-daily basal insulin with a flat profile and lower nocturnal hypoglycemia than NPH; biosimilars available
c.ci: Hypoglycemia; hypersensitivity to the insulin or its excipients
c.sae: Severe hypoglycemia / Hypokalemia / Anaphylaxis (rare)
c.info: Long-acting analogue that precipitates at neutral pH in tissue, giving slow release with no pronounced peak: about 24 h (U-100) and up to 36 h (U-300). U-300 is not unit-for-unit interchangeable with U-100.
c.caution: Inject once daily at the same time; never mix or dilute with other insulins and never give IV. U-300 pens must not be drawn into a syringe. When changing from U-100 to U-300 a higher dose (about 10–18%) may be needed. Keep unopened insulin in the refrigerator; in-use pens or vials are kept at room temperature for the time on the label (usually 28 days).
c.preg: Insulin is the treatment of choice in pregnancy; needs usually fall in the first trimester, rise in the second and third, and drop sharply after delivery. Compatible with breastfeeding (needs may fall).
c.renal: Insulin clearance falls in renal impairment, so requirements drop — reduce doses and monitor glucose closely. Hypoglycemia risk is also higher in liver disease.

ind: Type 1 and type 2 diabetes for basal glucose control (once or twice daily).
ae: Hypoglycemia, weight gain, injection-site reactions or lipodystrophy, mild edema when starting, hypokalemia
c.doc: Basal insulin with less weight gain than NPH; being discontinued in many markets
c.ci: Hypoglycemia; hypersensitivity to the insulin or its excipients
c.sae: Severe hypoglycemia / Hypokalemia / Anaphylaxis (rare)
c.info: Long-acting analogue with a fatty-acid chain that binds albumin, so its duration is dose-dependent (about 6–24 h). Manufacturing has been discontinued in many markets, so check availability.
c.caution: Inject once or twice daily; twice daily dosing is common in type 1 diabetes. Never mix with other insulins or give IV. Switching from NPH usually needs a unit-for-unit dose. Keep unopened insulin in the refrigerator; in-use pens or vials are kept at room temperature for the time on the label (usually 28 days).
c.preg: Insulin is the treatment of choice in pregnancy; needs usually fall in the first trimester, rise in the second and third, and drop sharply after delivery. Compatible with breastfeeding (needs may fall).
c.renal: Insulin clearance falls in renal impairment, so requirements drop — reduce doses and monitor glucose closely. Hypoglycemia risk is also higher in liver disease.

ind: Type 1 and type 2 diabetes for once-daily basal glucose control.
ae: Hypoglycemia, weight gain, injection-site reactions or lipodystrophy, mild edema when starting, hypokalemia
c.doc: Ultra-long-acting basal insulin with flexible dosing times and less hypoglycemia than glargine
c.ci: Hypoglycemia; hypersensitivity to the insulin or its excipients
c.sae: Severe hypoglycemia / Hypokalemia / Anaphylaxis (rare)
c.info: Ultra-long-acting analogue that forms soluble multi-hexamers in tissue: duration over 42 h, flat profile, and a half-life of about 25 h. Dosing time can vary by 8–40 h between doses.
c.caution: Inject once daily; allow at least 8 hours between doses when timing is changed. Never mix with other insulins or give IV. U-200 pens deliver the dose in the same units — do not convert. Keep unopened insulin in the refrigerator; in-use pens or vials are kept at room temperature for the time on the label (usually 28 days).
c.preg: Limited pregnancy data; use only if needed, otherwise NPH or detemir have more experience. Compatible with breastfeeding.
c.renal: Insulin clearance falls in renal impairment, so requirements drop — reduce doses and monitor glucose closely. Hypoglycemia risk is also higher in liver disease.

c.mn:
💊 Names: Glargine, Detemir, Degludec ('GDD' — longest last).
🎯 Used for: Once-daily basal insulin with a flat profile.
💡 Tip: Degludec lasts over 42 h and allows flexible dosing times; glargine U-300 is not unit-for-unit with U-100.

ind: Type 2 diabetes (first-line); prediabetes prevention; polycystic ovary syndrome (off-label).
ae: Diarrhea, nausea, abdominal discomfort, metallic taste, decreased appetite, vitamin B12 deficiency with long-term use
c.doc: First-line drug for type 2 diabetes; weight neutral with no hypoglycemia when used alone; cardiovascular safety
c.ci: eGFR below 30 mL/min/1.73 m², metabolic acidosis (including DKA), severe hepatic impairment, states of hypoxia or shock, heavy alcohol use
c.sae: Lactic acidosis (rare) / Vitamin B12 deficiency
c.info: Biguanide that lowers glucose mainly by reducing hepatic gluconeogenesis (AMPK activation, mitochondrial complex I inhibition) and improving insulin sensitivity. It does not stimulate insulin secretion. Not metabolised; excreted unchanged by the kidney.
c.caution: Take with meals and increase the dose slowly to limit GI side effects; XR once daily with the evening meal. Hold before iodinated contrast, major surgery and during dehydration or acute illness. Check vitamin B12 periodically on long-term use and limit alcohol.
c.preg: Commonly continued in gestational diabetes and pregnancy with type 2 diabetes or PCOS; crosses the placenta, and insulin is still the usual first choice in many guidelines. Small amounts pass into breast milk; compatible with breastfeeding.
c.renal: eGFR 45 or above: no change; eGFR 30–44: reduce to a maximum of about 1000 mg/day and reassess; eGFR below 30: contraindicated. Avoid in significant hepatic impairment.

c.mn:
💊 Names: Metformin (the only biguanide in use).
🎯 Used for: First-line type 2 diabetes, PCOS.
💡 Tip: No hypoglycemia alone, weight-neutral. Stop if eGFR falls below 30 (lactic acidosis); check B12 long-term.

ind: Type 2 diabetes, especially with insulin resistance; used off-label in fatty liver disease.
ae: Weight gain, edema, headache, upper respiratory infection, anemia, bone fractures
c.doc: Insulin-resistant type 2 diabetes as add-on therapy; may help nonalcoholic fatty liver; low hypoglycemia risk alone
c.ci: Symptomatic heart failure (NYHA III–IV), active bladder cancer, type 1 diabetes, DKA, active liver disease (ALT above 2.5 times normal)
c.sae: Congestive heart failure / Bone fractures / Macular edema / Bladder cancer signal
c.info: PPAR-γ agonist that improves insulin sensitivity in fat, muscle and liver; the full effect builds over 6–12 weeks. Metabolised by CYP2C8 (gemfibrozil raises levels).
c.caution: Once daily with or without food. Watch for weight gain, swelling and shortness of breath; check liver tests before and during use. Avoid combining with insulin where heart failure risk exists. Women may see restored ovulation — consider contraception.
c.preg: Not recommended in pregnancy or breastfeeding; use insulin.
c.renal: No dose adjustment for renal impairment (fluid retention can worsen edema). Avoid in active liver disease and monitor liver enzymes.

ind: Type 2 diabetes as add-on therapy.
ae: Weight gain, edema, headache, anemia, bone fractures
c.doc: Restricted add-on option where available; suspended in Europe in 2010 over cardiovascular concerns
c.ci: Heart failure (any grade), acute coronary syndrome, type 1 diabetes, DKA, active liver disease
c.sae: Congestive heart failure / Myocardial ischemia concern / Bone fractures / Macular edema
c.info: PPAR-γ agonist with more marked LDL-cholesterol rise than pioglitazone; metabolised by CYP2C8. Availability is limited in many markets after cardiovascular safety concerns.
c.caution: Once or twice daily. Check for heart failure signs before and during use. Available only in some markets, so check local rules. Do not combine with insulin in most regions.
c.preg: Not recommended in pregnancy or breastfeeding; use insulin.
c.renal: No adjustment needed for renal impairment but fluid retention may worsen; avoid in active liver disease.

c.mn:
💊 Names: Pioglitazone, Rosiglitazone (all end in '-glitazone').
🎯 Used for: Insulin-resistant type 2 diabetes.
💡 Tip: Cause fluid retention and weight gain, so avoid in heart failure; fractures in women.

ind: Type 2 diabetes (approved in China).
ae: Raised triglycerides, raised uric acid, hypoglycemia (uncommon), nausea, dizziness
c.doc: Glucokinase activator approved in China (2022) for type 2 diabetes; limited use elsewhere
c.ci: Type 1 diabetes, diabetic ketoacidosis, pregnancy, hypersensitivity to the drug
c.sae: Elevated lipids and uric acid / Hypoglycemia
c.info: Dual-acting glucokinase activator that acts on the pancreatic beta cell (improves glucose sensing and insulin secretion) and on the liver (glucose uptake). Approved only in China; global data are limited.
c.caution: Taken twice daily within an hour before meals per the local label. Monitor triglycerides and uric acid. Limited experience — check local labeling.
c.preg: No adequate human data; avoid in pregnancy and breastfeeding.
c.renal: Limited data in renal or hepatic impairment; use caution and follow the local label.

c.mn:
💊 Names: Dorzagliatin.
🎯 Used for: Type 2 diabetes (approved in China).
💡 Tip: A newer class acting on the beta cell and liver; watch triglycerides and uric acid.

ind: Type 2 diabetes; also used as a diagnostic test for insulinoma.
ae: Hypoglycemia, weight gain, nausea, rash, dizziness
c.doc: Older short-acting sulfonylurea; still used where cheaper options are limited
c.ci: Type 1 diabetes, diabetic ketoacidosis, severe renal or hepatic impairment, pregnancy, breastfeeding, sulfonylurea or sulfonamide hypersensitivity
c.sae: Prolonged severe hypoglycemia / Hemolytic anemia in G6PD deficiency / Cholestatic jaundice (rare)
c.info: First-generation sulfonylurea with a short half-life (4–6 h), so it carries a lower risk of prolonged hypoglycemia than other older agents. Metabolised in the liver to inactive metabolites; usually 500 mg two or three times daily.
c.caution: Take 30 minutes before meals. Alcohol can cause flushing and nausea. Warfarin and sulfonamides can potentiate the effect. Watch for hypoglycemia, particularly in the elderly.
c.preg: Avoid in pregnancy (prolonged neonatal hypoglycemia); switch to insulin before conception or as soon as pregnancy is found. Avoid while breastfeeding (infant hypoglycemia risk).
c.renal: Inactive metabolites make it relatively safer in mild renal impairment, but avoid in severe renal or hepatic impairment; start low in the elderly.

ind: Type 2 diabetes (rarely used now).
ae: Hypoglycemia, weight gain, nausea, rash, dizziness
c.doc: Obsolete; replaced by second-generation sulfonylureas
c.ci: Type 1 diabetes, diabetic ketoacidosis, severe renal or hepatic impairment, pregnancy, breastfeeding, sulfonylurea or sulfonamide hypersensitivity
c.sci: Elderly and renal impairment (prolonged hypoglycemia); SIADH
c.sae: Prolonged severe hypoglycemia / Hyponatremia (SIADH-like) / Disulfiram-like reaction with alcohol
c.info: First-generation sulfonylurea with a very long half-life (about 36 h) excreted unchanged by the kidney. It potentiates ADH (hyponatremia) and causes a disulfiram-like reaction with alcohol; largely obsolete.
c.caution: Avoid alcohol (flushing, nausea). Monitor sodium. Avoid in older adults and in renal impairment because of prolonged hypoglycemia. Usually replaced by safer agents.
c.preg: Avoid in pregnancy (prolonged neonatal hypoglycemia); switch to insulin before conception or as soon as pregnancy is found. Avoid while breastfeeding (infant hypoglycemia risk).
c.renal: Contraindicated or avoided in renal impairment because the drug is excreted unchanged and hypoglycemia is prolonged; avoid in hepatic impairment.

ind: Type 2 diabetes (historical).
ae: Hypoglycemia, weight gain, nausea, rash, dizziness
c.doc: Obsolete; discontinued in most markets
c.ci: Type 1 diabetes, diabetic ketoacidosis, severe renal or hepatic impairment, pregnancy, breastfeeding, sulfonylurea or sulfonamide hypersensitivity
c.sae: Prolonged severe hypoglycemia / Hemolytic anemia in G6PD deficiency / Cholestatic jaundice (rare)
c.info: First-generation sulfonylurea metabolised to the active hydroxyhexamide, which is excreted by the kidney. It has a mild uricosuric effect. Discontinued in most markets.
c.caution: Rarely available today — check local availability. Take before meals; monitor for hypoglycemia, especially in the elderly and in renal impairment.
c.preg: Avoid in pregnancy (prolonged neonatal hypoglycemia); switch to insulin before conception or as soon as pregnancy is found. Avoid while breastfeeding (infant hypoglycemia risk).
c.renal: Active metabolite accumulates in renal impairment, so avoid in renal impairment; avoid in hepatic impairment.

ind: Type 2 diabetes (historical).
ae: Hypoglycemia, weight gain, nausea, rash, dizziness
c.doc: Obsolete; replaced by second-generation sulfonylureas
c.ci: Type 1 diabetes, diabetic ketoacidosis, severe renal or hepatic impairment, pregnancy, breastfeeding, sulfonylurea or sulfonamide hypersensitivity
c.sae: Prolonged severe hypoglycemia / Hemolytic anemia in G6PD deficiency / Cholestatic jaundice (rare)
c.info: First-generation sulfonylurea with slow onset (4–6 h) and an intermediate duration (12–24 h), metabolised to weakly active metabolites. Discontinued in many markets.
c.caution: Take with breakfast (once or twice daily). Alcohol may cause flushing. Rarely used now; check local availability.
c.preg: Avoid in pregnancy (prolonged neonatal hypoglycemia); switch to insulin before conception or as soon as pregnancy is found. Avoid while breastfeeding (infant hypoglycemia risk).
c.renal: Use with caution in renal impairment (active metabolites); avoid in severe renal or hepatic impairment.

c.mn:
💊 Names: 'TCAT': Tolbutamide, Chlorpropamide, Acetohexamide, Tolazamide.
🎯 Used for: Historical type 2 diabetes therapy; rarely used now.
💡 Tip: Chlorpropamide lasts 36 h with hyponatremia and disulfiram-like reactions.

ind: Type 2 diabetes.
ae: Hypoglycemia, weight gain, nausea, rash, dizziness
c.dose: Oral tablet; dose per local label (limited availability)
c.doc: Rarely used second-generation sulfonylurea; limited availability and data
c.ci: Type 1 diabetes, diabetic ketoacidosis, severe renal or hepatic impairment, pregnancy, breastfeeding, sulfonylurea or sulfonamide hypersensitivity
c.sae: Prolonged severe hypoglycemia / Hemolytic anemia in G6PD deficiency / Cholestatic jaundice (rare)
c.info: Second-generation sulfonylurea (also called glycyclamide) that closes ATP-sensitive potassium channels in the pancreatic beta cell to stimulate insulin release. Limited clinical data and availability.
c.caution: Take before meals and watch for hypoglycemia. Follow the local label because data are limited.
c.preg: Avoid in pregnancy (prolonged neonatal hypoglycemia); switch to insulin before conception or as soon as pregnancy is found. Avoid while breastfeeding (infant hypoglycemia risk).
c.renal: Use caution in renal and hepatic impairment; avoid in severe impairment.

ind: Type 2 diabetes.
ae: Hypoglycemia, weight gain, nausea, rash, dizziness
c.doc: Potent second-generation sulfonylurea; avoided in older adults and renal impairment because of hypoglycemia
c.ci: Type 1 diabetes, diabetic ketoacidosis, severe renal or hepatic impairment, pregnancy, breastfeeding, sulfonylurea or sulfonamide hypersensitivity
c.sae: Prolonged severe hypoglycemia (higher risk than other sulfonylureas) / Hemolytic anemia in G6PD deficiency / Cholestatic jaundice (rare)
c.info: Second-generation sulfonylurea (glibenclamide) metabolised to active metabolites that accumulate in renal impairment. It has the highest hypoglycemia risk of the class, which is why guidelines advise against it in older adults.
c.caution: Take with breakfast (once or twice daily); micronised forms have different doses. Avoid in older adults; hypoglycemia can be prolonged. Bosentan is contraindicated with it.
c.preg: Used in gestational diabetes in some settings but insulin or metformin are preferred (placental transfer, neonatal hypoglycemia). Avoid while breastfeeding.
c.renal: Avoid in renal impairment (active metabolites accumulate); avoid in hepatic impairment.

ind: Type 2 diabetes.
ae: Hypoglycemia, weight gain, nausea, rash, dizziness
c.doc: Short-acting second-generation sulfonylurea with inactive metabolites; preferred in older adults and mild renal impairment
c.ci: Type 1 diabetes, diabetic ketoacidosis, severe renal or hepatic impairment, pregnancy, breastfeeding, sulfonylurea or sulfonamide hypersensitivity
c.sae: Prolonged severe hypoglycemia / Hemolytic anemia in G6PD deficiency / Cholestatic jaundice (rare)
c.info: Second-generation sulfonylurea with a half-life of 2–4 h and inactive metabolites, so hypoglycemia is less prolonged. XL form is an osmotic pump releasing the drug over 24 h.
c.caution: Take 30 minutes before a meal; XL is once daily with breakfast, swallow whole (the shell may appear in the stool). Start with low doses in older adults and monitor for hypoglycemia.
c.preg: Avoid in pregnancy (prolonged neonatal hypoglycemia); switch to insulin before conception or as soon as pregnancy is found. Avoid while breastfeeding (infant hypoglycemia risk).
c.renal: Preferred sulfonylurea in mild–moderate renal impairment because metabolites are inactive; use low doses and avoid in severe renal or hepatic impairment.

ind: Type 2 diabetes.
ae: Hypoglycemia, weight gain, nausea, rash, dizziness
c.doc: Sulfonylurea with lower hypoglycemia risk and weight gain than glyburide; widely used outside the US
c.ci: Type 1 diabetes, diabetic ketoacidosis, severe renal or hepatic impairment, pregnancy, breastfeeding, sulfonylurea or sulfonamide hypersensitivity; concomitant miconazole
c.sae: Prolonged severe hypoglycemia / Hemolytic anemia in G6PD deficiency / Cholestatic jaundice (rare)
c.info: Second-generation sulfonylurea with a selective effect on the beta cell receptor and mild antioxidant properties; metabolised in the liver to inactive metabolites. MR tablets give once-daily dosing.
c.caution: Take with breakfast (MR once daily, swallow whole). Miconazole strongly increases hypoglycemia risk and is contraindicated. Not marketed in the US.
c.preg: Avoid in pregnancy (prolonged neonatal hypoglycemia); switch to insulin before conception or as soon as pregnancy is found. Avoid while breastfeeding (infant hypoglycemia risk).
c.renal: Can be used in mild–moderate renal impairment at lower doses because metabolites are inactive; avoid in severe renal or hepatic impairment.

ind: Type 2 diabetes.
ae: Hypoglycemia, weight gain, nausea, rash, dizziness
c.doc: Sulfonylurea excreted mainly in bile, so suitable in renal impairment; used in Europe and Asia
c.ci: Type 1 diabetes, diabetic ketoacidosis, severe renal or hepatic impairment, pregnancy, breastfeeding, sulfonylurea or sulfonamide hypersensitivity
c.sae: Prolonged severe hypoglycemia / Hemolytic anemia in G6PD deficiency / Cholestatic jaundice (rare)
c.info: Second-generation sulfonylurea (30 mg tablets) with almost complete hepatic metabolism and biliary excretion (about 95%), making it useful in patients with renal impairment. Short duration.
c.caution: Take 15–30 minutes before meals, up to 3 times daily (maximum about 120 mg/day). Check local availability; not marketed in the US.
c.preg: Avoid in pregnancy (prolonged neonatal hypoglycemia); switch to insulin before conception or as soon as pregnancy is found. Avoid while breastfeeding (infant hypoglycemia risk).
c.renal: Can be used in mild–moderate renal impairment because elimination is mainly biliary; avoid in severe hepatic impairment.

ind: Type 2 diabetes.
ae: Hypoglycemia, weight gain, nausea, rash, dizziness
c.doc: Once-daily third-generation sulfonylurea with lower hypoglycemia risk than glyburide
c.ci: Type 1 diabetes, diabetic ketoacidosis, severe renal or hepatic impairment, pregnancy, breastfeeding, sulfonylurea or sulfonamide hypersensitivity
c.sae: Prolonged severe hypoglycemia / Hemolytic anemia in G6PD deficiency / Cholestatic jaundice (rare)
c.info: Sulfonylurea metabolised by CYP2C9 to an active M1 metabolite (renally cleared). It may have less effect on ischemic preconditioning than glyburide and is dosed once daily.
c.caution: Take once daily with breakfast or the first main meal; start at 1 mg. Watch for hypoglycemia, especially in older adults and with fluconazole or other CYP2C9 inhibitors.
c.preg: Avoid in pregnancy (prolonged neonatal hypoglycemia); switch to insulin before conception or as soon as pregnancy is found. Avoid while breastfeeding (infant hypoglycemia risk).
c.renal: Start at 1 mg once daily in mild–moderate renal impairment; avoid in severe renal or hepatic impairment.

c.mn:
💊 Names: Glyclopyramide, Glyburide, Glipizide, Gliclazide, Gliquidone, Glimepiride (all 'gli-').
🎯 Used for: Type 2 diabetes when insulin secretion is reduced.
💡 Tip: Glyburide = highest hypoglycemia risk; glipizide and gliclazide are safer in the elderly; gliquidone is biliary (renal-friendly).

ind: Type 2 diabetes (mealtime glucose control).
ae: Hypoglycemia, weight gain, upper respiratory infection, headache, diarrhea
c.doc: Short-acting secretagogue taken with meals; usable in renal impairment; skip the dose if the meal is skipped
c.ci: Type 1 diabetes, diabetic ketoacidosis, concurrent gemfibrozil, severe hepatic impairment, hypersensitivity
c.sae: Severe hypoglycemia / Ischemic cardiac events (rare)
c.info: Meglitinide (carbamoylmethyl benzoic acid) that closes beta cell potassium channels at a site separate from sulfonylureas, with onset in about 15 minutes and duration of 4–6 h. Metabolised by CYP2C8 and CYP3A4; hepatic elimination.
c.caution: Take 0–30 minutes before each main meal; skip the dose if you skip the meal. Gemfibrozil is contraindicated; clarithromycin and cyclosporine also raise levels.
c.preg: Not recommended in pregnancy or breastfeeding; use insulin.
c.renal: Start with 0.5 mg in severe renal impairment (CrCl 20–40 mL/min) and titrate carefully; use caution in hepatic impairment.

ind: Type 2 diabetes (mealtime glucose control).
ae: Hypoglycemia, upper respiratory infection, dizziness, back pain, diarrhea
c.doc: Rapid, short-acting secretagogue for postprandial glucose
c.ci: Type 1 diabetes, diabetic ketoacidosis, hypersensitivity, severe hepatic impairment
c.sae: Severe hypoglycemia (rare)
c.info: D-phenylalanine derivative that stimulates rapid, short insulin release: onset within 20 minutes, peak 1 h, duration about 4 h. Metabolised by CYP2C9 and CYP3A4.
c.caution: Take 1–30 minutes before meals; skip the dose if you skip the meal. Monitor glucose, since hypoglycemia can occur if meals are late.
c.preg: Not recommended in pregnancy or breastfeeding; use insulin.
c.renal: No adjustment in mild–moderate renal impairment; use caution in severe renal impairment (limited data) and avoid in severe hepatic impairment.

ind: Type 2 diabetes (mealtime glucose control; marketed mainly in Japan).
ae: Hypoglycemia, abdominal discomfort, liver enzyme elevation
c.doc: Rapid-acting meglitinide used in Japan for postprandial glucose
c.ci: Type 1 diabetes, diabetic ketoacidosis, severe infection, perioperative state, hypersensitivity
c.sae: Severe hypoglycemia / Liver dysfunction (rare)
c.info: Meglitinide with very fast onset (peak within about 15 minutes) and short duration; taken immediately before meals. Marketed mainly in Japan and other Asian countries.
c.caution: Take within 5 minutes before meals (10 mg three times daily in Japan); skip if the meal is skipped. Available mainly in Asia.
c.preg: Not recommended in pregnancy or breastfeeding; use insulin.
c.renal: Use caution in severe renal impairment (limited data); avoid in severe hepatic impairment.

c.mn:
💊 Names: Repaglinide, Nateglinide, Mitiglinide (all end in '-glinide').
🎯 Used for: Short-acting mealtime insulin release.
💡 Tip: Take just before meals and skip the dose if you skip the meal. Gemfibrozil is contraindicated with repaglinide.

ind: Type 2 diabetes (postprandial hyperglycemia).
ae: Flatulence, abdominal bloating, diarrhea, abdominal pain
c.doc: Add-on for after-meal glucose spikes; weight neutral and does not cause hypoglycemia alone
c.ci: Inflammatory bowel disease, colonic ulceration, intestinal obstruction, cirrhosis, CrCl below 25 mL/min, chronic digestive disorders
c.sae: Hypoglycemia when combined with other agents (treat with glucose, not sucrose) / Liver enzyme elevation (rare)
c.info: Pseudotetrasaccharide that competitively blocks intestinal α-glucosidase, delaying carbohydrate digestion so absorption is spread out. Almost no systemic absorption.
c.caution: Take with the first bite of each main meal. If hypoglycemia occurs on combination therapy, treat with glucose (dextrose), not sucrose. Start with a low dose to reduce flatulence.
c.preg: Not recommended in pregnancy (limited data); use insulin. Minimal absorption, but avoid while breastfeeding.
c.renal: Avoid when CrCl is below 25 mL/min; avoid in cirrhosis; monitor liver enzymes.

ind: Type 2 diabetes (postprandial hyperglycemia; marketed mainly in Japan and India).
ae: Flatulence, abdominal distension, diarrhea, loose stools
c.doc: Add-on for after-meal glucose spikes; widely used in Japan and India
c.ci: Severe ketosis, diabetic coma, severe infection, perioperative state, intestinal obstruction, hypersensitivity
c.sae: Hypoglycemia when combined with other agents / Intestinal obstruction-like symptoms (rare) / Liver enzyme elevation
c.info: α-Glucosidase inhibitor structurally related to valiolamine, more selective for sucrase and maltase. Negligible absorption.
c.caution: Take 0.2–0.3 mg immediately before each meal. Treat hypoglycemia with glucose. Start low to limit gas and bloating.
c.preg: Not recommended in pregnancy or breastfeeding; use insulin.
c.renal: Use caution in severe renal impairment; no formal adjustment in mild–moderate.

ind: Type 2 diabetes (postprandial hyperglycemia).
ae: Flatulence, diarrhea, abdominal pain, skin rash
c.doc: Add-on for after-meal glucose spikes; systemically absorbed, unlike acarbose
c.ci: Diabetic ketoacidosis, inflammatory bowel disease, colonic ulceration, intestinal obstruction, CrCl below 25 mL/min
c.sae: Hypoglycemia when combined with other agents (treat with glucose, not sucrose)
c.info: Deoxynojirimycin derivative that inhibits intestinal α-glucosidases; unlike acarbose it is absorbed and excreted unchanged by the kidney. It also lowers glucose only slightly at fasting.
c.caution: Take with the first bite of each main meal. Treat hypoglycemia with glucose, not sucrose. Start low and increase slowly.
c.preg: Not recommended in pregnancy (limited data); use insulin. Small amounts pass into breast milk — avoid.
c.renal: Avoid when CrCl is below 25 mL/min (accumulation); no adjustment above that.

c.mn:
💊 Names: Acarbose, Voglibose, Miglitol.
🎯 Used for: After-meal glucose spikes.
💡 Tip: Take with the first bite of the meal. Flatulence is common. Treat hypoglycemia with glucose, not sucrose.

c.st: Pen 5, 10 mcg per dose · ER 2 mg weekly
ind: Type 2 diabetes (adjunct to diet, exercise and other agents).
ae: Nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, constipation, decreased appetite, injection-site reactions, headache
c.dose: Pen 5, 10 mcg per dose · ER 2 mg weekly
c.doc: First GLP-1 agonist; twice-daily pen before meals or once-weekly extended-release; no cardiovascular benefit proven
c.ci: Personal or family history of medullary thyroid carcinoma, multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2 (MEN 2), prior pancreatitis or serious hypersensitivity, type 1 diabetes (not for DKA); severe gastroparesis; CrCl below 30 mL/min
c.sci: Medullary thyroid carcinoma / MEN 2 (boxed warning for most agents)
c.sae: Pancreatitis / Gallbladder disease / Thyroid C-cell tumors (animal data) / Acute kidney injury from dehydration
c.info: GLP-1 receptor agonist (synthetic exendin-4 from Gila monster saliva) that stimulates glucose-dependent insulin release, suppresses glucagon and slows gastric emptying. The extended-release microsphere form carries a boxed warning for thyroid C-cell tumors.
c.caution: Twice-daily form: inject within 60 minutes before the two main meals. Extended-release: once weekly, any time of day. Reconstitute ER powder fully and shake vigorously per instructions. Not with insulin unless directed. Rotate injection sites. Stop and seek help for severe, persistent abdominal pain (pancreatitis). Tell the anesthetist before procedures (delayed gastric emptying, aspiration risk).
c.preg: Not recommended in pregnancy — stop before planned conception (semaglutide about 2 months before) and use insulin. Avoid while breastfeeding (limited data).
c.renal: Avoid when CrCl is below 30 mL/min or in end-stage renal disease; use caution when CrCl is 30–50 mL/min. Acute kidney injury has occurred with vomiting and dehydration.

ind: Type 2 diabetes; reduction of major cardiovascular events in type 2 diabetes with established disease; a separate higher-dose product is used for weight management.
ae: Nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, constipation, decreased appetite, injection-site reactions, headache
c.doc: Daily GLP-1 agonist with proven cardiovascular benefit (LEADER trial); also lowers weight
c.ci: Personal or family history of medullary thyroid carcinoma, multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2 (MEN 2), prior pancreatitis or serious hypersensitivity, type 1 diabetes (not for DKA)
c.sci: Medullary thyroid carcinoma / MEN 2 (boxed warning for most agents)
c.sae: Pancreatitis / Gallbladder disease / Thyroid C-cell tumors (animal data) / Acute kidney injury from dehydration
c.info: Long-acting GLP-1 analogue with a fatty-acid chain that binds albumin (half-life about 13 h). The diabetes and weight-management products are different labelled doses.
c.caution: Once daily at any time, with or without food. Start at 0.6 mg for 1 week, then 1.2 mg, then 1.8 mg if needed. Do not use with another GLP-1 agonist or DPP-4 inhibitor. Rotate injection sites. Stop and seek help for severe, persistent abdominal pain (pancreatitis). Tell the anesthetist before procedures (delayed gastric emptying, aspiration risk).
c.preg: Not recommended in pregnancy — stop before planned conception (semaglutide about 2 months before) and use insulin. Avoid while breastfeeding (limited data).
c.renal: No dose adjustment in mild–moderate renal impairment; limited experience in severe impairment or end-stage disease. Monitor renal function if vomiting or dehydration occurs.

ind: Investigational only: type 2 diabetes (development stopped).
ae: Nausea, vomiting, injection-site reactions
c.dose: Investigational once-weekly subcutaneous injection; never marketed
c.doc: Obsolete / Never marketed
c.ci: Not applicable (development discontinued)
c.sae: Hypersensitivity reactions (including anaphylaxis) / Severe GI intolerance
c.info: Once-weekly GLP-1 analogue whose phase 3 program was stopped in 2010–2011 because of hypersensitivity reactions and GI intolerance. It was never approved; kept for historical reference.
c.caution: Not available for clinical use — retained for historical reference only.
c.preg: Not applicable; never marketed.
c.renal: Not applicable; never marketed.

ind: Type 2 diabetes (adjunct); available alone or in a fixed combination with insulin glargine.
ae: Nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, constipation, decreased appetite, injection-site reactions, headache
c.doc: Short-acting once-daily GLP-1 agonist that mainly lowers after-meal glucose; neutral for cardiovascular outcomes
c.ci: Personal or family history of medullary thyroid carcinoma, multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2 (MEN 2), prior pancreatitis or serious hypersensitivity, type 1 diabetes (not for DKA); severe gastroparesis; CrCl below 15 mL/min
c.sae: Pancreatitis / Gallbladder disease / Immunogenicity (antibodies) / Acute kidney injury from dehydration
c.info: Short-acting exendin-4-based GLP-1 agonist with a pronounced effect on gastric emptying and postprandial glucose; the single-agent product has been withdrawn in some markets, while the insulin combination remains.
c.caution: Inject once daily within 1 hour before the first meal of the day. Start at 10 mcg for 14 days, then 20 mcg. Do not take with other GLP-1 agonists. Rotate injection sites. Stop and seek help for severe, persistent abdominal pain (pancreatitis). Tell the anesthetist before procedures (delayed gastric emptying, aspiration risk).
c.preg: Not recommended in pregnancy — stop before planned conception (semaglutide about 2 months before) and use insulin. Avoid while breastfeeding (limited data).
c.renal: No adjustment in mild renal impairment; use caution in moderate impairment (CrCl 30–60); avoid in severe impairment (CrCl below 30) and end-stage renal disease.

ind: Type 2 diabetes; reduction of major cardiovascular events in type 2 diabetes.
ae: Nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, constipation, decreased appetite, injection-site reactions, headache
c.doc: Once-weekly GLP-1 agonist with cardiovascular benefit (REWIND trial); autoinjector pen
c.ci: Personal or family history of medullary thyroid carcinoma, multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2 (MEN 2), prior pancreatitis or serious hypersensitivity, type 1 diabetes (not for DKA)
c.sci: Medullary thyroid carcinoma / MEN 2 (boxed warning for most agents)
c.sae: Pancreatitis / Gallbladder disease / Thyroid C-cell tumors (animal data) / Acute kidney injury from dehydration
c.info: GLP-1 analogue fused to an IgG4 Fc fragment, giving a half-life of about 5 days and weekly dosing. Starting dose 0.75 mg weekly, titrated to 1.5, 3 or 4.5 mg.
c.caution: Inject once weekly on the same day, with or without food. If a dose is missed, give within 3 days. Do not shake the pen; use only as an autoinjector. Not for use with other GLP-1 agonists. Rotate injection sites. Stop and seek help for severe, persistent abdominal pain (pancreatitis). Tell the anesthetist before procedures (delayed gastric emptying, aspiration risk).
c.preg: Not recommended in pregnancy — stop before planned conception (semaglutide about 2 months before) and use insulin. Avoid while breastfeeding (limited data).
c.renal: No dose adjustment for renal impairment, including end-stage renal disease. Monitor renal function if GI losses occur.

ind: Type 2 diabetes; reduction of cardiovascular events and kidney outcomes in type 2 diabetes; separate higher-dose products are used for weight management.
ae: Nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, constipation, decreased appetite, injection-site reactions, headache
c.doc: Once-weekly injectable (and once-daily oral) GLP-1 agonist with cardiovascular benefit; largest HbA1c and weight reduction among GLP-1 agents
c.ci: Personal or family history of medullary thyroid carcinoma, multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2 (MEN 2), prior pancreatitis or serious hypersensitivity, type 1 diabetes (not for DKA)
c.sci: Medullary thyroid carcinoma / MEN 2 (boxed warning for most agents) / Diabetic retinopathy (worsening with rapid glucose fall)
c.sae: Pancreatitis / Gallbladder disease / Thyroid C-cell tumors (animal data) / Acute kidney injury from dehydration / Worsening diabetic retinopathy
c.info: Long-acting GLP-1 analogue (94% homology to human GLP-1) with an albumin-binding side chain, half-life about 1 week. The oral form is co-formulated with an absorption enhancer (SNAC). Injection: start 0.25 mg weekly, increase every 4 weeks to 0.5, 1 or 2 mg.
c.caution: Injection: once weekly, any time of day. Oral tablet: take first thing in the morning on an empty stomach with no more than 120 mL of plain water, and wait 30 minutes before eating or other medicines. Have dilated eye exams if you have retinopathy. Rotate injection sites. Stop and seek help for severe, persistent abdominal pain (pancreatitis). Tell the anesthetist before procedures (delayed gastric emptying, aspiration risk).
c.preg: Not recommended in pregnancy — stop before planned conception (semaglutide about 2 months before) and use insulin. Avoid while breastfeeding (limited data).
c.renal: No adjustment in renal impairment; monitor renal function if vomiting or dehydration occurs. Not recommended in severe hepatic impairment for the oral form (limited data).

c.mn:
💊 Names: All end in '-tide' or '-glutide': Exenatide, Liraglutide, Taspoglutide, Lixisenatide, Dulaglutide, Semaglutide.
🎯 Used for: Type 2 diabetes with weight loss and cardiovascular benefit (liraglutide, dulaglutide, semaglutide).
💡 Tip: Nausea early on; boxed warning for thyroid C-cell tumors; avoid with MTC or MEN2 history.

ind: Type 2 diabetes; a separate labelled product is used for weight management.
ae: Nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, constipation, decreased appetite, injection-site reactions, headache
c.doc: Dual GIP/GLP-1 receptor agonist with greater HbA1c and weight reduction than most GLP-1 agents; weekly pen
c.ci: Personal or family history of medullary thyroid carcinoma, multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2 (MEN 2), prior pancreatitis or serious hypersensitivity, type 1 diabetes (not for DKA)
c.sci: Medullary thyroid carcinoma / MEN 2 (boxed warning for most agents)
c.sae: Pancreatitis / Gallbladder disease / Thyroid C-cell tumors (animal data) / Acute kidney injury from dehydration / Worsening diabetic retinopathy
c.info: Single-molecule agonist of both GIP and GLP-1 receptors; half-life about 5 days. Start 2.5 mg weekly for 4 weeks, then 5 mg, increasing by 2.5 mg every 4 weeks as needed to a maximum of 15 mg.
c.caution: Inject once weekly on the same day, with or without food. Oral contraceptives may be less effective for 4 weeks after starting and after each dose increase — add a barrier method or switch to non-oral contraception. Rotate injection sites. Stop and seek help for severe, persistent abdominal pain (pancreatitis). Tell the anesthetist before procedures (delayed gastric emptying, aspiration risk).
c.preg: Not recommended in pregnancy — stop before planned conception (semaglutide about 2 months before) and use insulin. Avoid while breastfeeding (limited data).
c.renal: No adjustment in renal or hepatic impairment; monitor renal function if vomiting or dehydration occurs.

c.mn:
💊 Names: Tirzepatide (dual GIP + GLP-1).
🎯 Used for: Type 2 diabetes with large HbA1c and weight reduction.
💡 Tip: May reduce oral contraceptive absorption — use a backup method for 4 weeks after each dose increase.

ind: Type 2 diabetes (monotherapy or combination).
ae: Nasopharyngitis, headache, upper respiratory tract infection, nausea, joint pain
c.doc: Widely used oral add-on with a low hypoglycemia risk and weight-neutral effect; cardiovascular safety shown (TECOS)
c.ci: Prior serious hypersensitivity (anaphylaxis, angioedema, Stevens-Johnson); type 1 diabetes or DKA; history of pancreatitis (caution)
c.sae: Pancreatitis / Severe joint pain / Bullous pemphigoid / Heart failure (saxagliptin, alogliptin)
c.info: DPP-4 inhibitor that raises endogenous GLP-1 and GIP levels, boosting glucose-dependent insulin release and lowering glucagon. Mostly excreted unchanged in urine.
c.caution: 100 mg once daily, with or without food. Stop and seek review for severe persistent abdominal pain (pancreatitis) or blistering skin. Do not combine with a GLP-1 agonist.
c.preg: Limited human data; insulin is preferred, so avoid in pregnancy. Avoid while breastfeeding (limited data).
c.renal: 50 mg daily when eGFR is 30–<45; 25 mg daily when eGFR is below 30 or on dialysis.

ind: Type 2 diabetes (monotherapy or combination); not approved in the US.
ae: Nasopharyngitis, headache, upper respiratory tract infection, nausea, joint pain
c.doc: DPP-4 inhibitor widely used outside the US; twice-daily dosing (once daily with a sulfonylurea)
c.ci: Hypersensitivity, hepatic impairment (ALT above 3 times normal), type 1 diabetes, DKA
c.sci: Liver disease / Angioedema with ACE inhibitors
c.sae: Liver enzyme elevation and hepatitis / Pancreatitis / Bullous pemphigoid / Angioedema (with ACE inhibitors)
c.info: DPP-4 inhibitor with a short half-life (about 3 h) that increases GLP-1 and GIP; metabolised by hydrolysis rather than CYP enzymes, so few interactions.
c.caution: 50 mg twice daily (50 mg once daily when combined with a sulfonylurea). Check liver function before starting, every 3 months in the first year, then periodically. Not available in the US.
c.preg: Limited human data; insulin is preferred, so avoid in pregnancy. Avoid while breastfeeding (limited data).
c.renal: 50 mg once daily when CrCl is below 50 mL/min or in end-stage renal disease; avoid in hepatic impairment.

ind: Type 2 diabetes (monotherapy or combination).
ae: Nasopharyngitis, headache, upper respiratory tract infection, nausea, joint pain
c.doc: DPP-4 inhibitor; limited use because of a heart failure hospitalization signal
c.ci: Prior serious hypersensitivity (anaphylaxis, angioedema, Stevens-Johnson); type 1 diabetes or DKA; history of pancreatitis (caution); heart failure (caution)
c.sae: Pancreatitis / Severe joint pain / Bullous pemphigoid / Heart failure (saxagliptin, alogliptin)
c.info: DPP-4 inhibitor metabolised by CYP3A4/5 to an active metabolite; strong CYP3A4 inhibitors raise its levels. The SAVOR trial showed a higher rate of hospitalization for heart failure.
c.caution: 5 mg once daily; 2.5 mg with strong CYP3A4 inhibitors (ketoconazole, clarithromycin). Use caution in patients with heart failure risk factors. Report severe joint pain or blistering.
c.preg: Limited human data; insulin is preferred, so avoid in pregnancy. Avoid while breastfeeding (limited data).
c.renal: 2.5 mg once daily when CrCl is 45 mL/min or less, or on dialysis; avoid in severe hepatic impairment.

ind: Type 2 diabetes (monotherapy or combination).
ae: Nasopharyngitis, headache, upper respiratory tract infection, nausea, joint pain
c.doc: DPP-4 inhibitor needing no renal dose adjustment (mainly biliary elimination)
c.ci: Prior serious hypersensitivity (anaphylaxis, angioedema, Stevens-Johnson); type 1 diabetes or DKA; history of pancreatitis (caution)
c.sae: Pancreatitis / Severe joint pain / Bullous pemphigoid / Heart failure
c.info: DPP-4 inhibitor eliminated mainly via bile and gut (about 5% renal), so it can be used across renal function. Half-life over 100 h due to tight target binding.
c.caution: 5 mg once daily, with or without food. Strong CYP3A4/P-gp inducers (rifampicin) reduce its effect. Report severe abdominal pain or joint pain.
c.preg: Limited human data; insulin is preferred, so avoid in pregnancy. Avoid while breastfeeding (limited data).
c.renal: No dose adjustment in renal impairment or mild–moderate hepatic impairment.

ind: Type 2 diabetes (monotherapy or combination).
ae: Nasopharyngitis, headache, upper respiratory tract infection, nausea, joint pain
c.doc: DPP-4 inhibitor available alone or in fixed combinations with metformin or pioglitazone
c.ci: Prior serious hypersensitivity (anaphylaxis, angioedema, Stevens-Johnson); type 1 diabetes or DKA; history of pancreatitis (caution)
c.sae: Pancreatitis / Severe joint pain / Bullous pemphigoid / Heart failure (saxagliptin, alogliptin) / Hepatotoxicity (rare)
c.info: DPP-4 inhibitor eliminated mostly unchanged in urine with little CYP metabolism; a small increase in heart failure hospitalization was noted in some analyses.
c.caution: 25 mg once daily with or without food. Liver tests should be checked before starting and if symptoms appear. Use caution in heart failure.
c.preg: Limited human data; insulin is preferred, so avoid in pregnancy. Avoid while breastfeeding (limited data).
c.renal: 12.5 mg daily when CrCl is 30–<60 mL/min; 6.25 mg daily when CrCl is below 30 or on dialysis.

c.mn:
💊 Names: All end in '-gliptin': Sitagliptin, Vildagliptin, Saxagliptin, Linagliptin, Alogliptin.
🎯 Used for: Oral add-on with weight neutrality and a low hypoglycemia risk.
💡 Tip: Linagliptin needs no renal dose adjustment; saxagliptin and alogliptin carry a heart failure signal; all can rarely cause pancreatitis or joint pain.

ind: Adjunct to mealtime insulin in type 1 and type 2 diabetes.
ae: Nausea (common, usually early), vomiting, anorexia, headache, abdominal pain, fatigue
c.dose: Inj 600 mcg/mL pen (15–60 mcg per dose)
c.doc: Adjunct to mealtime insulin in patients not at goal; reduces after-meal glucose and weight
c.ci: Gastroparesis, hypoglycemia unawareness, hypersensitivity to pramlintide or metacresol
c.sae: Severe hypoglycemia (boxed warning) when used with insulin
c.info: Synthetic analogue of amylin (co-secreted with insulin by the beta cell) that slows gastric emptying, suppresses glucagon and increases satiety. Doses are 15 mcg (type 1) or 60 mcg (type 2) before major meals.
c.caution: Reduce the mealtime insulin dose by about 50% when starting to avoid severe hypoglycemia. Inject before major meals only (at least 250 kcal or 30 g carbohydrate); skip the dose if skipping the meal. Use a separate injection from insulin and do not mix.
c.preg: Limited data; avoid in pregnancy and breastfeeding; use insulin.
c.renal: No adjustment in mild–moderate renal impairment; limited data in severe impairment.

c.mn:
💊 Names: Pramlintide.
🎯 Used for: Adjunct to mealtime insulin.
💡 Tip: Cut the mealtime insulin dose by about 50% at the start to prevent severe hypoglycemia.

ind: Type 2 diabetes; heart failure; chronic kidney disease (with or without diabetes).
ae: Genital yeast infections, urinary tract infections, increased urination, thirst, volume depletion, dizziness on standing
c.doc: Oral SGLT2 inhibitor with proven benefits in heart failure and chronic kidney disease as well as glucose lowering
c.ci: Type 1 diabetes, diabetic ketoacidosis, severe renal impairment or dialysis, serious hypersensitivity to the drug
c.sci: Type 1 diabetes / DKA risk; volume depletion
c.sae: Euglycemic diabetic ketoacidosis / Fournier gangrene / Urosepsis and pyelonephritis / Acute kidney injury
c.info: Inhibits the sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 in the proximal tubule, so glucose is excreted in urine (about 70 g/day) independent of insulin. Also reduces blood pressure and weight and offers cardiovascular and renal protection.
c.caution: 5–10 mg once daily in the morning. Hold for at least 3 days before planned surgery and during acute illness or reduced intake (ketoacidosis risk); maintain hydration and genital hygiene. Watch for nausea, vomiting or abdominal pain even with normal glucose (euglycemic DKA).
c.preg: Not recommended in the second and third trimesters (renal effects in animal studies); use insulin. Avoid while breastfeeding (unknown milk transfer, possible harm to infant kidney development).
c.renal: Glucose-lowering effect falls as eGFR falls (limited below 45); it can be started for heart failure or CKD at lower eGFR (down to about 25) per label; stop or avoid on dialysis. No adjustment in hepatic impairment.

ind: Type 2 diabetes; diabetic kidney disease; reduction of major cardiovascular events.
ae: Genital yeast infections, urinary tract infections, increased urination, thirst, volume depletion, dizziness on standing
c.doc: SGLT2 inhibitor with cardiovascular and renal benefit; lower-extremity amputation risk noted in CANVAS
c.ci: Type 1 diabetes, diabetic ketoacidosis, severe renal impairment or dialysis, serious hypersensitivity to the drug; peripheral vascular disease with active foot ulcers (caution)
c.sci: Type 1 diabetes / DKA risk; volume depletion / Peripheral arterial disease
c.sae: Euglycemic diabetic ketoacidosis / Fournier gangrene / Urosepsis and pyelonephritis / Acute kidney injury / Lower-limb (toe) amputation / Bone fractures
c.info: SGLT2 inhibitor that also weakly inhibits intestinal SGLT1. CANVAS found more amputations (mainly toes); the boxed warning was later removed but foot care remains important.
c.caution: 100–300 mg once daily before the first meal. Hold for at least 3 days before planned surgery and during acute illness or reduced intake (ketoacidosis risk); maintain hydration and genital hygiene. Watch for nausea, vomiting or abdominal pain even with normal glucose (euglycemic DKA). Check feet regularly and report foot sores or pain.
c.preg: Not recommended in the second and third trimesters (renal effects in animal studies); use insulin. Avoid while breastfeeding (unknown milk transfer, possible harm to infant kidney development).
c.renal: Maximum 100 mg daily when eGFR is 30–60; do not start for glucose control if eGFR is below 30 (may continue for kidney protection); avoid on dialysis.

ind: Type 2 diabetes; reduction of cardiovascular death in type 2 diabetes with established disease; heart failure; chronic kidney disease.
ae: Genital yeast infections, urinary tract infections, increased urination, thirst, volume depletion, dizziness on standing
c.doc: SGLT2 inhibitor that reduced cardiovascular death and heart failure hospitalization (EMPA-REG); also used for CKD
c.ci: Type 1 diabetes, diabetic ketoacidosis, severe renal impairment or dialysis, serious hypersensitivity to the drug
c.sci: Type 1 diabetes / DKA risk; volume depletion
c.sae: Euglycemic diabetic ketoacidosis / Fournier gangrene / Urosepsis and pyelonephritis / Acute kidney injury
c.info: Highly selective SGLT2 inhibitor with modest blood-pressure and weight reduction and cardiorenal protection. Half-life about 12 h, once daily.
c.caution: 10 mg once daily in the morning, increasing to 25 mg if needed. Hold for at least 3 days before planned surgery and during acute illness or reduced intake (ketoacidosis risk); maintain hydration and genital hygiene. Watch for nausea, vomiting or abdominal pain even with normal glucose (euglycemic DKA).
c.preg: Not recommended in the second and third trimesters (renal effects in animal studies); use insulin. Avoid while breastfeeding (unknown milk transfer, possible harm to infant kidney development).
c.renal: Glucose lowering is limited when eGFR is below 45; can be used for heart failure or CKD to lower eGFR per label; avoid on dialysis. No adjustment in hepatic impairment.

ind: Type 2 diabetes (adjunct to diet and exercise).
ae: Genital yeast infections, urinary tract infections, increased urination, thirst, volume depletion, dizziness on standing
c.doc: SGLT2 inhibitor for glucose lowering; cardiovascular safety shown but no proven cardiovascular benefit (VERTIS-CV)
c.ci: Type 1 diabetes, diabetic ketoacidosis, severe renal impairment or dialysis, serious hypersensitivity to the drug
c.sci: Type 1 diabetes / DKA risk; volume depletion
c.sae: Euglycemic diabetic ketoacidosis / Fournier gangrene / Urosepsis and pyelonephritis / Acute kidney injury
c.info: SGLT2 inhibitor with once-daily dosing; noninferior to placebo for major cardiovascular events in VERTIS-CV, without demonstrated cardiovascular or heart failure benefit.
c.caution: 5 mg once daily in the morning, increasing to 15 mg if needed. Hold for at least 3 days before planned surgery and during acute illness or reduced intake (ketoacidosis risk); maintain hydration and genital hygiene. Watch for nausea, vomiting or abdominal pain even with normal glucose (euglycemic DKA).
c.preg: Not recommended in the second and third trimesters (renal effects in animal studies); use insulin. Avoid while breastfeeding (unknown milk transfer, possible harm to infant kidney development).
c.renal: Do not start when eGFR is below 45; contraindicated in severe renal impairment and dialysis. No adjustment in mild hepatic impairment.

c.mn:
💊 Names: All end in '-gliflozin': Dapagliflozin, Canagliflozin, Empagliflozin, Ertugliflozin.
🎯 Used for: Type 2 diabetes with heart failure and kidney protection.
💡 Tip: Cause sugar in the urine — genital yeast infections, euglycemic DKA, Fournier gangrene; hold 3 days before surgery.

c.st: Tab 10, 20, 40, 80 mg · Inj 1 mg/mL · LA cap 60–160 mg
Tab 30, 60, 90, 120 mg · SR 120–300 mg · Inj 5 mg/mL

ind: Acid neutralization; also used as an osmotic laxative at higher doses.
c.doc: Antacid combined with aluminum salts to offset laxative effect
c.ci: Renal failure
ae: Diarrhea, hypermagnesemia (in renal impairment)
c.sae: Hypermagnesemia with cardiac/CNS depression
c.info: Non-absorbable antacid; commonly paired with aluminum hydroxide to balance bowel effects.
c.caution: Shake the suspension. Higher doses have a laxative effect. Separate from other medicines by about 2 hours. Avoid daily long-term use; children's dose depends on age.
c.preg: Acceptable at usual doses; avoid prolonged high doses. Compatible with breastfeeding.
c.renal: Avoid in moderate to severe renal impairment (hypermagnesemia: weakness, low blood pressure, drowsiness).

ind: Acid neutralization; also binds phosphate in chronic kidney disease.
c.doc: Phosphate binder in CKD; antacid component in combinations
c.ci: Hypophosphatemia
ae: Constipation, phosphate depletion
c.sae: Osteomalacia (chronic phosphate depletion)
c.info: Slower onset, longer duration than magnesium salts; constipating, often combined with Mg(OH)2.
c.caution: Can cause constipation. Long-term use binds phosphate and can cause low phosphate (weakness, bone loss). Separate from other medicines by 2 hours. Avoid prolonged use unless prescribed as a phosphate binder.
c.preg: Acceptable short-term; avoid prolonged high doses (phosphate depletion). Acceptable while breastfeeding.
c.renal: Avoid long-term use in renal impairment (aluminium accumulation: encephalopathy, bone disease, anemia); if used as a phosphate binder, keep courses short and monitor aluminium.

ind: Acid neutralization; also used as a calcium supplement.
c.doc: OTC antacid / calcium supplementation
c.ci: Hypercalcemia, hypercalciuria
ae: Constipation, belching, acid rebound
c.sae: Milk-alkali syndrome (with excessive use)
c.info: Potent, fast-acting; causes acid rebound and gas from CO2 generation.
c.caution: Chew tablets with meals or when symptoms occur; stay within the label maximum. Can constipate and cause rebound acid. Excess calcium with vitamin D risks milk-alkali syndrome. Separate from levothyroxine, iron, quinolones and tetracyclines by 2–4 hours.
c.preg: Safe and often used in pregnancy (also a calcium source); avoid excessive doses. Compatible with breastfeeding.
c.renal: Use caution in chronic kidney disease (hypercalcemia, calcification); monitor calcium and avoid excess.

ind: Rapid, short-acting relief of acid indigestion and heartburn.
c.doc: Occasional/emergency acid neutralization
c.ci: Sodium restriction, metabolic alkalosis, severe renal impairment
ae: Belching, flatulence, sodium overload, systemic alkalosis
c.sae: Milk-alkali syndrome, metabolic alkalosis
c.info: Highly soluble, fast-acting but short-duration; systemically absorbed, so unsuitable for chronic use.
c.caution: Contains a lot of sodium (about 12 mmol per gram) — avoid in heart failure, hypertension, edema or salt restriction. Short-term use only (not more than 2 weeks); overuse causes metabolic alkalosis and high sodium. Causes gas and belching; do not use with a very full stomach. Separate from other medicines by 2 hours.
c.preg: Avoid regular use in pregnancy (sodium load, fluid retention, alkalosis); occasional use is acceptable. Occasional use is acceptable while breastfeeding.
c.renal: Avoid in renal impairment because of the sodium load and alkalosis; in chronic kidney disease with metabolic acidosis it is used deliberately under medical supervision.

c.mn:
💊 Names: Magnesium hydroxide, Aluminum hydroxide, Calcium carbonate, Sodium bicarbonate.
🎯 Used for: Heartburn and sour stomach — they neutralize acid within minutes.
