💡 Tip: Magnesium loosens the bowel, aluminum constipates, which is why they are combined. Bicarbonate adds a salt load. Fast but short-acting.

c.dose: Oral 300 mg QID or 800 mg HS
ind: Peptic ulcer disease, GERD, hypersecretory states (first H2 blocker developed).
c.doc: Largely superseded by ranitidine/famotidine due to interactions
c.ci: Known hypersensitivity
ae: Headache, dizziness, gynecomastia, diarrhea
c.sae: Antiandrogenic effects (gynecomastia, impotence), confusion in elderly
c.info: Potent inhibitor of CYP450 (1A2, 2C9, 3A4); significant drug interactions and antiandrogenic activity limit modern use.
c.st: Oral 300 mg QID or 800 mg HS
c.caution: Strong inhibitor of several liver enzymes — raises levels of warfarin, phenytoin, theophylline, lidocaine, carbamazepine and benzodiazepines. Long-term use can cause gynecomastia and impotence (anti-androgen effect). Confusion in the elderly. Take with meals and at bedtime.
c.preg: Limited human data; famotidine is preferred. It passes into breast milk in concentrated amounts, so famotidine is preferred while breastfeeding.
c.renal: Reduce the dose (for example 300 mg every 12 h) when CrCl is below 30 mL/min; confusion is more likely. Removed by hemodialysis.

c.dose: Oral 150 mg BID or 300 mg HS
ind: Peptic ulcer disease, GERD, hypersecretory states.
c.doc: Formerly first-line H2 blocker; withdrawn from many markets (2020) over NDMA carcinogen contamination
c.ci: Hypersensitivity
ae: Headache, constipation, diarrhea
c.sae: NDMA (carcinogen) contamination leading to global withdrawal
c.info: More potent and fewer interactions than cimetidine; pulled from market after detection of N-nitrosodimethylamine impurities that increase with storage/heat.
c.st: Oral 150 mg BID or 300 mg HS
c.caution: Withdrawn or suspended in many markets since 2020 after NDMA impurity findings; check the local regulatory status and use famotidine as the usual alternative. Do not store tablets in heat.
c.preg: Was widely used in pregnancy but is no longer recommended because of NDMA concerns — use famotidine instead. Passes into breast milk.
c.renal: If still available: give 150 mg once daily when CrCl is below 50 mL/min; confusion is more likely. Removed by hemodialysis.

ind: Peptic ulcer disease, GERD, hypersecretory states.
c.doc: Preferred H2 blocker (minimal CYP interaction, no antiandrogenic effect)
c.ci: Hypersensitivity
ae: Headache, dizziness, constipation
c.sae: Rare thrombocytopenia
c.info: Most potent H2 blocker per mg; does not inhibit hepatic CYP450, unlike cimetidine.
c.caution: 10–20 mg once or twice daily; for prevention take 1 h before a trigger meal. Confusion can occur in the elderly and in renal impairment. Long-term use may reduce iron and B12 absorption.
c.preg: Generally considered acceptable in pregnancy. Small amounts pass into breast milk; compatible with breastfeeding.
c.renal: When CrCl is below 50 mL/min, halve the dose or extend the interval to 36–48 h.

c.dose: Oral 150 mg BID or 300 mg HS
ind: Peptic ulcer disease, GERD.
c.doc: Alternative H2 blocker, complete oral bioavailability
c.ci: Hypersensitivity
ae: Headache, sweating, urticaria
c.sae: Rare hepatotoxicity
c.info: Nearly 100% oral bioavailability, unlike other H2 blockers; minimal hepatic first-pass metabolism.
c.st: Oral 150 mg BID or 300 mg HS
c.caution: Take with or without food; 300 mg at bedtime or 150 mg twice daily. Minimal effect on liver enzymes. High-dose aspirin levels can rise. May cause a false-positive urine urobilinogen test.
c.preg: Limited data; famotidine is preferred. Small amounts pass into breast milk.
c.renal: Halve the dose (150 mg once daily) when CrCl is 20–50 mL/min; give 150 mg every other day when CrCl is below 20 mL/min.

c.mn:
💊 Names: All end in '-tidine': Cimetidine, Ranitidine, Famotidine, Nizatidine.
🎯 Used for: Ulcers, reflux and night-time acid.
💡 Tip: Cimetidine = many interactions; Ranitidine = withdrawn (NDMA); Famotidine = the preferred one.

ind: GERD, peptic ulcer disease, H. pylori eradication (triple therapy), Zollinger-Ellison syndrome.
c.doc: Prototype PPI; first-line for acid-related disorders
c.ci: Hypersensitivity to substituted benzimidazoles
ae: Headache, abdominal pain, diarrhea, flatulence
c.sae: C. difficile infection, fracture risk, hypomagnesemia, B12 deficiency (long-term)
c.info: Irreversibly inhibits H+/K+-ATPase (proton pump) of gastric parietal cells; prodrug activated in acidic canaliculi.
c.caution: Take 30–60 minutes before breakfast and swallow the capsule whole. OTC use is limited to 14 days without advice. Long-term use may lower magnesium and B12 and raise fracture and C. difficile risk. Avoid with clopidogrel (CYP2C19).
c.preg: Data are reassuring; one of the best-studied PPIs and acceptable when needed. Small amounts pass into breast milk; compatible.
c.renal: No adjustment in renal impairment; limit to 10–20 mg/day in severe hepatic impairment.

ind: GERD, peptic ulcer disease, NSAID-associated ulcer prophylaxis.
c.doc: Alternative PPI, available as orally disintegrating tablet
c.ci: Hypersensitivity
ae: Headache, diarrhea, abdominal pain
c.sae: Hypomagnesemia (long-term)
c.info: Available in orally disintegrating and granule formulations, useful for patients with swallowing difficulty or NG-tube administration.
c.caution: Take 30 minutes before a meal. The orally disintegrating tablet dissolves on the tongue; the capsule can be opened onto applesauce. Long-term use has the same risks as other PPIs. Can slightly lower theophylline levels.
c.preg: Data are reassuring; acceptable when needed. Small amounts pass into breast milk; compatible.
c.renal: No adjustment in renal impairment; reduce to 15 mg/day in severe hepatic impairment.

ind: GERD, erosive esophagitis; available IV for hospitalized patients (e.g., GI bleed).
c.doc: Preferred PPI for IV use / critically ill patients
c.ci: Hypersensitivity
ae: Headache, diarrhea, arthralgia
c.sae: Hypomagnesemia, acute interstitial nephritis (rare)
c.info: Fewer CYP2C19-mediated drug interactions than omeprazole; stable IV formulation makes it favored for GI bleeding protocols.
c.caution: Swallow the delayed-release tablet whole, ideally 30 minutes before a meal. IV 40 mg is given over 2–15 minutes. Less interaction with clopidogrel than omeprazole. Same long-term risks as other PPIs (low magnesium and B12, fractures, C. difficile).
c.preg: Limited data but generally considered acceptable when needed; omeprazole has more data. Small amounts pass into breast milk.
c.renal: No adjustment in renal impairment; limit to 20 mg/day in severe hepatic impairment.

ind: GERD, peptic ulcer disease, H. pylori eradication.
c.doc: Alternative PPI with rapid onset
c.ci: Hypersensitivity
ae: Headache, diarrhea, flatulence
c.sae: Hypomagnesemia (long-term)
c.info: Fastest onset of acid suppression among PPIs; metabolism less CYP2C19-dependent, giving more predictable effect.
c.caution: Swallow the delayed-release tablet whole (do not crush or chew), with or without food. Rapid onset and less dependent on CYP2C19. Long-term use has the same risks as other PPIs. Used in H. pylori regimens.
c.preg: Limited data; use only if clearly needed, and prefer omeprazole if suitable. Excretion into breast milk is unknown; use with caution.
c.renal: No adjustment in renal impairment or mild–moderate hepatic impairment; use caution in severe hepatic impairment (higher exposure).

ind: GERD, erosive esophagitis, H. pylori eradication.
c.doc: Alternative when higher/steadier acid suppression desired
c.ci: Hypersensitivity to substituted benzimidazoles
ae: Headache, diarrhea, nausea
c.sae: Hypomagnesemia, fracture risk (long-term)
c.info: S-isomer of omeprazole; slower hepatic clearance gives greater bioavailability and more sustained acid suppression.
c.caution: Take 20–40 mg once daily at least 1 hour before a meal. Swallow whole, or open the capsule and sprinkle the granules on applesauce. Avoid with clopidogrel (CYP2C19). Long-term use can lower magnesium and B12 and raise fracture and C. difficile risk — use the lowest dose for the shortest time.
c.preg: Data are reassuring, though omeprazole and lansoprazole have the most experience; use when clearly needed. Small amounts pass into breast milk; compatible.
c.renal: No adjustment in renal impairment; limit to 20 mg/day in severe hepatic impairment (Child-Pugh C).

c.mn:
💊 Names: All end in '-prazole': Omeprazole, Esomeprazole, Pantoprazole, Lansoprazole, Rabeprazole.
🎯 Used for: Reflux, ulcers, H. pylori regimens and stomach protection with NSAIDs.
💡 Tip: Strongest acid suppressors — take 30–60 min before meals. Long-term use lowers magnesium and B12. Omeprazole and esomeprazole weaken clopidogrel.

ind: Motion sickness, vertigo, mild chemotherapy/postoperative nausea.
c.doc: Motion sickness prophylaxis; adjunct antiemetic
c.ci: Narrow-angle glaucoma, BPH
ae: Sedation, dry mouth, blurred vision
c.sae: Anticholinergic toxicity/delirium in elderly
c.info: H1 antagonist with anticholinergic activity; blocks vestibular input to vomiting center.

ind: Motion sickness, vertigo (e.g., Meniere disease).
c.doc: First-line for vertigo/motion sickness
c.ci: Hypersensitivity
ae: Drowsiness, dry mouth
c.sae: Rare anticholinergic toxicity
c.info: Less sedating piperazine antihistamine; long duration allows once-daily dosing.

ind: Motion sickness prophylaxis, postoperative nausea/vomiting.
c.doc: Preferred for prolonged motion sickness prophylaxis (e.g., sea travel)
c.ci: Narrow-angle glaucoma, GI/urinary obstruction
ae: Dry mouth, blurred vision, drowsiness
c.sae: Acute angle-closure glaucoma, anticholinergic delirium
c.info: Muscarinic antagonist acting on vestibular apparatus and vomiting center; transdermal route provides sustained levels.

ind: Nausea and vomiting of pregnancy.
c.doc: First-line pharmacotherapy for nausea/vomiting of pregnancy (with vitamin B6)
c.ci: Hypersensitivity, MAOI use
ae: Sedation, dry mouth
c.sae: Excess sedation impairing daytime function
c.info: Combination doxylamine/pyridoxine is the only FDA-approved regimen specifically for pregnancy-related nausea.

c.st: Tab 10, 25 mg · Syrup 5 mg/5 mL · Inj 25 mg/mL
ind: Nausea/vomiting, motion sickness, sedation.
c.doc: Broad-spectrum antiemetic including postoperative nausea
c.ci: Children <2 years, comatose states
ae: Sedation, dry mouth, EPS
c.sae: Severe tissue injury with extravasation (IV), respiratory depression in young children
c.info: Phenothiazine with strong H1-antagonist and antidopaminergic activity; IV extravasation can cause severe local tissue necrosis.

c.st: Tab 5, 10 mg · Inj 5 mg/mL · Supp 25 mg
ind: Nausea/vomiting, migraine-associated nausea.
c.doc: General-purpose antiemetic, including postoperative and migraine-related nausea
c.ci: Severe CNS depression, comatose states
ae: Sedation, hypotension, EPS
c.sae: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome, tardive dyskinesia
c.info: Phenothiazine D2 antagonist acting at the chemoreceptor trigger zone; also has antihistaminic/anticholinergic activity.

ind: Diabetic gastroparesis, GERD, chemotherapy-induced nausea, prokinetic before anesthesia.
c.doc: Gastroparesis; also promotes gastric emptying
c.ci: GI obstruction/perforation, seizure disorder, pheochromocytoma
ae: Drowsiness, restlessness, diarrhea
c.sae: Extrapyramidal symptoms, tardive dyskinesia (black box warning)
c.info: D2 antagonist with prokinetic action via enhanced acetylcholine release in the gut; crosses blood-brain barrier causing EPS.

ind: Gastroparesis, nausea/vomiting; used to augment lactation in some countries.
c.doc: Alternative prokinetic where available (not FDA-approved in US)
c.ci: QT prolongation, cardiac disease, hepatic impairment
ae: Dry mouth, headache, galactorrhea
c.sae: QT prolongation, cardiac arrhythmia/sudden death
c.info: Does not readily cross blood-brain barrier, so fewer EPS than metoclopramide; carries cardiac arrhythmia risk.

ind: Chemotherapy-induced nausea/vomiting (adjunct, especially highly emetogenic regimens).
c.doc: Add-on for refractory or breakthrough CINV
c.ci: Hypersensitivity
ae: Sedation, weight gain, hyperglycemia
c.sae: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome (rare)
c.info: Atypical antipsychotic blocking multiple receptors (D2, 5-HT3, 5-HT2A, H1); increasingly used in CINV prevention protocols.

ind: Chemotherapy/radiotherapy-induced and postoperative nausea/vomiting.
c.doc: First-line for chemotherapy-induced nausea/vomiting (CINV)
c.ci: Congenital long QT syndrome
ae: Headache, constipation, QT prolongation
c.sae: QT prolongation, torsades de pointes
c.info: Selective 5-HT3 antagonist blocking serotonin at vagal afferents in the gut and chemoreceptor trigger zone.

ind: Chemotherapy-induced nausea/vomiting.
c.doc: Alternative 5-HT3 antagonist, longer half-life
c.ci: Hypersensitivity
ae: Headache, constipation
c.sae: QT prolongation (less than ondansetron)
c.info: Longer receptor binding and half-life than ondansetron; transdermal patch option for multi-day chemo regimens.

ind: Prevention of acute and delayed CINV, postoperative nausea/vomiting.
c.doc: Preferred for delayed-phase CINV (highly/moderately emetogenic chemo)
c.ci: Hypersensitivity
ae: Headache, constipation, dizziness
c.sae: QT prolongation (minimal risk)
c.info: Second-generation agent with ~40-hour half-life and higher receptor-binding affinity, uniquely effective for delayed-phase CINV.

ind: Chemotherapy-induced and postoperative nausea/vomiting.
c.doc: IV form withdrawn due to QT risk; oral form remains
c.ci: Congenital long QT syndrome
ae: Headache, diarrhea
c.sae: QT prolongation (IV formulation discontinued in the US)
c.info: Active metabolite hydrodolasetron responsible for effect; IV formulation withdrawn from US market over dose-dependent QT prolongation.

c.dose: Oral 125 mg day 1, then 80 mg days 2-3
ind: Prevention of acute and delayed CINV with highly emetogenic chemotherapy (combined with 5-HT3 antagonist + dexamethasone).
c.doc: Triple therapy component for highly emetogenic chemotherapy
c.ci: Concurrent pimozide
ae: Fatigue, hiccups, diarrhea
c.sae: Severe hypersensitivity (rare)
c.info: Blocks substance P/NK1 receptors in the CNS, targeting the delayed phase of CINV; moderate CYP3A4 inhibitor with many interactions.

ind: Prevention of CINV (IV prodrug of aprepitant).
c.doc: IV alternative when oral aprepitant not feasible
c.ci: Concurrent pimozide
ae: Infusion site reactions, fatigue
c.sae: Hypersensitivity/anaphylaxis (rare)
c.info: Water-soluble prodrug rapidly converted to aprepitant after IV administration; single-dose regimen improves adherence.

ind: Prevention of delayed CINV.
c.doc: Alternative NK1 antagonist, longer half-life
c.ci: Concurrent thioridazine
ae: Neutropenia, hiccups, decreased appetite
c.sae: Neutropenia
c.info: Very long half-life (~7 days) and does not inhibit CYP3A4, reducing interaction potential compared to aprepitant.

ind: Refractory chemotherapy-induced nausea/vomiting, appetite stimulation in AIDS-related anorexia.
c.doc: Second-line for CINV refractory to standard antiemetics
c.ci: Hypersensitivity to cannabinoids/sesame oil
ae: Euphoria, dizziness, dry mouth
c.sae: Psychiatric disturbance, tachycardia
c.info: Synthetic delta-9-THC acting on CB1 receptors; abuse potential limits first-line use.

ind: Chemotherapy-induced nausea/vomiting refractory to conventional antiemetics.
c.doc: Second-line synthetic cannabinoid for refractory CINV
c.ci: Hypersensitivity
ae: Drowsiness, dry mouth, vertigo
c.sae: Psychosis, severe hypotension
c.info: Synthetic cannabinoid analog structurally related to THC; CB1 agonism reduces vomiting center activity.

ind: Adjunct antiemetic in chemotherapy regimens (combined with 5-HT3/NK1 antagonists).
c.doc: Standard component of multi-drug CINV prophylaxis
c.ci: Systemic fungal infection
ae: Insomnia, hyperglycemia, agitation
c.sae: Adrenal suppression (repeated use), hyperglycemic crisis
c.info: Exact antiemetic mechanism unclear; thought to reduce prostaglandin production and inhibit CTZ; synergizes with 5-HT3/NK1 antagonists.

ind: Chronic constipation, irritable bowel syndrome, maintenance of regular bowel habit.
c.doc: First-line laxative for chronic constipation/IBS
c.ci: Bowel obstruction, fecal impaction
c.sci: Esophageal stricture (choking risk if taken without water)
ae: Bloating, flatulence, abdominal cramping
c.sae: Esophageal/intestinal obstruction if inadequate fluid intake
c.info: Absorbs water to form a gel, increasing stool bulk and softness; requires adequate fluid intake, onset 1-3 days.
c.caution: Take with at least a full glass (240 mL) of water — swallowing dry can cause choking or obstruction. Works in 12–72 hours; increase the dose gradually to limit gas and keep fluid intake up. Separate from other medicines by about 2 hours.
c.preg: Not absorbed; safe in pregnancy and breastfeeding, and a first-line choice for constipation.
c.renal: No adjustment; keep fluid intake adequate and check the potassium content of some products in advanced kidney disease.

ind: Chronic constipation.
c.doc: Alternative bulk laxative for patients with psyllium sensitivity
c.ci: Bowel obstruction
ae: Bloating, flatulence (less than psyllium)
c.sae: Intestinal obstruction (inadequate fluids)
c.info: Semi-synthetic, non-fermentable fiber, causing less gas/bloating than psyllium.
c.caution: Take with at least a full glass (240 mL) of water — swallowing dry can cause choking or obstruction. Works in 12–72 hours; increase the dose gradually to limit gas and keep fluid intake up. Separate from other medicines by about 2 hours. Suitable for people sensitive to psyllium.
c.preg: Not absorbed; safe in pregnancy and breastfeeding.
c.renal: No adjustment; keep fluid intake adequate.

c.mn:
💊 Names: Psyllium and Methylcellulose.
🎯 Used for: Chronic constipation and IBS — they add water and bulk to stool.
💡 Tip: Always take with a full glass of water. Slow (12–72 h) but the safest for long-term use.

ind: Chronic constipation; also used to lower ammonia in hepatic encephalopathy.
c.doc: Drug of choice for hepatic encephalopathy (ammonia reduction)
c.ci: Galactosemia, bowel obstruction
ae: Bloating, flatulence, abdominal cramps
c.sae: Severe diarrhea with electrolyte loss
c.info: Non-absorbable synthetic disaccharide fermented by colonic bacteria to acidify stool, trapping ammonia as ammonium and drawing water osmotically.
c.caution: Takes 24–48 h to work; gas, bloating and cramps are common early on. Drink plenty of fluids; can be mixed with juice. Avoid in galactosemia. In hepatic encephalopathy, adjust the dose to 2–3 soft stools daily.
c.preg: Not absorbed; considered safe in pregnancy and breastfeeding.
c.renal: No adjustment; monitor fluids and electrolytes if diarrhea develops.

c.dose: Oral 17 g in water OD (maintenance); 4 L for bowel prep
ind: Chronic constipation, bowel preparation for colonoscopy.
c.doc: First-line for chronic constipation; standard bowel preparation agent
c.ci: Bowel obstruction, GI perforation, ileus
c.sci: Toxic megacolon, severe inflammatory bowel disease
ae: Bloating, cramping, nausea
c.sae: Electrolyte disturbances (large-volume bowel prep)
c.info: Non-absorbable osmotic agent that retains water in stool without significant electrolyte shifts; well tolerated for daily use.
c.caution: Mix the powder in 120–240 mL of fluid; effect in 1–3 days for maintenance. Bowel-prep regimens must be followed exactly (usually split doses) with adequate hydration. Avoid in bowel obstruction, perforation or toxic colitis. Rare allergic reactions occur.
c.preg: Not absorbed; considered safe for constipation in pregnancy and breastfeeding. Bowel preparation only when clearly needed.
c.renal: No adjustment for PEG 3350; PEG-electrolyte preps are preferred over sodium phosphate preps in kidney disease (phosphate nephropathy). Use caution with large-volume preps in heart or kidney failure.

ind: Acute constipation, bowel preparation.
c.doc: Fast-acting osmotic laxative for acute relief/bowel prep
c.ci: Renal failure, bowel obstruction
ae: Cramping, diarrhea
c.sae: Hypermagnesemia (renal impairment), dehydration
c.info: Poorly absorbed magnesium salt draws water into the bowel lumen osmotically; onset within 30 minutes-3 hours.
c.st: Oral soln 1.745 g/30 mL (about 300 mL bottle)
c.caution: Chill to improve the taste. Single dose; works in 30 minutes to 6 hours. Drink extra fluids and avoid daily use. Separate from other medicines by about 2 hours. Avoid in bowel obstruction or unexplained abdominal pain.
c.preg: Occasional use is acceptable; avoid frequent use (electrolyte disturbance). Compatible with breastfeeding.
c.renal: Avoid in moderate to severe renal impairment (hypermagnesemia: weakness, low blood pressure, drowsiness).

ind: Constipation (less costly alternative to lactulose).
c.doc: Cost-effective osmotic laxative alternative to lactulose
c.ci: Fructose intolerance, bowel obstruction
ae: Bloating, flatulence, cramping
c.sae: Severe diarrhea and dehydration
c.info: Non-absorbable sugar alcohol with osmotic laxative effect similar to lactulose, at lower cost.
c.caution: Causes gas, bloating and cramps; dilute before taking and start with a small dose. Avoid in hereditary fructose intolerance. Sugar-free products containing sorbitol can cause diarrhea. Works in about 24 hours.
c.preg: Not absorbed; considered safe in pregnancy and breastfeeding.
c.renal: No adjustment; avoid excessive use (dehydration and electrolyte loss).

c.mn:
💊 Names: Polyethylene glycol, Lactulose, Magnesium citrate, Sorbitol.
🎯 Used for: Constipation, bowel preparation, hepatic encephalopathy (lactulose).
💡 Tip: They hold water in the bowel. Lactulose also lowers ammonia. Avoid magnesium products in kidney disease.

c.dose: Oral 5-15 mg HS; PR suppository 10 mg
ind: Acute constipation, bowel preparation.
c.doc: First-line stimulant laxative for short-term/occasional use
c.ci: Bowel obstruction, acute abdomen, severe dehydration
ae: Abdominal cramping, diarrhea
c.sae: Electrolyte imbalance with chronic use, melanosis coli
c.info: Diphenylmethane derivative that directly stimulates enteric nerves, increasing colonic motility and secretion; onset 6-12 h oral, 15-60 min PR.
c.caution: Swallow enteric-coated tablets whole; do not take with milk or antacids. Oral works in 6–12 h, so take at bedtime; suppositories work in 15–60 min. Use for no more than about 7 days to avoid dependence and electrolyte loss. Avoid in bowel obstruction or undiagnosed abdominal pain.
c.preg: Little is absorbed; short-term use is acceptable if bulk laxatives fail. Compatible with breastfeeding.
c.renal: No adjustment for short courses; avoid prolonged use in renal impairment (electrolyte disturbances).

ind: Constipation, especially opioid-induced constipation.
c.doc: First-line for opioid-induced constipation (with stool softener)
c.ci: Bowel obstruction, acute abdominal pain
ae: Abdominal cramps, diarrhea, urine discoloration
c.sae: Melanosis coli, laxative dependency (chronic use)
c.info: Anthraquinone glycoside metabolized by colonic bacteria to active compounds that stimulate motility and fluid secretion.
c.caution: Take at bedtime; works in 6–12 h. Short-term use only (usually under a week) unless advised. May cause cramps; urine may turn reddish-brown. Avoid in bowel obstruction.
c.preg: Generally acceptable short-term if bulk laxatives fail. Small amounts in milk; infant loose stool possible but compatible with breastfeeding.
c.renal: Avoid long-term use in renal impairment (fluid loss, low potassium).

ind: Acute constipation (rarely used, historical bowel prep).
c.doc: Largely historical; occasionally used for acute bowel evacuation
c.ci: Pregnancy (uterine stimulant), bowel obstruction
ae: Severe cramping, nausea
c.sae: Fluid/electrolyte depletion, can induce labor
c.info: Hydrolyzed to ricinoleic acid in the small intestine, which stimulates intestinal motility; unpleasant taste and strong action limit use.
c.caution: Take on an empty stomach, chilled or mixed with juice to hide the taste; works in 2–6 hours. Single dose only. Avoid in bowel obstruction or unexplained abdominal pain. Do not use to induce labor except under medical supervision.
c.preg: Avoid in pregnancy (stimulates uterine contractions). Avoid while breastfeeding.
c.renal: Avoid repeated use in renal impairment (dehydration and electrolyte loss).

c.mn:
💊 Names: 'BSC': Bisacodyl, Senna, Castor oil.
🎯 Used for: Short-term constipation, opioid-induced constipation, bowel preparation.
💡 Tip: Take at bedtime (effect in 6–12 h). Short courses only to avoid dependence and electrolyte loss. Avoid castor oil in pregnancy.

ind: Prevention of straining/constipation (postoperative, postpartum, cardiac patients).
c.doc: Stool softener for prevention (not treatment) of constipation
c.ci: Bowel obstruction, acute abdominal pain
ae: Mild cramping, diarrhea
c.sae: Rare hepatotoxicity (with long-term high dose)
c.info: Anionic surfactant that lowers stool surface tension, allowing water/fat to penetrate stool; weak laxative effect alone, often combined with a stimulant.
c.caution: Stool softener with weak evidence; works in 1–3 days. Take with a full glass of water. Do not combine with mineral oil. Often paired with senna for opioid-induced constipation.
c.preg: Minimal absorption; considered safe. Compatible with breastfeeding.
c.renal: No adjustment; avoid excessive use (electrolyte loss).

ind: Constipation, fecal impaction (lubricant).
c.doc: Lubricant laxative for fecal impaction/short-term use
c.ci: Dysphagia, bedridden/aspiration risk patients
ae: Anal leakage, decreased fat-soluble vitamin absorption
c.sae: Lipoid pneumonia (aspiration), malabsorption of vitamins A/D/E/K
c.info: Indigestible oil that coats and lubricates stool; aspiration risk, especially in elderly/bedridden patients, limits use.
c.caution: Take on an empty stomach at bedtime, not with meals and never lying down (aspiration and lipoid pneumonia risk). Avoid in young children, the elderly and people with swallowing problems. Short-term use only (up to about 1 week); it reduces absorption of fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K) and other medicines.
c.preg: Avoid prolonged use (vitamin K and other fat-soluble vitamin depletion); occasional use only. Not absorbed, so breastfeeding is compatible.
c.renal: No adjustment; avoid chronic use.

ind: Acute constipation, especially in children and elderly.
c.doc: Rapid-acting rectal laxative for acute relief
c.ci: Rectal fissures/hemorrhoids (irritation)
ae: Rectal irritation, cramping
c.sae: None significant at recommended use
c.info: Hyperosmotic agent drawing water into the rectum and lubricating stool passage; acts within 15-60 minutes.
c.caution: Moisten the suppository with water, insert fully and retain for 15–30 minutes; works in 15–60 minutes. Short-term use only. Do not use with rectal bleeding or severe abdominal pain.
c.preg: Minimal absorption; safe in pregnancy and breastfeeding.
c.renal: No adjustment.

c.mn:
💊 Names: Docusate sodium, Mineral oil, Glycerin.
🎯 Used for: Softening stool and easing straining (after surgery, hemorrhoids).
💡 Tip: Docusate has weak evidence; mineral oil can cause aspiration pneumonia and blocks vitamin absorption; glycerin suppositories work in minutes.

c.dose: Oral 524 mg (2 tabs/30 mL) q30-60min PRN (max 8 doses/day)
ind: Acute diarrhea, traveler's diarrhea prophylaxis, dyspepsia.
c.doc: Traveler's diarrhea prophylaxis and symptomatic treatment
c.ci: Aspirin/salicylate allergy, children with viral illness (Reye syndrome risk)
ae: Black stool/tongue, tinnitus (high dose)
c.sae: Salicylate toxicity (overdose), Reye syndrome (children)
c.info: Has antisecretory, antimicrobial, and anti-inflammatory actions; salicylate component confers aspirin-related risks and interactions.
c.st: Chew Tab 262 mg · Liquid 262, 524 mg/15 mL
c.caution: Chew tablets or shake the liquid. It can turn the tongue and stool black (harmless but can mimic bleeding). It contains salicylate — avoid with aspirin, warfarin and in aspirin allergy, and do not give to children or teenagers with viral illness (Reye syndrome). Limit to 2 days for diarrhea. Ringing in the ears signals excess.
c.preg: Avoid in pregnancy and breastfeeding because of the salicylate content.
c.renal: Avoid in renal impairment (salicylate and bismuth can accumulate).

ind: Acute nonspecific diarrhea.
c.doc: Alternative to loperamide for acute diarrhea
c.ci: Bloody diarrhea/dysentery, pseudomembranous colitis, obstructive jaundice
ae: Dry mouth, drowsiness, constipation
c.sae: CNS/respiratory depression (overdose, especially children), toxic megacolon
c.info: Opioid agonist combined with subtherapeutic atropine to discourage abuse/overdose; crosses blood-brain barrier more than loperamide at high dose.
c.st: Tab 2.5 mg/0.025 mg · Liq 2.5 mg/0.025 mg per 5 mL
c.caution: Opioid-based (controlled substance): keep away from children — overdose in young children can be fatal (breathing depression). Do not use in bloody diarrhea, high fever, dysentery or C. difficile. Stop if no improvement in 48 hours. Avoid alcohol and sedatives; atropine can cause dry mouth and blurred vision. Not for children under 6.
c.preg: Limited data; avoid near term (neonatal opioid effects) and use only if needed. Small amounts pass into breast milk; avoid.
c.renal: Use caution in renal impairment (metabolites accumulate); avoid in severe liver disease and obstructive jaundice.

c.dose: Oral 4 mg initially, then 2 mg after each loose stool (max 16 mg/day)
ind: Acute and chronic diarrhea (including traveler's diarrhea, IBS-D).
c.doc: First-line OTC antidiarrheal for uncomplicated acute diarrhea
c.ci: Bloody diarrhea/dysentery, pseudomembranous colitis, bacterial enterocolitis
ae: Constipation, abdominal cramping, dizziness
c.sae: Toxic megacolon (in infectious colitis), QT prolongation (high/abused doses)
c.info: Peripheral opioid mu-receptor agonist acting on intestinal muscle; minimal CNS penetration/abuse potential at normal doses, but high doses can cause cardiotoxicity.
c.caution: Do not exceed 8 mg/day OTC (16 mg prescription). High doses cause serious heart rhythm problems (QT prolongation). Avoid in bloody diarrhea, high fever, dysentery or C. difficile. Not for children under 12 (OTC). Stop if no better after 48 hours.
c.preg: Limited data; avoid in the first trimester if possible. Short-term use later is acceptable if needed. Very little passes into breast milk.
c.renal: No adjustment for renal impairment; use caution in severe hepatic impairment (higher levels).

ind: Severe secretory diarrhea (e.g., carcinoid syndrome, VIPoma, chemotherapy-induced, AIDS-related).
c.doc: Refractory/secretory diarrhea unresponsive to standard agents
c.ci: Hypersensitivity
ae: Injection site pain, nausea, gallstones
c.sae: Cholelithiasis, bradycardia, hyperglycemia/hypoglycemia
c.info: Somatostatin analog that inhibits secretion of multiple GI hormones (VIP, gastrin, serotonin), reducing intestinal secretion and motility.
c.caution: Subcutaneous injection: rotate sites and let the vial reach room temperature. Start with 50 mcg two or three times daily for secretory diarrhea. Monitor glucose (both high and low), thyroid function, heart rate (bradycardia) and gallbladder (gallstones) with long-term use. LAR depot is given monthly by a clinician after a short trial of SC doses.
c.preg: Limited data; use only if clearly needed. Excretion into breast milk is unknown; avoid breastfeeding.
c.renal: Clearance falls in severe renal impairment and cirrhosis; start with lower doses and monitor.

ind: Acute diarrhea (adjunct to oral rehydration).
c.doc: Antisecretory adjunct where available (not marketed in US)
c.ci: Hypersensitivity
ae: Headache, rash
c.sae: Angioedema (rare)
c.info: Enkephalinase inhibitor with purely antisecretory (not antimotility) action, reducing intestinal fluid loss without causing constipation or ileus.
c.caution: Give with the first main meal; capsules can be opened into food. Use together with oral rehydration — it does not replace fluids. Child dose is 1.5 mg/kg three times daily. Stop after a maximum of about 7 days. Rare angioedema and skin reactions; higher risk with ACE inhibitors. Not marketed in the US.
c.preg: Not recommended in pregnancy or breastfeeding (no data).
c.renal: Use caution in severe renal or hepatic impairment (limited data).

c.mn:
💊 Names: Loperamide, Diphenoxylate/Atropine, Bismuth subsalicylate, Racecadotril, Octreotide.
🎯 Used for: Acute and chronic diarrhea.
💡 Tip: Avoid opioid-type agents (loperamide, diphenoxylate) in bloody diarrhea or fever. Keep diphenoxylate away from children. Bismuth turns stool black.

ind: Peptic ulcer disease, stress ulcer prophylaxis.
c.doc: Stress ulcer prophylaxis in critically ill patients (low systemic risk)
c.ci: Hypersensitivity
ae: Constipation, dry mouth
c.sae: Bezoar formation (rare), aluminum toxicity in renal failure
c.info: Aluminum sucrose sulfate that forms a protective viscous gel over ulcer base in acidic environment; requires acidic pH and separate dosing from antacids/PPIs.

ind: Component of quadruple therapy for H. pylori eradication.
c.doc: Bismuth quadruple therapy (with PPI, tetracycline, metronidazole)
c.ci: Salicylate allergy
ae: Black stool/tongue, nausea
c.sae: Salicylate toxicity (overdose)
c.info: Coats ulcer base and has direct antibacterial activity against H. pylori; key component of quadruple eradication therapy.

ind: Prevention of NSAID-induced gastric ulcers; also used in obstetrics (labor induction, medical abortion).
c.doc: Prophylaxis of NSAID-induced ulcers in high-risk patients
c.ci: Pregnancy (unless used for obstetric indication)
c.sci: Women of childbearing age not using contraception
ae: Diarrhea, abdominal cramping
c.sae: Uterine contractions/miscarriage (contraindicated in pregnancy for GI indication)
c.info: Synthetic PGE1 analog that restores prostaglandin-mediated mucosal protection (mucus/bicarbonate secretion) suppressed by NSAIDs.

ind: Mild-moderate ulcerative colitis, rheumatoid arthritis.
c.doc: First-line for mild-moderate ulcerative colitis maintenance
c.ci: Sulfonamide/salicylate hypersensitivity, G6PD deficiency
ae: Nausea, headache, oligospermia (reversible)
c.sae: Stevens-Johnson syndrome, agranulocytosis, hepatotoxicity
c.info: Prodrug split by colonic bacteria into sulfapyridine (carrier, causes most side effects) and 5-aminosalicylic acid (active anti-inflammatory moiety).

c.dose: Oral 800 mg-1.2 g TID or delayed-release formulations OD; also PR suppository/enema
ind: Ulcerative colitis induction and maintenance (mild-moderate), some use in Crohn disease.
c.doc: First-line for mild-moderate ulcerative colitis (better tolerated than sulfasalazine)
c.ci: Salicylate hypersensitivity
ae: Headache, abdominal pain, diarrhea
c.sae: Interstitial nephritis, mesalamine-induced pericarditis (rare)
c.info: Pure 5-ASA without the sulfapyridine carrier, reducing side effects; various delivery systems (pH-dependent release, sustained-release, rectal) target different bowel segments.

ind: Mild-moderate ulcerative colitis.
c.doc: Alternative 5-ASA prodrug for colitis
c.ci: Salicylate hypersensitivity
ae: Headache, abdominal pain, diarrhea
c.sae: Interstitial nephritis (rare)
c.info: Prodrug releasing 5-ASA specifically in the colon via bacterial azo-bond cleavage, sparing an inert carrier (unlike sulfapyridine).

ind: Maintenance of remission in ulcerative colitis.
c.doc: Alternative for maintenance in sulfasalazine-intolerant patients
c.ci: Salicylate hypersensitivity
ae: Diarrhea (dose-related, especially early treatment)
c.sae: Interstitial nephritis (rare)
c.info: Two 5-ASA molecules linked by an azo bond, cleaved by colonic bacteria to release active drug specifically in the colon.

ind: Maintenance of remission in Crohn disease and ulcerative colitis (steroid-sparing).
c.doc: Steroid-sparing maintenance therapy for moderate-severe IBD
c.ci: Pregnancy (relative), concurrent allopurinol without dose reduction
c.sci: TPMT deficiency (check enzyme activity before starting)
ae: Nausea, leukopenia, hepatotoxicity
c.sae: Bone marrow suppression, pancreatitis, lymphoma risk (long-term)
c.info: Prodrug of 6-mercaptopurine; metabolized via thiopurine methyltransferase (TPMT) - genetic testing recommended before initiation to avoid severe myelosuppression.

c.dose: IV 5 mg/kg at weeks 0, 2, 6, then q8 weeks
ind: Moderate-severe Crohn disease and ulcerative colitis refractory to conventional therapy.
c.doc: First-line biologic for moderate-severe IBD, especially fistulizing Crohn disease
c.ci: Active serious infection, untreated latent TB, moderate-severe heart failure
ae: Infusion reactions, headache
c.sae: Reactivation of latent TB/hepatitis B, serious infections, lymphoma (rare)
c.info: Chimeric monoclonal antibody neutralizing tumor necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-alpha); screening for latent TB required before initiation.

c.dose: SC 160 mg week 0, 80 mg week 2, then 40 mg q2weeks
ind: Moderate-severe Crohn disease and ulcerative colitis.
c.doc: Self-administered anti-TNF alternative to infliximab
c.ci: Active serious infection, untreated latent TB
ae: Injection site reactions, headache
c.sae: Serious infections, TB reactivation, lymphoma (rare)
c.info: Fully human anti-TNF-alpha monoclonal antibody; subcutaneous self-injection allows outpatient/home administration unlike infliximab.

c.dose: IV 300 mg at weeks 0, 2, 6, then q8 weeks
ind: Moderate-severe ulcerative colitis and Crohn disease, especially when anti-TNF fails.
c.doc: Gut-selective biologic for anti-TNF-refractory IBD
c.ci: Active severe infection
ae: Headache, arthralgia, nasopharyngitis
c.sae: Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (theoretical, rare), infusion reactions
c.info: Monoclonal antibody against alpha4-beta7 integrin, blocking lymphocyte trafficking specifically to the gut, giving gut-selective immunosuppression with a favorable safety profile.

c.dose: IV weight-based induction, then SC 90 mg q8weeks
ind: Moderate-severe Crohn disease and ulcerative colitis.
c.doc: Alternative biologic for IBD refractory to anti-TNF/anti-integrin therapy
c.ci: Active serious infection
ae: Nasopharyngitis, headache, injection site reactions
c.sae: Serious infections, malignancy (theoretical)
c.info: Monoclonal antibody targeting the shared p40 subunit of IL-12 and IL-23, blocking Th1/Th17-mediated inflammation.

ind: Moderate-severe ulcerative colitis refractory to anti-TNF therapy.
c.doc: Oral option for ulcerative colitis after biologic failure
c.ci: Active serious infection, prior thrombosis (relative)
ae: Headache, nasopharyngitis, elevated lipids
c.sae: Venous thromboembolism, major cardiovascular events, malignancy (boxed warning)
c.info: Oral Janus kinase (JAK) inhibitor blocking cytokine signaling; boxed warning for thrombosis/cardiovascular events, especially in older patients with risk factors.

ind: Mild-to-moderate pain, headache, fever in adults, and antiplatelet prophylaxis for cardiovascular events.
c.doc: Secondary cardiovascular/cerebrovascular event prevention (low dose 75-100 mg)
c.ci: Children and teenagers with viral infections (Reye syndrome), active bleeding, hemophilia
ae: Gastric irritation, occult GI bleeding, tinnitus, bruising
c.sae: Reye syndrome in children / Salicylism in toxicity
c.info: Irreversibly acetylates COX-1 and COX-2, permanently blocking thromboxane A2 synthesis in platelets for their lifespan (~7-10 days).
c.caution: Take with or after food and a full glass of water; use enteric-coated tablets for long-term low-dose therapy. Do not give to children under 16 unless prescribed. Stop before surgery as advised (usually 5–7 days) unless taken for secondary prevention. Avoid other NSAIDs at the same time.
c.preg: Avoid analgesic doses, especially from 20 weeks and in the third trimester (fetal kidney dysfunction, ductus closure, bleeding, prolonged labor). Low-dose aspirin (75–150 mg) is used deliberately from about 12 weeks to reduce pre-eclampsia risk in high-risk women. Low-dose exposure through breast milk is small and generally acceptable; avoid regular analgesic doses while breastfeeding.
c.renal: Avoid analgesic doses in severe renal impairment (CrCl below 10–30 mL/min) because of fluid retention, AKI and hyperkalemia; low-dose antiplatelet use is generally tolerated. Avoid in severe hepatic impairment (bleeding risk).

ind: Fast temporary surface anesthesia for severe toothache, canker sores, and denture irritation.
c.doc: Topical immediate numbing for localized oral/gum mucosa and canker sores
c.ci: Hypersensitivity to ester local anesthetics, infants <2 years
c.sci: Infants and teething babies (risk of life-threatening methemoglobinemia)
ae: Local burning, tingling, contact dermatitis, altered taste
c.sae: Methemoglobinemia
c.info: Ester-type local anesthetic that blocks voltage-gated sodium channels in sensory nerve endings, preventing generation and conduction of pain impulses.
c.caution: Use the smallest amount on intact skin or mucosa and no longer than 7 days. Do not use teething gels in children under 2 years. Stop and seek urgent help if lips or nails turn blue/gray, or if breathing is difficult (methemoglobinemia).
c.preg: Limited data; small-area topical use is low risk and generally acceptable in pregnancy. Systemic absorption is minimal, so it is compatible with breastfeeding at usual amounts.
c.renal: No adjustment for topical use at recommended amounts; avoid large mucosal areas in severe renal or hepatic disease.

c.st: Tab 500, 650 mg, 1 g · Susp 120, 250 mg/5 mL · Supp 80–1000 mg · Inj 10 mg/mL
c.dose: Tab 500 mg, 650 mg, 1 g · Syr 120 mg/5 mL, 250 mg/5 mL · Drops 100 mg/mL
ind: First-line antipyretic and analgesic for fever, headache, body aches, and mild dental pain.
c.doc: First-line antipyretic in pregnancy, pediatrics, and dengue/viral fevers
c.ci: Severe active hepatic disease, hypersensitivity
c.sci: Acute hepatic failure (toxic metabolite NAPQI accumulation in overdose)
ae: Nausea, rash, elevated liver enzymes with high doses
c.sae: Centrilobular hepatic necrosis in overdose
c.info: Centrally acting inhibitor of prostaglandin synthesis with minimal peripheral anti-inflammatory action; metabolized via glucuronidation and sulfation.
c.caution: Adults 500 mg–1 g every 4–6 h, maximum 4 g/day (3 g/day or less with chronic alcohol use, malnutrition or low weight). Children 10–15 mg/kg every 4–6 h, maximum 60 mg/kg/day. Check combination cold and flu products to avoid double dosing. Overdose is an emergency even if the person feels well — seek urgent care.
c.preg: Preferred analgesic and antipyretic in pregnancy at the lowest effective dose for the shortest time; some observational studies have raised questions about prolonged use, but regulators still consider it acceptable when needed. Small amounts pass into breast milk; compatible with breastfeeding.
c.renal: No adjustment in mild renal impairment; in severe impairment (CrCl below 10 mL/min) extend the interval to at least 8 h (IV: 6 h when CrCl is 30 mL/min or less). In liver disease, chronic alcohol use or malnutrition, reduce the maximum daily dose (2–3 g).

ind: Treatment and prevention of gingivitis, oral candidiasis, mouth ulcers, and post-dental surgical disinfection.
c.doc: Gold standard anti-plaque and antiseptic mouthwash for acute gingivitis and oral surgery care
c.ci: Hypersensitivity to chlorhexidine
c.sci: Direct application to the middle ear or eyes (ototoxicity/corneal damage)
ae: Brown staining of teeth/tongue, altered taste sensation, transient oral mucosa peeling
c.sae: Reversible extrinsic tooth staining and taste alteration
c.info: Cationic bisbiguanide that binds negatively charged bacterial cell walls, causing cytoplasmic membrane rupture and broad bactericidal action.
c.caution: Rinse 10–15 mL for 30 seconds and spit out; do not swallow, and do not rinse with water or eat for 30 minutes. May stain teeth and tongue brown and change taste; use for up to 2 weeks unless directed. Keep out of eyes and ears.
c.preg: Minimal absorption; acceptable in pregnancy and breastfeeding as a mouthwash or skin antiseptic (rinse the nipple before nursing).
c.renal: Negligible absorption; no adjustment.

ind: Painful mouth ulcers, denture friction sores, and inflamed gums.
c.doc: Topical analgesic and anti-inflammatory gel for painful aphthous ulcers and denture irritation
c.ci: Aspirin allergy, active ulceration in children <16 years (Reye syndrome risk)
c.sci: Children under 16 years (theoretical salicylate Reye syndrome link)
ae: Local tingling on application, mild temporary numbness
c.sae: Salicylate toxicity on excessive chronic swallowing
c.info: Water-soluble salicylate salt that rapidly penetrates oral mucous membranes to suppress local prostaglandin synthesis without stinging.
c.caution: Apply a pea-sized amount to the ulcer with a clean finger, at most every 3 hours (up to 6 times/day). Not for children under 16 because of the salicylate (Reye syndrome). Avoid in aspirin allergy.
c.preg: Small amounts of salicylate are absorbed — avoid in the third trimester; use a non-salicylate mouth gel instead. Occasional use while breastfeeding is generally acceptable.
c.renal: Avoid frequent use in severe renal impairment; systemic exposure is small.

ind: Short-term relief of acute dental pain, primary dysmenorrhea, and inflammatory headaches.
c.doc: Primary dysmenorrhea and acute post-dental extraction pain
c.ci: Active GI ulceration, inflammatory bowel disease, severe renal disease
c.sci: Treatment duration >7 days (risk of severe diarrhea and renal papillary necrosis)
ae: Diarrhea, dyspepsia, drowsiness, abdominal cramps
c.sae: Severe steatorrhea/diarrhea / Autoimmune hemolytic anemia
c.info: Anthranilic acid derivative that inhibits COX enzymes and directly blocks prostaglandin receptors on target tissues.
c.caution: Take with food. Usual adult dose 500 mg once, then 250 mg every 6 h, for no more than 7 days. Stop if diarrhea or rash develops. Keep away from children — overdose can cause seizures.
c.preg: Avoid from 20 weeks (risk of fetal kidney dysfunction and low amniotic fluid) and in the third trimester (premature closure of the ductus arteriosus, bleeding, prolonged labor); earlier in pregnancy use only if clearly needed, at the lowest dose for the shortest time. Passes into breast milk in small amounts; short-term use is acceptable, though prefer ibuprofen.
c.renal: NSAIDs lower renal prostaglandins and can cause acute kidney injury, fluid retention and hyperkalemia — avoid in severe renal impairment (CrCl below 30 mL/min), and be careful with dehydration, diuretics and ACE inhibitors/ARBs. Contraindicated in severe hepatic impairment; monitor renal function during longer use.

ind: Acute inflammatory pain, toothache, fever, dysmenorrhea, and musculoskeletal aches.
c.doc: First-line NSAID for inflammatory toothache and pediatric fever refractory to paracetamol
c.ci: Active peptic ulcer, third-trimester pregnancy, severe renal impairment, aspirin-induced asthma
c.sci: Third-trimester pregnancy (premature closure of ductus arteriosus)
ae: Dyspepsia, heartburn, GI ulceration, fluid retention, nausea
c.sae: Gastrointestinal bleeding and acute kidney injury
c.info: Non-selective reversible inhibitor of COX-1 and COX-2; reduces peripheral prostaglandin synthesis to suppress inflammation and pain.
c.caution: Take with food or milk. Take low-dose aspirin at least 30 minutes before, or 8 hours after, ibuprofen. Children: 5–10 mg/kg every 6–8 h (maximum 40 mg/kg/day); give under 3 months only on medical advice. Avoid when dehydrated or during chickenpox.
c.preg: Avoid from 20 weeks (risk of fetal kidney dysfunction and low amniotic fluid) and in the third trimester (premature closure of the ductus arteriosus, bleeding, prolonged labor); earlier in pregnancy use only if clearly needed, at the lowest dose for the shortest time. Ibuprofen is the preferred NSAID during breastfeeding — very low milk levels, compatible with nursing.
c.renal: NSAIDs lower renal prostaglandins and can cause acute kidney injury, fluid retention and hyperkalemia — avoid in severe renal impairment (CrCl below 30 mL/min), and be careful with dehydration, diuretics and ACE inhibitors/ARBs. Avoid in severe hepatic impairment; caution in cirrhosis (fluid retention and renal failure).

c.st: Tab 25, 50, 75, 100 mg · Inj 75 mg/3 mL · Gel 1%
c.dose: Tab 25, 50 mg · SR Tab 75, 100 mg · Gel 1% · Inj 75 mg/3 mL
ind: Moderate-to-severe dental pain, acute musculoskeletal injuries, and post-traumatic inflammation.
c.doc: Acute dental and post-surgical inflammatory pain (diclofenac potassium for rapid onset)
c.ci: Established ischemic heart disease, peripheral arterial disease, congestive heart failure
c.sci: Established cardiovascular disease (highest thrombotic risk among non-selective NSAIDs)
ae: Epigastric distress, fluid retention, headache, elevated transaminases
c.sae: Increased thrombotic cardiovascular events
c.info: Potent phenylacetic acid derivative with balanced COX-1/COX-2 inhibition and mild inhibition of the arachidonic acid lipoxygenase pathway.
c.caution: Take with or after food; swallow enteric-coated and modified-release tablets whole. Use the lowest dose for the shortest time and check liver enzymes with long-term use. IM injection can damage tissue — use only when needed. Topical gel: thin layer on intact skin, wash hands.
c.preg: Avoid from 20 weeks (risk of fetal kidney dysfunction and low amniotic fluid) and in the third trimester (premature closure of the ductus arteriosus, bleeding, prolonged labor); earlier in pregnancy use only if clearly needed, at the lowest dose for the shortest time. Very low levels in breast milk; generally acceptable while breastfeeding at usual doses.
c.renal: NSAIDs lower renal prostaglandins and can cause acute kidney injury, fluid retention and hyperkalemia — avoid in severe renal impairment (CrCl below 30 mL/min), and be careful with dehydration, diuretics and ACE inhibitors/ARBs. Hepatotoxic — monitor liver enzymes and avoid in severe hepatic impairment.

c.st: Tab 250, 375, 500 mg · Na salt 275, 550 mg · Susp 125 mg/5 mL
ind: Sustained dental pain, osteoarthritis, acute gout flares, and tension headache.
c.doc: Preferred long-acting NSAID for patients needing 12-hour pain relief with lowest relative cardiovascular risk
c.ci: Active peptic ulcer, CABG perioperative pain, severe renal failure
ae: Epigastric pain, headache, edema, dizziness
c.sae: GI ulceration / Microscopic bleeding
c.info: Propionic acid derivative with a long elimination half-life (~14 hours); provides prolonged anti-inflammatory and analgesic coverage.
c.caution: Take with food or milk. Do not take naproxen and naproxen sodium products together. OTC naproxen sodium: 220 mg every 8–12 h, maximum 660 mg/day. Report black stools or vomiting blood.
c.preg: Avoid from 20 weeks (risk of fetal kidney dysfunction and low amniotic fluid) and in the third trimester (premature closure of the ductus arteriosus, bleeding, prolonged labor); earlier in pregnancy use only if clearly needed, at the lowest dose for the shortest time. Present in breast milk and its long half-life may cause accumulation in the infant; prefer ibuprofen, especially for newborns.
c.renal: NSAIDs lower renal prostaglandins and can cause acute kidney injury, fluid retention and hyperkalemia — avoid in severe renal impairment (CrCl below 30 mL/min), and be careful with dehydration, diuretics and ACE inhibitors/ARBs. Avoid in severe hepatic impairment.

ind: Topical emergency relief for pulpitis pain, deep cavity ache, and localized dry socket discomfort.
c.doc: Traditional immediate home/chairside relief for acute open dental cavities and dry socket
c.ci: Hypersensitivity, damaged or deep soft tissue lacerations, unguided pediatric use
c.sci: Ingestion of concentrated oil (severe hepatotoxicity and CNS depression)
ae: Local mucosal irritation, burning sensation, gum erythema
c.sae: Chemical burn/necrosis of delicate gingival tissues on direct spill
c.info: Natural phenolic compound with local anesthetic properties via sodium channel blockade, weak anti-inflammatory action, and broad antimicrobial efficacy.
c.caution: Never swallow concentrated oil. Dilute it, apply a tiny amount on cotton to the tooth only (not the gums) and keep away from children (liver injury, seizures). Stop if burning occurs and see a dentist.
c.preg: Avoid concentrated oil in pregnancy and breastfeeding; food-flavoring amounts are fine. Dental use should be brief until you see a dentist.
c.renal: Avoid ingestion in renal or hepatic impairment; tiny topical dental amounts have no established adjustment.

c.dose: Tab 30, 60 mg · ER Tab 120, 240 mg · Syr 30 mg/5 mL
ind: Nasal congestion, sinus pressure, and eustachian tube congestion caused by colds or allergies.
c.doc: Oral systemic decongestant of choice for severe nasal and sinus congestion without rebound rhinitis
c.ci: Severe uncontrolled hypertension, severe coronary artery disease, MAOI use within 14 days
c.sci: Severe uncontrolled hypertension / Acute myocardial ischemia
ae: Insomnia, palpitations, tachycardia, nervousness, hypertension, urinary hesitation
c.sae: Hypertensive crisis and cardiac arrhythmias
c.info: Direct and indirect sympathomimetic amine; stimulates alpha-adrenergic receptors causing vasoconstriction of swollen nasal mucosal blood vessels.
c.st: Tab 30, 60 mg · ER Tab 120, 240 mg · Syr 30 mg/5 mL
c.caution: Take earlier in the day (can cause insomnia). Avoid in uncontrolled hypertension, coronary disease, hyperthyroidism, glaucoma and prostate enlargement, and with MAO inhibitors. Adults 60 mg every 4–6 h (maximum 240 mg/day) or ER 120 mg every 12 h. Raises blood pressure and heart rate.
c.preg: Avoid in the first trimester (gastroschisis association) and generally avoid throughout pregnancy. Small amounts pass into breast milk and may reduce milk supply or make the infant irritable.
c.renal: Cleared by the kidneys — reduce the dose and avoid in severe renal impairment.

ind: Symptomatic relief of nasal congestion associated with acute rhinitis and sinusitis.
c.doc: OTC oral substitute for restricted pseudoephedrine and topical rapid nasal decongestant
c.ci: Severe hypertension, ventricular tachycardia, narrow-angle glaucoma, MAOI therapy
ae: Reflex bradycardia, elevated blood pressure, restlessness, insomnia, local rebound congestion (topical)
c.sae: Hypertension and topical rebound congestion
c.info: Direct-acting selective alpha-1 adrenergic receptor agonist causing local vascular constriction; oral bioavailability is low (~38%) due to extensive gut/liver monoamine oxidase metabolism.
c.caution: An FDA advisory committee judged oral OTC phenylephrine ineffective as a decongestant (2023); regulatory status is under review, so check the local position. Nasal sprays work, but limit to 3 days to avoid rebound congestion. Can raise blood pressure.
c.preg: Limited data; avoid oral use in the first trimester if possible and use non-drug measures or saline first. Breastfeeding data are limited.
c.renal: No formal adjustment; use caution in hypertension and severe renal impairment.

c.st: Cap/Tab 25, 50 mg · Syrup 12.5 mg/5 mL · Inj 50 mg/mL
ind: Acute allergic reactions, allergic insomnia, motion sickness, and nighttime cough from cold.
c.doc: Acute mild-to-moderate systemic allergic reactions and short-term OTC sleep aid for allergy sufferers
c.ci: Neonates/premature infants, narrow-angle glaucoma, severe asthma exacerbation
c.sci: Elderly patients (high risk of anticholinergic confusion, delirium, and falls)
ae: Pronounced sedation, dry mouth, urinary retention, thick bronchial secretions, constipation
c.sae: Anticholinergic delirium and marked central depression
c.info: Ethanolamine-class first-generation antihistamine with potent central H1-antagonism, muscarinic receptor blockade, and anti-emetic properties.
c.caution: Causes drowsiness — avoid driving and alcohol. Avoid in older adults (confusion, urinary retention, falls) and do not give to children under 6 for cough and cold. Adults 25–50 mg every 4–6 h, maximum 300 mg/day.
c.preg: Long history of use; generally considered acceptable at usual doses if needed. Passes into breast milk and can cause infant drowsiness and reduce milk supply — avoid regular use while breastfeeding.
c.renal: Extend the dosing interval in severe renal impairment; use caution in liver disease.

ind: Acute symptom relief in common cold, allergic rhinitis, insect bites, and acute urticaria.
c.doc: Nighttime symptomatic control for cold-related runny nose and acute pruritic flares
c.ci: Narrow-angle glaucoma, benign prostatic hyperplasia, concurrent MAOI use
c.sci: Narrow-angle glaucoma and acute urinary retention
ae: Marked drowsiness, dry mouth, blurred vision, urinary retention, dizziness
c.sae: Significant sedation and anticholinergic side effects
c.info: First-generation alkylamine H1-blocker that readily crosses the blood-brain barrier; exhibits significant central sedative and peripheral anticholinergic properties.
c.caution: Drowsiness — avoid alcohol and driving. Avoid in children under 6 and in the elderly (anticholinergic effects). Adults 4 mg every 4–6 h, maximum 24 mg/day.
c.preg: Long experience without a clear risk; acceptable when needed at usual doses. Passes into breast milk and may cause infant irritability or drowsiness and reduce milk supply — use occasionally.
c.renal: Lengthen the interval in severe renal impairment; use caution in liver disease.

c.dose: Tab 200, 400 mg · ER Tab 600, 1200 mg · Syr 100 mg/5 mL
ind: Chest congestion and productive cough with thick, tenacious phlegm.
c.doc: First-line oral expectorant to thin respiratory tract secretions in productive wet cough
c.ci: Hypersensitivity, persistent chronic cough from smoking or emphysema without diagnosis
c.sci: Use in chronic cough without adequate daily water hydration
ae: Nausea, vomiting, stomach pain, mild dizziness, headache
c.sae: Nausea and GI upset with high doses
c.info: Increases the volume and reduces the viscosity of respiratory secretions by stimulating bronchial secretory glands, facilitating mucus clearance via ciliary action.
c.st: Tab 200, 400 mg · ER Tab 600, 1200 mg · Syr 100 mg/5 mL
c.caution: Drink plenty of fluids. Adults 200–400 mg every 4 h (maximum 2.4 g/day) or extended-release 600–1200 mg every 12 h; swallow ER tablets whole. See a doctor if cough lasts more than 7 days or comes with fever or rash. Not for children under 4.
c.preg: Limited data; avoid in the first trimester if possible and use only if needed. Breastfeeding: probably compatible, with limited data.
c.renal: No specific adjustment for short courses; use caution in severe renal impairment.

ind: Symptomatic suppression of non-productive dry, irritating, and tickly cough.
c.doc: First-line non-narcotic cough suppressant for disturbing dry nocturnal cough
c.ci: Concurrent or recent (within 14 days) MAOI use, productive phlegmy cough, asthma/COPD
c.sci: Concurrent MAOI or SSRI use (precipitates life-threatening Serotonin Syndrome)
ae: Drowsiness, dizziness, nausea, mild stomach distress
c.sae: Serotonin syndrome / Dissociative abuse liability at massive doses
c.info: d-Isomer of codeine analog that acts centrally on the medullary cough center to elevate threshold; acts as an NMDA receptor antagonist and weak serotonin reuptake blocker.
c.caution: Do not use with MAO inhibitors or within 14 days of stopping one. Avoid with SSRIs, bupropion and quinidine (serotonin syndrome, higher levels). Not for children under 6. Adults 10–20 mg every 4 h, maximum 120 mg/day. Not for chronic cough from smoking or asthma. High doses are misused.
c.preg: Limited data but no clear risk; acceptable for short-term use if needed. Very little passes into breast milk; occasional use is compatible.
c.renal: No adjustment for short courses; use caution in severe hepatic impairment (higher levels).

ind: Severe acute nasal congestion, acute sinusitis, and eustachian tube block.
c.doc: Emergency topical spray for severe acute nasal blockage (strict maximum use: 3-5 consecutive days)
c.ci: Rhinitis sicca, transsphenoidal surgery, concurrent MAOI use
c.sci: Use beyond 3 to 5 consecutive days (causes severe rhinitis medicamentosa / rebound congestion)
ae: Nasal stinging, dryness, sneezing, headache, profound rebound congestion upon cessation
c.sae: Rhinitis medicamentosa (rebound chemical nasal congestion)
c.info: Direct-acting imidazoline alpha-1 and alpha-2 adrenergic agonist causing potent rapid constriction of dilated mucosal arterioles; excessive use downregulates alpha receptors.
c.caution: Use for no more than 3 days — longer causes rebound congestion (rhinitis medicamentosa). 2–3 sprays per nostril, no more than twice daily. Not for children under 6. Avoid with MAO inhibitors. Accidental swallowing by children is dangerous (slow heart rate, low BP).
c.preg: Limited data; a short course is acceptable if needed, but saline is preferred first. Short-term use while breastfeeding is acceptable.
c.renal: No adjustment for short topical use; use caution in severe hypertension or heart disease.

ind: Allergic rhinitis, hay fever, chronic urticaria, itchy watery eyes, and allergic sneezing.
c.doc: First-line rapid-acting once-daily antihistamine for seasonal allergic rhinitis and urticaria
c.ci: End-stage renal disease (CrCl <10 mL/min), hypersensitivity to hydroxyzine
c.sci: Severe renal failure without dose reduction
ae: Mild drowsiness, dry mouth, fatigue, headache
c.sae: Sedation at higher doses compared to other 2nd-gen antihistamines
c.info: Second-generation piperazine H1-receptor antagonist with low blood-brain barrier penetration, conferring selective peripheral antihistaminic action.
c.caution: 10 mg once daily; some people feel drowsy, especially at 10 mg — take at bedtime and avoid alcohol. Can be taken with or without food. Intense itching can occur after stopping long-term use.
c.preg: Generally considered acceptable when needed (with loratadine, a preferred second-generation antihistamine). Small amounts pass into breast milk; occasional use is fine, watch the infant for drowsiness.
c.renal: Reduce to 5 mg once daily when CrCl is below about 30 mL/min or in hepatic impairment; avoid in end-stage renal disease unless on dialysis and directed.

c.dose: Tab 10 mg · Syr 5 mg/5 mL · ODT 10 mg
ind: Allergic rhinitis, environmental allergies, and allergic skin hives.
c.doc: Preferred non-sedating oral daytime antihistamine for drivers, students, and active workers
c.ci: Severe hepatic failure, hypersensitivity
c.sci: Co-administration with severe liver failure without dose adjustment
ae: Headache, dry mouth, fatigue (very low incidence)
c.sae: Extremely low central sedation profile
c.info: Long-acting tricyclic second-generation H1-antagonist metabolized into the active metabolite desloratadine; lacks sedative central anticholinergic effects.
c.st: Tab 10 mg · Syr 5 mg/5 mL · ODT 10 mg
c.caution: 10 mg once daily, with or without food; less sedating than older antihistamines. Rarely causes palpitations or headache. Allergy testing should be delayed until it has been stopped for several days.
c.preg: Widely used and considered acceptable in pregnancy when needed; a possible hypospadias signal has not been confirmed. Low levels in breast milk; compatible with breastfeeding.
c.renal: Give 10 mg every other day when CrCl is below 30 mL/min or in significant hepatic impairment.

ind: Seasonal allergic rhinitis, ocular allergy symptoms, and chronic idiopathic urticaria.
c.doc: First-line completely non-sedating antihistamine (zero blood-brain barrier penetration)
c.ci: Hypersensitivity
c.sci: Ingestion with fruit juices (OATP1A2 inhibition drastically impairs absorption)
ae: Headache, nausea, dizziness, dyspepsia
c.sae: Drug-food interaction reducing efficacy with acidic juices
c.info: Active carboxylated metabolite of terfenadine; does not cross the blood-brain barrier and possesses zero cardiac HERG channel toxicity.
c.caution: Take with water, not fruit juice (grapefruit, orange and apple juice reduce absorption). Separate from aluminium/magnesium antacids by 2 hours. Usual dose 120–180 mg once daily or 60 mg twice daily.
c.preg: Limited data; loratadine or cetirizine have more experience, but use is acceptable when needed. Small amounts in breast milk; generally compatible.
c.renal: Start at 60 mg once daily in renal impairment.

ind: Nasal dryness, crusted nasal passages, gentle mucus thinning, and adjunct in allergic rhinitis.
c.doc: Safe first-line nasal cleanser and moisturizer in infants, pregnant women, and chronic sinus sufferers
c.ci: Hypersensitivity to preservatives (for preserved formulations)
c.sci: Use of non-sterile tap water for home irrigation (Amebic meningoencephalitis risk)
ae: Transient mild nasal stinging with hypertonic formulations
c.sae: Virtually free of systemic toxicity
c.info: Isotonic or hypertonic salt solution that mechanically irrigates allergen and viral particles while restoring normal mucosal ciliary beat frequency and epithelial hydration.
c.caution: Safe for repeated use. Use a clean or single-use device. For nasal rinsing use distilled, sterile or boiled-and-cooled water only (risk of rare amoeba infection from tap water). Babies: use drops.
c.preg: Safe in pregnancy and breastfeeding; first choice for pregnancy rhinitis.
c.renal: No adjustment; negligible sodium absorption.

c.dose: Chew Tab 262 mg · Liquid 262, 524 mg/15 mL
ind: Traveler's diarrhea prevention/treatment, upset stomach, nausea, indigestion, and diarrhea.
c.doc: First-line prophylaxis and therapy for traveler's diarrhea and mild infectious gastrointestinal upset
c.ci: Salicylate hypersensitivity, children/teens recovering from viral infections (Reye syndrome), bleeding disorders
c.sci: Children with chickenpox or influenza symptoms (Reye syndrome risk from salicylate component)
ae: Harmless dark/black staining of tongue and stools, constipation, tinnitus in high doses
c.sae: Salicylate toxicity and Reye syndrome in pediatric viral recovery
c.info: Undergoes stomach cleavage into bismuth oxychloride (exerts direct antimicrobial and toxin-binding action) and salicylic acid (provides anti-secretory and anti-inflammatory action).
c.st: Chew Tab 262 mg · Liquid 262, 524 mg/15 mL
c.caution: Chew tablets or shake the liquid. It can turn the tongue and stool black (harmless but can mimic bleeding). It contains salicylate — avoid with aspirin, warfarin and in aspirin allergy, and do not give to children or teenagers with viral illness (Reye syndrome). Limit to 2 days for diarrhea. Ringing in the ears signals excess.
c.preg: Avoid in pregnancy and breastfeeding because of the salicylate content.
c.renal: Avoid in renal impairment (salicylate and bismuth can accumulate).

ind: Fast chewable relief of acid indigestion, heartburn, and sour stomach.
c.doc: Fast-acting chewable antacid with added dietary calcium benefit
c.ci: Hypercalcemia, severe hypercalciuria, calcium renal calculi
c.sci: Hypercalcemia and concurrent high-dose Vitamin D therapy
ae: Constipation, flatulence from CO2 release, acid rebound, belching
c.sae: Milk-alkali syndrome with chronic heavy consumption
c.info: Reacts with gastric acid to form calcium chloride, carbon dioxide, and water; has high neutralizing capacity but can cause secondary acid rebound due to gastrin stimulation.
c.caution: Chew tablets with meals or when symptoms occur; stay within the label maximum. Can constipate and cause rebound acid. Excess calcium with vitamin D risks milk-alkali syndrome. Separate from levothyroxine, iron, quinolones and tetracyclines by 2–4 hours.
c.preg: Safe and often used in pregnancy (also a calcium source); avoid excessive doses. Compatible with breastfeeding.
c.renal: Use caution in chronic kidney disease (hypercalcemia, calcification); monitor calcium and avoid excess.

c.dose: Suspension 200/200 mg per 5 mL · Chewable Tab
ind: Immediate neutralization of gastric acidity in acute heartburn, sour stomach, and dyspepsia.
c.doc: First-line immediate symptomatic relief for postprandial acute acid indigestion and heartburn
c.ci: Severe renal impairment, appendicitis symptoms, hypophosphatemia
c.sci: Severe chronic kidney disease (risk of magnesium toxicity and aluminum encephalopathy)
ae: Balanced bowel action (Mg causes diarrhea, Al causes constipation), chalky taste, belching
c.sae: Hypermagnesemia or aluminum accumulation in renal failure
c.info: Chemical combination of fast-acting magnesium hydroxide and slower-acting aluminum hydroxide; neutralizes gastric HCl to form non-absorbable salts while balancing bowel motility effects.
c.st: Suspension 200/200 mg per 5 mL · Chewable Tab
c.caution: Take 1–3 h after meals and at bedtime. Separate from other medicines by about 2 hours (reduces absorption of tetracyclines, quinolones, levothyroxine, iron). Shake the suspension. Do not use continuously for more than 2 weeks without advice; aluminium can constipate and magnesium can loosen stool.
c.preg: Acceptable intermittently at recommended doses; avoid prolonged high doses. Compatible with breastfeeding.
c.renal: Avoid regular use in severe renal impairment — magnesium and aluminium accumulate (hypermagnesemia, aluminium bone disease).

c.dose: Chew Tab 80, 125 mg · Softgel 125, 180 mg · Drops 40 mg/0.6 mL
ind: Relief of painful gas, abdominal bloating, post-operative flatulence, and infant colic.
c.doc: First-line completely safe defoaming agent for infant colic and adult abdominal gas/bloating
c.ci: Known hypersensitivity, suspected intestinal perforation or mechanical obstruction
c.sci: Use as monotherapy in undiagnosed mechanical bowel obstruction
ae: Loose stools (rare), mild belching, nausea
c.sae: Inert non-toxic agent with virtually no systemic adverse effects
c.info: Physiologically inert surface-active silicone polymer that decreases the surface tension of gas bubbles in the GI tract, causing them to coalesce into larger bubbles expelled via belching or flatus.
c.st: Chew Tab 80, 125 mg · Softgel 125, 180 mg · Drops 40 mg/0.6 mL
c.caution: Chew tablets thoroughly; can be taken after meals and at bedtime. Infant drops can be mixed with a feed. It is not absorbed. Proof of benefit for infant colic is limited.
c.preg: Not absorbed; considered safe in pregnancy and breastfeeding.
c.renal: Not absorbed; no adjustment.

ind: Control and symptomatic relief of acute non-specific diarrhea and chronic diarrhea in IBS-D.
c.doc: First-line rapid-acting antimotility drug for acute uncomplicated watery traveler's diarrhea
c.ci: Infectious dysentery (bloody stools and high fever), acute ulcerative colitis flare, children <2 years
c.sci: Invasive bacterial enteritis / C. difficile colitis (risk of precipitating Toxic Megacolon)
ae: Constipation, abdominal cramping, dizziness, dry mouth, nausea
c.sae: Toxic megacolon in inflammatory/infectious diarrhea; fatal cardiac arrhythmias at massive abused doses
c.info: Peripheral mu-opioid receptor agonist in the myenteric plexus that inhibits circular and longitudinal bowel smooth muscle tone, slowing transit time and enhancing fluid resorption.
c.caution: Do not exceed 8 mg/day OTC (16 mg prescription). High doses cause serious heart rhythm problems (QT prolongation). Avoid in bloody diarrhea, high fever, dysentery or C. difficile. Not for children under 12 (OTC). Stop if no better after 48 hours.
c.preg: Limited data; avoid in the first trimester if possible. Short-term use later is acceptable if needed. Very little passes into breast milk.
c.renal: No adjustment for renal impairment; use caution in severe hepatic impairment (higher levels).

c.dose: Tab 10, 20, 40 mg · Oral Susp 40 mg/5 mL
ind: Treatment and prevention of meal-induced heartburn, GERD, and gastric acid hypersecretion.
c.doc: Preferred H2 blocker for on-demand meal-triggered heartburn prevention with zero CYP450 interactions
c.ci: Hypersensitivity to H2 blockers, severe renal failure without dose adjustment
c.sci: Unadjusted dosing in severe renal impairment (causes CNS confusion)
ae: Headache, dizziness, constipation, diarrhea, mild fatigue
c.sae: Reversible mental confusion in elderly or renally impaired patients
c.info: Potent, competitive, reversible antagonist of histamine H2-receptors on gastric parietal cells; suppresses both basal and food-stimulated acid secretion without anti-androgenic effects.
c.st: Tab 10, 20, 40 mg · Oral Susp 40 mg/5 mL
c.caution: 10–20 mg once or twice daily; for prevention take 1 h before a trigger meal. Confusion can occur in the elderly and in renal impairment. Long-term use may reduce iron and B12 absorption.
c.preg: Generally considered acceptable in pregnancy. Small amounts pass into breast milk; compatible with breastfeeding.
c.renal: When CrCl is below 50 mL/min, halve the dose or extend the interval to 36–48 h.

ind: Frequent heartburn (>=2 days/week), gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD), and gastritis.
c.doc: Gold standard first-line acid suppression for chronic GERD, erosive esophagitis, and peptic ulcer disease
c.ci: Known hypersensitivity to benzimidazoles, concurrent rilpivirine-containing regimens
c.sci: Concurrent use with Clopidogrel (CYP2C19 inhibition reduces clopidogrel antiplatelet activation)
ae: Headache, abdominal pain, diarrhea, flatulence, nausea
c.sae: Hypomagnesemia, B12 deficiency, and increased fracture/C. difficile risk with long-term use
c.info: Irreversibly inhibits the gastric parietal cell H+/K+-ATPase pump; prodrug activated in acidic canaliculi to provide long-lasting acid suppression despite a short plasma half-life.
c.caution: Take 30–60 minutes before breakfast and swallow the capsule whole. OTC use is limited to 14 days without advice. Long-term use may lower magnesium and B12 and raise fracture and C. difficile risk. Avoid with clopidogrel (CYP2C19).
c.preg: Data are reassuring; one of the best-studied PPIs and acceptable when needed. Small amounts pass into breast milk; compatible.
c.renal: No adjustment in renal impairment; limit to 10–20 mg/day in severe hepatic impairment.

c.dose: Powder sachet for 200 mL, 500 mL, 1 L solution (75 mEq/L Na+)
ind: Prevention and treatment of clinical dehydration resulting from acute diarrhea and vomiting.
c.doc: Gold standard life-saving therapy for fluid and electrolyte replenishment in acute diarrheal illness
c.ci: Intractable paralytic ileus, severe uncorrectable persistent vomiting, severe hemodynamic shock
c.sci: Intractable shock requiring urgent intravenous fluid resuscitation
ae: Vomiting if administered too rapidly, mild hypernatremia if mixed in incorrect water volumes
c.sae: Hypernatremia if concentrated powder is consumed without prescribed water dilution
c.info: Leverages the intact sodium-glucose cotransport system (SGLT-1) in the intestinal brush border, enabling rapid passive water absorption even in severe secretory cholera-like diarrhea.
c.st: Powder sachet for 200 mL, 500 mL, 1 L solution (75 mEq/L Na+)
c.caution: Mix exactly in the stated volume of clean (boiled and cooled) water — never add sugar or salt or dilute further. Give small frequent sips (about 5 mL every 1–2 min for a child) and keep breastfeeding. Discard after 24 hours. Seek care for no urine, sunken eyes, blood in stool or persistent vomiting.
c.preg: Safe and recommended for dehydration in pregnancy and breastfeeding.
c.renal: Use under medical guidance in severe renal failure or heart failure (sodium and water load); monitor fluids and electrolytes.

c.dose: Tab 50 mg · Liquid 12.5 mg/5 mL · Chew Tab 25 mg
ind: Prevention and treatment of nausea, vomiting, dizziness, and vertigo associated with motion sickness.
c.doc: First-line OTC agent for travel-related motion sickness and nausea taken 30-60 minutes pre-travel
c.ci: Narrow-angle glaucoma, severe prostatic hypertrophy, children <2 years
c.sci: Concurrent use with ototoxic drugs (aminoglycosides) as it masks early signs of ototoxicity
ae: Marked drowsiness, dry mouth, blurred vision, dizziness, uncoordination
c.sae: Significant sedation and impaired motor coordination for driving
c.info: 1:1 salt combination of diphenhydramine and 8-chlorotheophylline; central H1-antagonism and anticholinergic action in the vestibular apparatus blocks emetic signaling to the CTZ.
c.st: Tab 50 mg · Liquid 12.5 mg/5 mL · Chew Tab 25 mg
c.caution: Take 30–60 minutes before travel. Causes drowsiness — avoid alcohol and driving. Adults 50–100 mg every 4–6 h, maximum 400 mg/day. Can mask ear toxicity from other drugs. Use caution in the elderly.
c.preg: Used for nausea and motion sickness in pregnancy at usual doses; high doses near term may stimulate uterine contractions. May make a breastfed infant drowsy and reduce milk supply; use occasionally.
c.renal: Extend the interval in severe renal impairment; use caution in liver disease.

ind: Short-term relief of acute constipation and bowel evacuation prior to medical procedures.
c.doc: Fast-acting predictable stimulant laxative for acute occasional constipation and colon cleansing
c.ci: Bowel obstruction, acute appendicitis, acute surgical abdomen, undiagnosed rectal bleeding
c.sci: Suspected mechanical bowel obstruction or acute surgical abdomen
ae: Abdominal cramping, griping pain, diarrhea, nausea, rectal burning (suppository)
c.sae: Severe hypokalemia and laxative dependence with chronic unmonitored abuse
c.info: Diphenylmethane stimulant laxative that directly irritates sensory nerve endings in the colonic mucosa, stimulating rhythmic peristaltic contractions and accumulating luminal water/electrolytes.
c.caution: Swallow enteric-coated tablets whole; do not take with milk or antacids. Oral works in 6–12 h, so take at bedtime; suppositories work in 15–60 min. Use for no more than about 7 days to avoid dependence and electrolyte loss. Avoid in bowel obstruction or undiagnosed abdominal pain.
c.preg: Little is absorbed; short-term use is acceptable if bulk laxatives fail. Compatible with breastfeeding.
c.renal: No adjustment for short courses; avoid prolonged use in renal impairment (electrolyte disturbances).

ind: Prevention of hard dry stools and straining in post-MI, postpartum, anal fissure, and hemorroid patients.
c.doc: Prophylactic stool softener to prevent dangerous straining after myocardial infarction, eye surgery, or childbirth
c.ci: Concomitant use of mineral oil, intestinal obstruction, acute abdominal pain
c.sci: Concurrent administration with mineral oil (enhances systemic mineral oil tissue absorption)
ae: Mild abdominal cramping, bitter taste, throat irritation (liquid), diarrhea
c.sae: Very low toxicity profile; ineffective for acute rapid constipation treatment
c.info: Anionic surfactant that reduces stool surface tension, permitting water and lipid penetration into hardened fecal masses to produce soft, easily passed stools.
c.caution: Stool softener with weak evidence; works in 1–3 days. Take with a full glass of water. Do not combine with mineral oil. Often paired with senna for opioid-induced constipation.
c.preg: Minimal absorption; considered safe. Compatible with breastfeeding.
c.renal: No adjustment; avoid excessive use (electrolyte loss).

ind: Chronic constipation and prevention/treatment of hepatic encephalopathy.
c.doc: First-line gentle osmotic laxative for chronic constipation in elderly/pregnancy and DOC for Hepatic Encephalopathy
c.ci: Galactosemia, mechanical bowel obstruction, patients requiring low galactose diet
ae: Flatulence, abdominal distention, belching, intestinal cramps, sweet taste aversion
c.sae: Severe diarrhea leading to dehydration and electrolyte depletion in high doses
c.info: Non-absorbable synthetic disaccharide degraded by colonic flora into lactic and acetic acids; acidifies colonic contents (trapping NH3 as non-absorbable NH4+) and exerts osmotic water draw.
