c.caution: Takes 24–48 h to work; gas, bloating and cramps are common early on. Drink plenty of fluids; can be mixed with juice. Avoid in galactosemia. In hepatic encephalopathy, adjust the dose to 2–3 soft stools daily.
c.preg: Not absorbed; considered safe in pregnancy and breastfeeding.
c.renal: No adjustment; monitor fluids and electrolytes if diarrhea develops.

ind: Acute constipation, opioid-induced constipation, and bowel evacuation.
c.doc: First-line stimulant choice for opioid-induced bowel dysfunction (combined with stool softener)
c.ci: Intestinal obstruction, ulcerative colitis, Crohn disease, undiagnosed abdominal pain
c.sci: Mechanical intestinal obstruction or acute ileus
ae: Abdominal cramps, diarrhea, nausea, reddish-brown urine discoloration
c.sae: Melanosis coli (benign brownish pigmentation of colon mucosa on chronic use)
c.info: Anthraquinone prodrug unabsorbed in upper GI; cleaved by colonic bacterial enzymes into active rheinanthrone which directly stimulates the myenteric plexus and fluid secretion.
c.caution: Take at bedtime; works in 6–12 h. Short-term use only (usually under a week) unless advised. May cause cramps; urine may turn reddish-brown. Avoid in bowel obstruction.
c.preg: Generally acceptable short-term if bulk laxatives fail. Small amounts in milk; infant loose stool possible but compatible with breastfeeding.
c.renal: Avoid long-term use in renal impairment (fluid loss, low potassium).

c.dose: Topical Ointment (400 U Bacitracin + 3.5 mg Neomycin + 5000 U Polymyxin B per gram)
ind: First aid prevention of bacterial infection in minor cuts, scrapes, abrasions, and superficial burns.
c.doc: Broad-spectrum topical antibacterial ointment for contaminated minor domestic cuts and abrasions
c.ci: Hypersensitivity to aminoglycosides/neomycin, deep puncture wounds, animal bites
c.sci: Application over large denuded body surface areas (risk of systemic Neomycin nephro/ototoxicity)
ae: Allergic contact dermatitis (frequently driven by the neomycin component), local erythema, itching
c.sae: Allergic contact sensitization (Neomycin-induced hypersensitivity rash)
c.info: Synergistic combination: Bacitracin inhibits Gram-positive cell wall synthesis, Neomycin causes Gram-negative bacterial ribosomal misreading, and Polymyxin B disrupts Gram-negative outer cell membranes. Note: standard Polyfax is a dual-antibiotic ointment (Polymyxin B + Bacitracin only, no Neomycin) and is not equivalent to this triple formulation.
c.st: Topical Ointment (400 U Bacitracin + 3.5 mg Neomycin + 5000 U Polymyxin B per gram)
c.caution: Apply a thin layer 1–3 times daily to a small area for up to 7 days. Neomycin allergic contact dermatitis is common — stop if a rash appears. Not for deep wounds, burns or eyes; avoid large areas because absorbed neomycin and polymyxin can harm kidneys and hearing.
c.preg: Small-area, short-term use is acceptable; avoid large areas. Acceptable while breastfeeding on small areas, but not on the nipples.
c.renal: Avoid large-area or prolonged use in renal impairment (neomycin and polymyxin are nephrotoxic and ototoxic when absorbed).

ind: Temporary relief of itching, skin inflammation, eczema, dermatitis, and insect bite reactions.
c.doc: First-line OTC mild topical corticosteroid for facial and intertriginous skin itching/eczema
c.ci: Untreated bacterial/fungal/viral (herpes) skin infections, open weeping wounds
c.sci: Untreated cutaneous fungal or viral infections (causes rapid pathogen proliferation)
ae: Local burning, dryness, folliculitis; skin atrophy and telangiectasia with prolonged continuous use
c.sae: Skin thinning (atrophy) and striae on chronic misuse
c.info: Low-potency Class VII short-acting glucocorticoid that diffuses into cells, binding cytoplasmic receptors to downregulate pro-inflammatory cytokines and leukocyte migration.
c.caution: Apply a thin layer once or twice daily for up to 7 days (up to 2 weeks in some guidance). Do not use on the face, groin, anal area or infected skin, acne or rosacea without advice. Avoid occlusive dressings. Stop if irritation occurs.
c.preg: Low-potency topical steroids are acceptable in pregnancy at the lowest effective amount. Compatible with breastfeeding, but do not apply to the breast right before nursing.
c.renal: Negligible systemic absorption on small areas for a short time; avoid extensive or prolonged use (systemic steroid effects).

c.dose: Topical Solution 10% (1% available iodine) · Ointment 10% · Surgical Scrub 7.5%
ind: Skin antisepsis for minor cuts, scrapes, burns, wound dressing, and pre-operative skin preparation.
c.doc: Gold standard broad-spectrum topical antiseptic for superficial wounds and pre-surgical skin prep
c.ci: Hypersensitivity to iodine, premature neonates, thyroid disorders (extensive long-term use)
c.sci: Large open wound application in patients with thyroid disease or premature infants (systemic iodine absorption)
ae: Local skin irritation, yellow-brown skin staining (washable), contact dermatitis
c.sae: Systemic iodine absorption causing thyroid dysfunction with massive application
c.info: Water-soluble complex of polyvinylpyrrolidone and elemental iodine; slowly liberates free iodine to oxidize microbial protoplasmic proteins, fatty acids, and nucleotides.
c.st: Topical Solution 10% (1% available iodine) · Ointment 10% · Surgical Scrub 7.5%
c.caution: Apply to skin before procedures and allow to dry. Not for deep wounds, burns or large areas; iodine can be absorbed and disturb thyroid function. Avoid in newborns and preterm infants, and with lithium. Do not use under occlusion (chemical burns).
c.preg: Avoid repeated or large-area use in pregnancy and breastfeeding (iodine reaches the fetus and breast milk and can cause neonatal hypothyroidism). A single small-area use is acceptable.
c.renal: Avoid repeated use over large areas in severe renal impairment (iodine accumulation).

c.st: Cream 1% · Vaginal tab 100, 500 mg · Troche 10 mg
c.dose: Topical Cream 1% · Topical Soln 1% · Vaginal Tab 100, 500 mg
ind: Tinea pedis (athlete's foot), tinea cruris (jock itch), tinea corporis (ringworm), and cutaneous candidiasis.
c.doc: First-line broad-spectrum topical antifungal for common dermatophyte and Candida infections
c.ci: Hypersensitivity to imidazole antifungals
ae: Local skin irritation, erythema, burning, stinging, peeling
c.sae: Local contact dermatitis and hypersensitivity
c.info: Imidazole antifungal that inhibits fungal cytochrome P450 enzyme 14-alpha-demethylase, blocking conversion of lanosterol to ergosterol and disrupting fungal cell membrane integrity.
c.caution: Apply cream thinly 2–3 times daily for 2–4 weeks and finish the course. Vaginal tablets: insert at night; the cream and tablets can weaken latex condoms and diaphragms. Troche: let it dissolve slowly. Keep out of eyes. See a doctor if no improvement in 7 days.
c.preg: Topical use is acceptable; for vaginal thrush a 7-day course is preferred in pregnancy, using the applicator gently. Topical use is compatible with breastfeeding.
c.renal: Negligible absorption from topical or vaginal use; no adjustment. Troche: monitor liver tests in hepatic impairment.

c.dose: Topical Cream 2% · Oral Gel 20 mg/g · Powder 2% · Vaginal Supp 100, 200 mg
ind: Fungal skin infections, vulvovaginal candidiasis, and oral thrush (oral gel formulation).
c.doc: Topical treatment for localized fungal skin folds and OTC oral gel for oral candidiasis
c.ci: Hypersensitivity, co-administration of oral gel with Warfarin
c.sci: Oral gel co-administration with Warfarin (systemic absorption strongly inhibits CYP2C9, causing severe bleeding)
ae: Local burning, pruritus, pelvic cramping (vaginal), nausea (oral gel)
c.sae: Marked INR elevation and hemorrhage when oral gel is taken with Warfarin
c.info: Broad-spectrum synthetic imidazole antifungal that disrupts ergosterol synthesis and alters membrane permeability, resulting in intracellular organelle leakage and fungal death.
c.caution: Apply cream twice daily and continue 2 weeks after clearing. Oral gel and other forms can raise warfarin's effect (INR) — avoid or monitor. Oral gel in infants carries a choking risk. The cream and pessaries can weaken latex condoms.
c.preg: Topical use is acceptable; vaginal use in short courses is acceptable. Compatible with breastfeeding (wipe the nipple before feeding).
c.renal: Negligible absorption; no adjustment. Use caution with the oral gel in hepatic impairment.

c.dose: Topical Lotion 8% Zinc Oxide + 0.5% Ferric Oxide
ind: Soothing relief of itching and discomfort from poison ivy, chickenpox lesions, sunburn, and insect stings.
c.doc: First-line safe protective soothing and cooling lotion for chickenpox, insect bites, and weeping skin rashes
c.ci: Known hypersensitivity to components, application to open weeping deep wounds or eyes
c.sci: Application into eyes or mucosal surfaces
ae: Mild local skin dryness, chalky residue on drying
c.sae: Completely non-toxic soothing preparation with negligible adverse effects
c.info: Basic zinc oxide formulation with ferric oxide imparting pink color; functions as a mild astringent and protective soothing agent that evaporates rapidly to produce cutaneous cooling.
c.st: Topical Lotion 8% Zinc Oxide + 0.5% Ferric Oxide
c.caution: Shake well and apply to intact skin. Keep out of eyes and mouth; not for open or oozing wounds. Stop if irritation occurs. Versions with diphenhydramine should not be used over large areas.
c.preg: Minimal absorption; safe in pregnancy and breastfeeding.
c.renal: Not absorbed; no adjustment.

c.st: Inj 250 mg, 500 mg (imipenem) with an equal amount of cilastatin
c.dose: Inj 250 mg, 500 mg, always given as imipenem-cilastatin 1:1 · usual adult 500 mg IV q6h (or 1 g q8h)
ind: Serious polymicrobial infections: lower respiratory tract, intra-abdominal, gynecologic, skin and soft tissue, bone and joint, complicated UTI, endocarditis and septicemia; also used empirically in febrile neutropenia.
c.doc: Polymicrobial intra-abdominal sepsis and ESBL-producing Enterobacterales; hospital-acquired pneumonia and febrile neutropenia when Pseudomonas, Enterococcus faecalis and anaerobes all need cover
c.ci: Hypersensitivity to any carbapenem; severe reaction to another beta-lactam
c.sci: Seizure disorder or CNS lesions; renal impairment without dose reduction; valproate co-therapy
ae: Nausea, vomiting (especially with fast infusion), diarrhea, rash, infusion-site phlebitis, transient transaminase rise, seizures (dose- and renal-function-related)
c.sae: Seizures (highest among carbapenems) / C. difficile colitis / Anaphylaxis
c.info: The original carbapenem (derived from thienamycin). It is broken down by renal dehydropeptidase-I (DHP-I) in the proximal tubule, so it is always co-formulated with cilastatin, a DHP-I inhibitor that raises urinary levels and blocks a nephrotoxic metabolite. Very broad activity including Enterococcus faecalis and anaerobes, but not MRSA or E. faecium. Not recommended for meningitis because of its seizure risk.
c.caution: Reconstitute per the label; infuse IV over 20–30 minutes (250–500 mg) or 40–60 minutes (1 g) — rapid infusion causes nausea, vomiting and dizziness. Not for meningitis. Avoid with valproate; if unavoidable, add another antiseizure medicine.
c.preg: Human data are limited but reassuring, and animal studies have not shown teratogenicity; reserve for serious infections where safer beta-lactams are unsuitable. Small amounts reach breast milk with poor infant oral absorption — generally acceptable, but watch the infant for diarrhea or thrush.
c.renal: Cleared by the kidney — reduce the dose or extend the interval as creatinine clearance falls (label tables are stepped by CrCl). Accumulation sharply raises seizure risk; avoid if CrCl <15 mL/min unless dialysis is started within 48 hours.

c.dose: Inj 500 mg, 1 g · usual adult 1 g IV q8h (2 g q8h in meningitis)
ind: Complicated skin and skin-structure infections, complicated intra-abdominal infections and bacterial meningitis; widely used for hospital-acquired pneumonia, febrile neutropenia and ESBL sepsis.
c.doc: Bacterial meningitis (the carbapenem with a lower seizure risk); ESBL-producing Enterobacterales bacteremia (MERINO trial); Pseudomonas aeruginosa sepsis
c.ci: Hypersensitivity to meropenem or other carbapenems; anaphylaxis to beta-lactams
c.sci: Valproate co-therapy (levels fall sharply); CNS disorders; renal impairment
ae: Diarrhea, nausea, vomiting, headache, rash, injection-site inflammation; seizures are uncommon
c.sae: Seizures (rare) / C. difficile colitis / Loss of valproate seizure control
c.info: The 1-beta-methyl group makes it stable to renal DHP-I, so no cilastatin is needed. Less seizure-prone than imipenem and licensed for meningitis. Strong gram-negative activity including Pseudomonas aeruginosa and ESBL/AmpC producers. Like all carbapenems it misses MRSA, Enterococcus faecium, Stenotrophomonas maltophilia and atypical organisms.
c.caution: Reconstitute per the label; give as an IV infusion over 15–30 minutes or a slow bolus over 3–5 minutes. Extended (3-hour) infusions are used in critically ill patients to keep drug levels above the MIC longer. Avoid with valproate.
c.preg: Human data are limited but reassuring, and animal studies have not shown teratogenicity; reserve for serious infections where safer beta-lactams are unsuitable. Small amounts reach breast milk with poor infant oral absorption — generally acceptable, but watch the infant for diarrhea or thrush.
c.renal: Cleared by the kidney — reduce the dose or extend the interval when creatinine clearance is 50 mL/min or lower; no routine hepatic adjustment.

c.dose: Inj 1 g · usual adult 1 g IV or IM once daily
ind: Complicated intra-abdominal and skin/skin-structure infections (including diabetic foot without osteomyelitis), community-acquired pneumonia, complicated UTI/pyelonephritis, acute pelvic infections, and surgical prophylaxis in elective colorectal surgery.
c.doc: ESBL-producing Enterobacterales infections treated as an outpatient (OPAT) with once-daily dosing; colorectal surgery prophylaxis
c.ci: Hypersensitivity to carbapenems; IM use contraindicated in allergy to amide-type local anesthetics (the diluent is lidocaine)
c.sci: Amide local anesthetic allergy (IM route); valproate co-therapy; seizure history; CrCl 30 mL/min or lower needs a lower dose
ae: Diarrhea, nausea, headache, infusion-site reactions, rash, vaginitis; seizures are uncommon
c.sae: Seizures / C. difficile colitis / Hypersensitivity
c.info: Group 1 carbapenem: once-daily dosing is possible because it is highly protein-bound (about 85–95%) with a longer half-life (~4 h). It lacks reliable activity against Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Acinetobacter and Enterococcus — the Group 2 carbapenems (imipenem, meropenem, doripenem) cover those.
c.caution: IV: infuse over 30 minutes. IM: reconstitute with 1% lidocaine (without epinephrine) only — never inject that preparation IV. Give 500 mg daily if CrCl is 30 mL/min or lower. Avoid with valproate.
c.preg: Human data are limited but reassuring, and animal studies have not shown teratogenicity; reserve for serious infections where safer beta-lactams are unsuitable. Small amounts reach breast milk with poor infant oral absorption — generally acceptable, but watch the infant for diarrhea or thrush.
c.renal: Cleared by the kidney — reduce to 500 mg once daily when creatinine clearance is 30 mL/min or lower; give after hemodialysis on dialysis days.

c.dose: Inj 250 mg, 500 mg · usual adult 500 mg IV q8h, infused over 1 hour
ind: Complicated intra-abdominal infections and complicated urinary tract infections including pyelonephritis (use in ventilator-associated pneumonia was withdrawn after a trial showed worse outcomes).
c.doc: Complicated intra-abdominal sepsis and pyelonephritis; historically noted for very low MICs against Pseudomonas aeruginosa
c.ci: Hypersensitivity to doripenem or other carbapenems
c.sci: Valproate co-therapy; seizure history; renal impairment (CrCl 50 mL/min or lower)
ae: Headache, nausea, diarrhea, rash, phlebitis, raised liver enzymes
c.sae: Seizures / C. difficile colitis / Hypersensitivity
c.info: Group 2 carbapenem, stable to renal DHP-I and very potent against Pseudomonas aeruginosa in vitro. Availability is now limited in many markets, so it is mostly of historical or regional interest.
c.caution: Reconstitute and dilute per the label; infuse over 1 hour. Reduce the dose when CrCl is 50 mL/min or lower. Avoid with valproate.
c.preg: Human data are limited but reassuring, and animal studies have not shown teratogenicity; reserve for serious infections where safer beta-lactams are unsuitable. Small amounts reach breast milk with poor infant oral absorption — generally acceptable, but watch the infant for diarrhea or thrush.
c.renal: Cleared by the kidney — reduce the dose when creatinine clearance is 50 mL/min or lower.

c.sp:
Gram-positive: Streptococcus pneumoniae, Streptococcus pyogenes, Staphylococcus aureus (MSSA), Enterococcus faecalis (imipenem, doripenem best)
Gram-negative: Escherichia coli, Klebsiella, Enterobacter, Serratia, Proteus (including ESBL and AmpC producers), Haemophilus influenzae, Neisseria, Pseudomonas aeruginosa (imipenem, meropenem, doripenem — not ertapenem), Acinetobacter baumannii (variable)
Anaerobes: Bacteroides fragilis, Clostridium (not C. difficile), Peptostreptococcus
Not covered: MRSA, Enterococcus faecium, Stenotrophomonas maltophilia, atypicals (Mycoplasma, Chlamydia, Legionella)
c.mn:
💊 Names: All end in “-penem”: Imipenem, Meropenem, Ertapenem, Doripenem. Imipenem always comes with cilastatin.
🦠 Kills: The widest beta-lactam net — Gram-positives, Gram-negatives (including ESBL producers and Pseudomonas) and anaerobes. Misses MRSA, Enterococcus faecium, Stenotrophomonas and atypicals.
🎯 Used for: Severe hospital infections, sepsis, febrile neutropenia and ESBL infections; meropenem for meningitis; ertapenem for once-daily outpatient therapy.
💡 Tip: Imipenem is the seizure-prone one (needs cilastatin). Meropenem is the meningitis one. Ertapenem is the once-a-day one that skips Pseudomonas. All carbapenems + valproate = seizures.

c.st: Inj 250 mg, 500 mg (panipenem) with an equal amount of betamipron
c.dose: Inj 250 mg, 500 mg · usual adult 0.5 g IV twice daily (Japan labeling)
ind: Respiratory, urinary, intra-abdominal, gynecologic, skin and bone infections and sepsis in the markets where it is licensed (Japan and parts of Asia).
c.doc: Serious mixed aerobic–anaerobic infections in Japanese and Asian practice
c.ci: Hypersensitivity to carbapenems
c.sci: Valproate co-therapy; seizure history; renal impairment
ae: Diarrhea, rash, nausea, raised liver enzymes; seizures are uncommon
c.sae: Seizures / C. difficile colitis / Loss of valproate seizure control
c.info: Carbapenem always co-formulated with betamipron, which competes for renal organic anion transporters so less panipenem enters proximal tubule cells, lowering the risk of kidney injury. Betamipron itself is not an antibacterial.
c.caution: Reconstitute and dilute per local labeling; infuse IV over 30–60 minutes. Avoid with valproate. Availability depends on the market.
c.preg: Human data are limited but reassuring, and animal studies have not shown teratogenicity; reserve for serious infections where safer beta-lactams are unsuitable. Small amounts reach breast milk with poor infant oral absorption — generally acceptable, but watch the infant for diarrhea or thrush.
c.renal: Cleared by the kidney — reduce the dose as creatinine clearance falls.

c.dose: Inj 300 mg · usual adult 300 mg IV twice daily (Japan labeling)
ind: Pneumonia, lung abscess, complicated UTI, intra-abdominal and gynecologic infections, and sepsis in the markets where it is licensed (Japan, China and some other Asian markets).
c.doc: ESBL-producing Enterobacterales and mixed anaerobic infections in Asian practice; multidrug-resistant Pseudomonas aeruginosa
c.ci: Hypersensitivity to carbapenems
c.sci: Valproate co-therapy; seizure history; renal impairment
ae: Diarrhea, rash, nausea, raised liver enzymes, phlebitis; seizures are uncommon
c.sae: Seizures / C. difficile colitis / Loss of valproate seizure control
c.info: A 1-beta-methyl carbapenem that is stable to renal DHP-I (no cilastatin needed), with a wide spectrum including Pseudomonas aeruginosa and anaerobes. Like the other Group 2 carbapenems it does not cover MRSA.
c.caution: Reconstitute and dilute per local labeling; infuse IV over 30–60 minutes. Avoid with valproate. Availability depends on the market.
c.preg: Human data are limited but reassuring, and animal studies have not shown teratogenicity; reserve for serious infections where safer beta-lactams are unsuitable. Small amounts reach breast milk with poor infant oral absorption — generally acceptable, but watch the infant for diarrhea or thrush.
c.renal: Cleared by the kidney — reduce the dose as creatinine clearance falls.

c.sp:
Gram-negative: KPC-producing Klebsiella pneumoniae and other CRE, ESBL and AmpC producers, Pseudomonas aeruginosa (imipenem-relebactam, including many imipenem-resistant strains)
Gram-positive and anaerobes: as for the parent carbapenem
Not covered: metallo-beta-lactamase producers (NDM, VIM, IMP), most OXA-48 producers, reliably-resistant Acinetobacter baumannii, MRSA, Enterococcus faecium
c.mn:
💊 Names: Meropenem + Vaborbactam (Vabomere); Imipenem + Cilastatin + Relebactam (Recarbrio). The inhibitor names end in “-bactam”. Regional: Biapenem, Panipenem (with betamipron).
🦠 Kills: KPC-producing CRE — the superbugs that beat plain carbapenems. Does NOT kill NDM/VIM/IMP (metallo-beta-lactamase) makers.
🎯 Used for: Complicated UTI, intra-abdominal infection and hospital pneumonia when carbapenem resistance is likely.
💡 Tip: KPC = Klebsiella Producing Carbapenemase — these combinations beat it. Metallo-enzymes need cefiderocol or ceftazidime-avibactam + aztreonam.

c.dose: Tab 150 mg, 200 mg · dosing varies by market and indication; follow local labeling
ind: Respiratory tract infections, urinary tract infections, skin and soft tissue infections and otitis media in the markets where it is licensed (for example Japan and India).
c.doc: Oral therapy for respiratory and urinary infections in regions where it is licensed; carbapenem cross-resistance is a stewardship concern
c.ci: Hypersensitivity to faropenem, other penems/carbapenems or severe beta-lactam allergy
c.sci: Valproate co-therapy (a carbapenem class interaction that may extend to penems — check local labeling); seizure history
ae: Diarrhea, loose stools, nausea, abdominal pain, rash, raised liver enzymes
c.sae: C. difficile colitis / Hypersensitivity
c.info: An oral penem (sulfur is kept in the ring, unlike carbapenems) that is stable to many beta-lactamases including ESBLs, with activity against S. pneumoniae, H. influenzae, M. catarrhalis, anaerobes and many Enterobacterales. There is concern that widespread use may select cross-resistance to true carbapenems, so it is not a first-line choice.
c.caution: Take as directed with a full glass of water and report severe or persistent diarrhea. Use should follow local stewardship guidance because of carbapenem cross-resistance concerns.
c.preg: Human data are lacking — use in pregnancy only if clearly needed and no better-studied option exists. Breastfeeding data are limited; watch the infant for diarrhea or thrush if used.
c.renal: Renally excreted in part — check local labeling for dose adjustment in severe renal impairment.

c.sp:
Gram-positive: Streptococcus pneumoniae, Streptococcus pyogenes, Staphylococcus aureus (MSSA)
Gram-negative: Escherichia coli, Klebsiella, Proteus (including many ESBL producers), Haemophilus influenzae, Moraxella catarrhalis
Anaerobes: Bacteroides, Clostridium (faropenem)
Not covered: MRSA, Pseudomonas aeruginosa (not reliable), Enterococcus faecium
c.mn:
💊 Names: Faropenem, Sulopenem (with probenecid). Penems, not carbapenems — sulfur stays in the ring.
🦠 Kills: Respiratory bugs, E. coli/Klebsiella (including ESBL), and anaerobes; unreliable on Pseudomonas.
🎯 Used for: Oral step-down for respiratory and urinary infections; sulopenem only for uncomplicated UTI with few options.
💡 Tip: Penem = sulfur in the ring, oral. Carbapenem = carbon in place of sulfur, injection.

ov.moa: Beta-lactam antibiotics of the carbapenem family (a carbon replaces the sulfur of the penicillin ring). They bind penicillin-binding proteins (PBPs) to block peptidoglycan cross-linking, causing bacterial lysis; bactericidal (time-dependent killing) and stable against most beta-lactamases, including ESBLs and AmpC.
ov.ind: Reserved for serious or multidrug-resistant infections: hospital-acquired and ventilator-associated pneumonia, complicated intra-abdominal and urinary tract infections, sepsis, febrile neutropenia and ESBL-producing Enterobacterales. Meropenem is used for meningitis; ertapenem allows once-daily outpatient therapy but misses Pseudomonas, Acinetobacter and Enterococcus. Newer inhibitor combinations (meropenem-vaborbactam, imipenem-relebactam) treat KPC-producing CRE. Not active against MRSA, Enterococcus faecium, Stenotrophomonas maltophilia or atypical organisms.
ov.ae: Nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, rash, headache and infusion-site phlebitis; seizures (most with imipenem, higher with renal impairment or CNS disease); C. difficile colitis; superinfection with Candida or resistant organisms; rarely hypersensitivity/anaphylaxis.
ov.ci: Contraindicated with serious hypersensitivity to any carbapenem; cross-reactivity with penicillin allergy is low (about 1%) but use caution after a severe beta-lactam reaction. Carbapenems sharply lower valproate levels and can bring seizures back — avoid the combination. Adjust the dose in renal impairment.
ov.counsel: Given by injection in hospital or clinic; report rash, swelling, breathing difficulty, seizures or severe/persistent diarrhea at once. Tell your prescriber if you take valproate (sodium valproate/valproic acid) — carbapenems can make seizures return. Complete the prescribed course.

ind: Aerobic gram-negative infections: complicated UTI, lower respiratory tract, intra-abdominal, gynecologic, skin infections and septicemia.
c.doc: Gram-negative infections in patients with severe penicillin/cephalosporin allergy; metallo-beta-lactamase (NDM, VIM, IMP) producers when paired with a partner drug
c.ci: Hypersensitivity to aztreonam
c.sci: Ceftazidime or cefiderocol allergy (identical side chain); renal impairment
ae: Nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, rash, injection-site phlebitis, transient transaminase rise
c.sae: C. difficile colitis / Hypersensitivity (cross-reaction with ceftazidime)
c.info: The only clinically used monobactam (single beta-lactam ring). Binds PBP3 of aerobic gram-negatives; no activity against gram-positives or anaerobes. Stable to metallo-beta-lactamases but hydrolyzed by ESBLs, AmpC and KPC. Little cross-allergy with other beta-lactams except the ceftazidime/cefiderocol side chain.
c.caution: IV infusion over 20–60 minutes or IM. Reduce dose in renal impairment. Add a gram-positive/anaerobic agent when the infection is mixed.
c.preg: Limited human data; animal studies show no fetal harm. Crosses the placenta and can be used when clearly needed (for example, gram-negative infection in a severely beta-lactam-allergic patient). Excreted into breast milk in very small amounts (well under 1% of maternal serum levels); generally considered compatible with breastfeeding, though watch the infant for diarrhea or thrush.
c.renal: Renally eliminated — after the usual loading dose, give about 50% of the maintenance dose at the same interval when CrCl is 10–30 mL/min and about 25% when CrCl is below 10 mL/min; give a supplemental dose after hemodialysis. Reduce the dose by 20–25% in chronic liver disease such as cirrhosis.

c.sp:
Gram-negative aerobes only: Escherichia coli, Klebsiella, Enterobacter, Proteus, Serratia, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Haemophilus, Neisseria
Not covered: gram-positives, anaerobes; ESBL/AmpC/KPC producers unless combined with avibactam
c.mn:
💊 Names: Aztreonam (+ avibactam).
🦠 Kills: Gram-negatives only, including NDM/VIM/IMP makers (when paired with avibactam).
🎯 Used for: Gram-negative sepsis in penicillin/cephalosporin allergy; metallo-enzyme superbugs.
💡 Tip: Aztreonam = the beta-lactam that ignores penicillin allergy (except ceftazidime).

ov.moa: Monocyclic beta-lactam (monobactam) that binds PBP3 of aerobic gram-negative bacteria to block cell wall synthesis; bactericidal.
ov.ind: Serious aerobic gram-negative infections, especially where penicillin or cephalosporin allergy rules out other beta-lactams; combined with avibactam for metallo-beta-lactamase producers. Inactive against gram-positives and anaerobes, so mixed infections need an added agent.
ov.ae: Nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, rash, phlebitis, transaminase rise; C. difficile colitis; rarely hypersensitivity.
ov.ci: Contraindicated in aztreonam hypersensitivity. Low cross-reactivity with other beta-lactams, but ceftazidime and cefiderocol share its side chain. Adjust dose in renal impairment.
ov.counsel: Given by injection; report rash, swelling, breathing difficulty or severe diarrhea. Tell your prescriber about any ceftazidime allergy.

c.st: Inj 500 mg, 1 g · Cap 125, 250 mg (oral, for C. difficile)
c.dose: Inj 500 mg, 1 g · Cap 125, 250 mg (oral, for C. difficile)
ind: MRSA infections, serious gram-positive infections in beta-lactam allergy, endocarditis, bacterial meningitis (with ceftriaxone), and oral therapy for C. difficile colitis.
c.doc: MRSA bacteremia and endocarditis; ampicillin-resistant Enterococcus faecium; C. difficile infection (oral)
c.ci: Hypersensitivity to vancomycin
c.sci: Renal impairment, hearing loss, concurrent aminoglycosides or piperacillin-tazobactam
ae: Infusion reaction (flushing, rash, itching), nephrotoxicity, ototoxicity, neutropenia, phlebitis
c.sae: Nephrotoxicity / Vancomycin infusion reaction / Ototoxicity
c.info: Binds D-Ala-D-Ala termini of peptidoglycan precursors, blocking cell wall cross-linking. Too large to be absorbed from the gut, so oral use acts only in the intestine. VRE change the target to D-Ala-D-Lac. Dosing is guided by levels (AUC 400–600 mg·h/L or trough) to avoid kidney injury.
c.caution: Infuse slowly, at most 10 mg/min or over at least 60 minutes, to prevent the infusion reaction. Monitor renal function and levels.
c.preg: Limited data; IV vancomycin is used in pregnancy when clearly needed (MRSA infection, or prophylaxis in beta-lactam-allergic women, e.g. for group B streptococcus). Reports of fetal harm are rare and unconfirmed, but monitor maternal levels and renal function. Oral vancomycin is barely absorbed, so fetal exposure is minimal. Milk levels are low and infant oral absorption is poor; compatible with breastfeeding — watch for diarrhea or thrush.
c.renal: Nephrotoxic and cleared almost entirely by the kidneys — IV doses must be reduced or the interval extended according to CrCl, and guided by levels (AUC-guided or trough monitoring); in hemodialysis, dose by pre-dialysis levels. Avoid combining with other nephrotoxic drugs. Oral vancomycin for C. difficile needs no adjustment because absorption is negligible.

ind: Serious gram-positive infections including MRSA: bone and joint, endocarditis, skin and soft tissue, and prophylaxis in surgery.
c.doc: MRSA bone and joint infections and endocarditis with once-daily or thrice-weekly dosing
c.ci: Hypersensitivity to teicoplanin
c.sci: Vancomycin allergy (cross-reaction possible); renal impairment; thrombocytopenia
ae: Rash, fever, injection-site pain, raised liver enzymes, thrombocytopenia, mild nephrotoxicity
c.sae: Thrombocytopenia / Hypersensitivity
c.info: Glycopeptide with the same target as vancomycin but a longer half-life and IM route. Lower rates of infusion reaction and nephrotoxicity, but needs loading doses. Not available in the US.
c.caution: Add the solvent slowly and roll the vial gently — do not shake, to avoid foaming. Give IV as a bolus over 3–5 minutes or an infusion over 30 minutes, or IM. The loading doses (usually 12-hourly for the first 3–5 doses) are essential for effective levels. Monitor trough levels, blood counts, and renal and liver function; check hearing with prolonged courses. Cross-sensitivity with vancomycin can occur.
c.preg: Limited human data; animal studies at high doses suggested toxicity, so use only if the benefit clearly outweighs the risk and when safer options are unsuitable. Excretion into breast milk is unknown, but oral absorption by the infant is expected to be poor; use with caution and watch for diarrhea or thrush.
c.renal: Renally eliminated. Keep the loading doses unchanged; from about day 4 onward reduce the dose or extend the interval in moderate–severe renal impairment, guided by trough levels. It is not removed by hemodialysis. Use with caution alongside aminoglycosides or other nephrotoxic drugs.

c.sp:
Gram-positive only: MRSA, MSSA, S. epidermidis, streptococci, Enterococcus faecalis, Clostridioides difficile (oral vancomycin)
Not covered: gram-negatives, VRE (VanA/VanB), mycobacteria
c.mn:
💊 Names: Vancomycin, Teicoplanin.
🦠 Kills: MRSA and other gram-positives; oral vancomycin kills C. difficile.
🎯 Used for: MRSA sepsis/endocarditis; C. difficile.
💡 Tip: Vanco = infuse SLOW (red man), watch kidneys and ears. Teico = the long-acting IM cousin.

ind: Acute bacterial skin and skin-structure infections (ABSSSI) caused by gram-positive organisms including MRSA.
c.doc: Once-weekly or single-dose therapy for ABSSSI; long-acting outpatient option for osteomyelitis (off-label)
c.ci: Hypersensitivity to dalbavancin
c.sci: Glycopeptide allergy; hepatic impairment; renal impairment (CrCl <30 mL/min)
ae: Nausea, diarrhea, headache, rash, infusion-site reactions, raised transaminases
c.sae: Hypersensitivity / infusion reactions / C. difficile colitis
c.info: Semisynthetic lipoglycopeptide; a lipophilic tail anchors to the membrane and gives an extremely long half-life (~ 14 days), allowing one or two doses to complete a course.
c.caution: Reconstitute with sterile water, then dilute only in 5% dextrose (incompatible with saline). Infuse over 30 minutes; flush the line with 5% dextrose. Rapid infusion can cause an infusion reaction. Watch for diarrhea (C. difficile) and hepatic enzyme rises. Because of the long half-life, effects of any adverse reaction can persist for weeks.
c.preg: No adequate human data; animal studies at high doses showed effects on fetal development. Use only if the benefit outweighs the risk. Excreted into animal milk; human milk data are lacking, though oral absorption in the infant is expected to be poor — use with caution.
c.renal: No adjustment needed for CrCl of 30 mL/min or above or in patients on regular hemodialysis. Reduce the dose by about 25% when CrCl is below 30 mL/min and not on dialysis. Caution in moderate–severe hepatic impairment (no dose adjustment established).

ind: Acute bacterial skin and skin-structure infections (ABSSSI) caused by gram-positive organisms including MRSA.
c.doc: Single-dose therapy for ABSSSI, including MRSA
c.ci: Hypersensitivity to oritavancin; IV unfractionated heparin within 120 hours (Orbactiv only)
c.sci: Vancomycin allergy; warfarin therapy (falsely prolongs coag tests)
ae: Headache, nausea, infusion reactions, limb abscess, phlebitis
c.sae: Infusion reactions / Hypersensitivity / Osteomyelitis
c.info: Lipoglycopeptide with three mechanisms (blocks transglycosylation and transpeptidation, disrupts membrane); active against VanA VRE. A single dose is enough. It artificially prolongs aPTT and PT/INR for hours to days, so avoid heparin and interpret coagulation tests with caution.
c.caution: Reconstitute with sterile water and dilute only in 5% dextrose (not saline). Infuse over 3 hours (Orbactiv) or 1 hour (Kimyrsa). Avoid IV unfractionated heparin for 120 hours after Orbactiv. It falsely prolongs aPTT for up to 120 hours and PT/INR for up to 12 hours — use alternative coagulation tests where possible, and be careful with warfarin.
c.preg: No adequate human data; animal studies showed no fetal harm. Use only if clearly needed. Excreted into animal milk; human data are lacking, though infant oral absorption is expected to be poor. Because the drug persists for weeks, weigh this when deciding on breastfeeding.
c.renal: No dose adjustment in mild–moderate renal impairment; not studied in severe impairment, and it is not removed by hemodialysis. No adjustment in mild–moderate hepatic impairment.

c.sp:
Gram-positive: MRSA, MSSA, streptococci, Enterococcus faecalis (oritavancin also VRE)
Not covered: gram-negatives
c.mn:
💊 Names: Dalbavancin, Oritavancin (telavancin is the third).
🦠 Kills: MRSA and streptococci; oritavancin also kills VRE.
🎯 Used for: Skin infections with one or two doses.
💡 Tip: -vancin = glycopeptide; dal/ori = long-acting, one and done.

ov.moa: Glycopeptides bind the D-Ala-D-Ala terminus of peptidoglycan precursors and block cell wall polymerization; bactericidal (time-dependent) against gram-positives. Lipoglycopeptides add a lipophilic tail that anchors to the membrane and extends half-life.
ov.ind: MRSA and other serious gram-positive infections: bacteremia, endocarditis, bone and joint, pneumonia, meningitis and skin infections; oral vancomycin for C. difficile colitis. Lipoglycopeptides allow one- or two-dose therapy for skin infections. No gram-negative activity.
ov.ae: Vancomycin infusion reaction (flushing from rapid infusion), nephrotoxicity, ototoxicity, neutropenia, phlebitis; teicoplanin thrombocytopenia; oritavancin distorts coagulation tests.
ov.ci: Avoid or monitor closely with other nephrotoxic drugs (aminoglycosides, piperacillin-tazobactam). Adjust dose and monitor levels in renal impairment.
ov.counsel: Given by slow injection or infusion; report rash, itching, flushing, hearing changes, ringing in the ears or reduced urine. Oral vancomycin capsules are for gut infection only.

ind: Serious gram-positive infections, especially in penicillin-allergic patients, where clindamycin is not available.
c.doc: Older lincosamide used when clindamycin is unavailable; mostly replaced by clindamycin
c.ci: Hypersensitivity to lincomycin or clindamycin
c.sci: Current or past C. difficile or colitis; liver disease
ae: Diarrhea, nausea, rash, glossitis, injection-site pain
c.sae: C. difficile-associated diarrhea / pseudomembranous colitis (boxed warning)
c.info: The parent lincosamide from Streptomyces lincolnensis; clindamycin is its chlorinated, better-absorbed derivative. Same 50S mechanism, poorer absorption and higher colitis rates, so it is now rarely used.
c.caution: Give IM or by slow IV infusion (dilute; never push — rapid IV can cause hypotension or cardiac arrest). Take capsules with a full glass of water, 1–2 hours before or after food, since food lowers absorption. Stop and seek review for persistent or bloody diarrhea (C. difficile colitis); higher colitis rates than clindamycin.
c.preg: Crosses the placenta; limited data. Clindamycin is the preferred lincosamide in pregnancy, so use lincomycin only if clearly needed. Excreted into breast milk; may cause infant diarrhea or sensitization, so use with caution and watch the infant for loose or bloody stools.
c.renal: Half-life is prolonged in renal and hepatic impairment — in severe renal impairment give about 25–30% of the usual dose. Monitor closely in liver disease.

c.st: Cap 75, 150, 300 mg · Inj 150 mg/mL (300, 600, 900 mg) · Topical gel/lotion · Vaginal cream
c.dose: Cap 75, 150, 300 mg · Inj 150 mg/mL (300, 600, 900 mg) · Topical gel/lotion · Vaginal cream
ind: Anaerobic and gram-positive infections: skin and soft tissue (including community MRSA), bone and joint, dental, pelvic, lung abscess, and toxic shock; also topical for acne and vaginal cream for bacterial vaginosis.
c.doc: Anaerobic infections above the diaphragm, necrotizing/toxic shock syndromes (toxin suppression), MSSA/MRSA osteomyelitis, and penicillin-allergic dental or surgical prophylaxis
c.ci: Hypersensitivity to clindamycin or lincomycin
c.sci: Current or past C. difficile or colitis; severe liver disease
ae: Diarrhea, nausea, rash, metallic taste; C. difficile colitis
c.sae: C. difficile-associated diarrhea / pseudomembranous colitis (boxed warning)
c.info: Binds the 50S ribosomal subunit and blocks translocation; bacteriostatic. Good bone and abscess penetration, poor CNS penetration (not for meningitis). Erythromycin-resistant staphylococci may carry inducible resistance (positive D-test). Highest C. difficile risk among common antibiotics.
c.caution: Give IV over 10–60 minutes (do not push); take capsules with a full glass of water. Stop and seek review for persistent diarrhea.
c.preg: Generally considered acceptable in all trimesters when indicated (for example bacterial vaginosis, group B streptococcus prophylaxis in penicillin-allergic women), with no consistent increase in malformations. Small amounts pass into breast milk; compatible with breastfeeding, but watch the infant for diarrhea, blood in the stool, or thrush.
c.renal: Mostly metabolized by the liver, so no routine adjustment in renal impairment (half-life increases modestly in severe renal failure); not removed by dialysis. Use with caution and consider level monitoring in severe hepatic impairment.

c.sp:
Gram-positive: Staphylococcus aureus (MSSA, community MRSA), streptococci (not enterococci)
Anaerobes: Bacteroides fragilis, Clostridium (not C. difficile), Peptostreptococcus
Other: Toxoplasma, Plasmodium and Babesia (with other drugs)
Not covered: gram-negative aerobes, Enterococcus, MRSA hospital strains (variable)
c.mn:
💊 Names: Clindamycin, Lincomycin.
🦠 Kills: Anaerobes above the belt, staph and strep; stops toxin production.
🎯 Used for: Abscesses, dental, bone, toxic shock; acne and BV topically.
💡 Tip: Clinda = C. diff (causes diarrhea); D-test for hidden resistance.

ov.moa: Bind the 50S ribosomal subunit (23S rRNA) and inhibit peptide translocation; bacteriostatic, sometimes bactericidal at high concentrations, and suppress bacterial toxin production.
ov.ind: Anaerobic and gram-positive infections (skin/soft tissue including community MRSA, bone and joint, dental, lung abscess, pelvic infections), toxic shock and necrotizing infections as adjunct, and penicillin-allergic prophylaxis; topical use for acne and vaginal use for bacterial vaginosis.
ov.ae: Diarrhea, nausea, rash, metallic taste; C. difficile colitis can be severe and appear weeks after stopping.
ov.ci: Boxed warning for C. difficile colitis; avoid with a history of colitis. Erythromycin can antagonize its action. Not for meningitis (poor CNS penetration).
ov.counsel: Take capsules with a full glass of water. Stop the drug and call your prescriber for watery or bloody diarrhea, even after finishing the course.

c.st: Tab 400, 600 mg · Inj 600 mg/300 mL · Susp 100 mg/5 mL
c.dose: Tab 400, 600 mg · Inj 600 mg/300 mL · Susp 100 mg/5 mL
ind: Vancomycin-resistant Enterococcus faecium infections, nosocomial and community pneumonia, complicated skin infections including MRSA; also used in drug-resistant tuberculosis.
c.doc: VRE infections and MRSA pneumonia; MDR/XDR tuberculosis regimens
c.ci: Non-selective MAO inhibitors within 14 days
c.sci: Uncontrolled hypertension, pheochromocytoma, carcinoid, thyrotoxicosis, SSRIs or other serotonergic drugs; baseline cytopenias; use beyond 2 weeks
ae: Diarrhea, nausea, headache, thrombocytopenia, taste change; peripheral and optic neuropathy and lactic acidosis with long courses
c.sae: Myelosuppression (thrombocytopenia) / Serotonin syndrome / Optic and peripheral neuropathy / Lactic acidosis
c.info: Binds the 50S subunit at the P-site and stops the 70S initiation complex forming — unique so no cross-resistance with other ribosomal drugs. About 100% oral bioavailability, so IV-to-oral switch uses the same dose. Weak reversible MAO inhibitor. Check blood counts weekly beyond 2 weeks.
c.caution: Same dose IV and oral, with or without food. Avoid large amounts of tyramine-rich food (aged cheese, cured meats). Weekly complete blood count for courses longer than 2 weeks.
c.preg: Limited human data; animal studies showed embryo-fetal toxicity at high doses. Use only when the benefit clearly outweighs the risk and alternatives are unsuitable (e.g. VRE or drug-resistant tuberculosis). Excreted into breast milk; where possible avoid or pause breastfeeding, otherwise watch the infant for diarrhea, vomiting, and poor feeding.
c.renal: No dose adjustment in renal impairment, but the two main metabolites accumulate — monitor blood counts closely in severe renal impairment or dialysis, since myelosuppression is more likely. Linezolid is removed by hemodialysis, so give the dose after the session. No adjustment in mild–moderate hepatic impairment.

ind: Acute bacterial skin and skin-structure infections (ABSSSI) caused by susceptible gram-positives including MRSA.
c.doc: Six-day, once-daily ABSSSI therapy with less blood-count and MAO effects than linezolid
c.ci: Hypersensitivity to tedizolid or linezolid
c.sci: Neutropenia; use beyond 6 days is not studied
ae: Nausea, headache, diarrhea, vomiting, dizziness
c.sae: Hypersensitivity / C. difficile colitis
c.info: Next-generation oxazolidinone prodrug (tedizolid phosphate) with greater potency, once-daily dosing, and less myelosuppression and MAO inhibition. It can work on some linezolid-resistant strains carrying cfr.
c.caution: Take tablets with or without food; give IV over 1 hour. Fewer blood-count and MAO effects than linezolid, but still avoid combining with other serotonergic drugs where possible. Report new diarrhea (C. difficile). Treatment course is 6 days.
c.preg: No adequate human data; animal studies showed decreased fetal weight and delayed skeletal development at high exposures. Use only if clearly needed. Excreted into animal milk; human data are lacking — use with caution.
c.renal: No dose adjustment in renal impairment (including hemodialysis, which does not remove it) or in hepatic impairment.

c.sp:
Gram-positive: MRSA, MSSA, Enterococcus faecium and faecalis (including VRE), streptococci (including penicillin-resistant pneumococci); Mycobacterium tuberculosis (linezolid)
Not covered: gram-negatives
c.mn:
💊 Names: Linezolid, Tedizolid (all end in -zolid).
🦠 Kills: VRE, MRSA and resistant strep; also drug-resistant TB.
🎯 Used for: VRE/MRSA infections; 100% oral so IV = oral.
💡 Tip: Linezolid = low platelets and serotonin syndrome; stop SSRIs and MAOIs.

ov.moa: Bind the 50S ribosomal subunit at the P-site, blocking formation of the 70S initiation complex and protein synthesis; bacteriostatic against most gram-positives (bactericidal vs some streptococci).
ov.ind: Resistant gram-positive infections: vancomycin-resistant Enterococcus, MRSA pneumonia and skin infections; drug-resistant tuberculosis (linezolid). Excellent oral bioavailability allows early IV-to-oral switch.
ov.ae: Diarrhea, nausea, headache; myelosuppression (thrombocytopenia) with courses beyond 2 weeks; peripheral and optic neuropathy, lactic acidosis; serotonin syndrome with serotonergic drugs.
ov.ci: Avoid with MAO inhibitors and with SSRIs/SNRIs/tramadol unless monitored. Watch blood counts; caution with uncontrolled hypertension, pheochromocytoma or carcinoid.
ov.counsel: Take with or without food; limit tyramine-rich foods. Report bleeding or bruising, vision changes, numbness/tingling, agitation, fever or fast heartbeat.

c.st: Tab 200, 400, 500 mg · Inj 500 mg/100 mL · Susp 200 mg/5 mL · Vaginal/topical gel
c.dose: Tab 200, 400, 500 mg · Inj 500 mg/100 mL · Susp 200 mg/5 mL · Vaginal/topical gel
ind: Anaerobic infections, amoebiasis, giardiasis, trichomoniasis, bacterial vaginosis, H. pylori eradication regimens and C. difficile (second line); topical for rosacea.
c.doc: Intra-abdominal and pelvic anaerobic infection (with a gram-negative agent); amoebic liver abscess; trichomoniasis and BV
c.ci: Hypersensitivity to nitroimidazoles; disulfiram within the last 2 weeks
c.sci: Alcohol during and for 48–72 h after; liver disease; Cockayne syndrome; seizure or CNS disease; warfarin
ae: Metallic taste, nausea, headache, dark urine, glossitis; peripheral neuropathy and CNS effects with long courses
c.sae: Peripheral neuropathy and encephalopathy with prolonged use / Disulfiram-like reaction with alcohol
c.info: Prodrug reduced by anaerobes’ nitroreductases into radicals that break DNA; bactericidal against anaerobes and protozoa. About 100% oral bioavailability; excellent tissue and CNS penetration. Inhibits warfarin metabolism (CYP2C9), raising INR.
c.caution: Avoid alcohol during and for at least 72 hours after. Take with food to reduce nausea. Limit courses to what is needed because of neuropathy risk.
c.preg: Many labels advise avoiding it in the first trimester unless clearly needed, but large studies show no increase in birth defects, and it is used at any stage for symptomatic trichomoniasis and bacterial vaginosis. Passes into breast milk at levels close to maternal plasma; short courses are acceptable. After a large single dose some guidance suggests pausing breastfeeding for 12–24 hours; watch the infant for diarrhea, thrush, and rarely neutropenia.
c.renal: No adjustment in mild–moderate renal impairment; in severe renal failure (CrCl below 10 mL/min) metabolites accumulate, so consider a dose reduction. Hemodialysis removes it, so give the dose after the session. Reduce the dose by about 50% in severe hepatic impairment (Child-Pugh C).

ind: Trichomoniasis, giardiasis, amoebiasis and bacterial vaginosis; also anaerobic infections and surgical prophylaxis in some regions.
c.doc: Single-dose therapy for trichomoniasis and giardiasis
c.ci: Hypersensitivity to nitroimidazoles; first trimester of pregnancy; alcohol during and 3 days after
c.sci: Blood dyscrasias, CNS disease, liver disease
ae: Metallic taste, nausea, vomiting, dizziness, fatigue
c.sae: Disulfiram-like reaction with alcohol / Peripheral neuropathy / Carcinogenic in rodents (boxed warning in US)
c.info: Second-generation nitroimidazole with a longer half-life (12–14 h) allowing once-daily or single-dose regimens; same DNA-damaging mechanism as metronidazole.
c.caution: Take with food to reduce nausea. Avoid alcohol during treatment and for 3 days after. Avoid in the first trimester. Carcinogenic in animal studies, so avoid unnecessary or prolonged use. Report numbness, tingling, or unsteadiness.
c.preg: Avoid in the first trimester; use later only if clearly needed, since metronidazole has more safety data. Excreted into breast milk — pause breastfeeding during treatment and for 3 days after the last dose.
c.renal: No adjustment in renal impairment. It is removed by hemodialysis, so give a supplemental dose after the session. Use caution and consider dose reduction in severe hepatic impairment.

ind: Amoebiasis, giardiasis, trichomoniasis, bacterial vaginosis and anaerobic infections in the markets where it is licensed (not approved in the US).
c.doc: Amoebic dysentery and liver abscess in South Asian practice; often combined with ofloxacin/ciprofloxacin for diarrhea (fixed-dose products)
c.ci: Hypersensitivity to imidazoles
c.sci: Alcohol; CNS disease or seizures; liver disease; first trimester
ae: Nausea, dizziness, headache, metallic taste, drowsiness
c.sae: CNS effects (ataxia, vertigo, seizures) / Peripheral neuropathy
c.info: Nitroimidazole with a longer half-life than metronidazole (~ 12–14 h) and the same mechanism; often used as twice-daily or once-daily therapy.
c.caution: Take after food to reduce nausea and metallic taste; avoid alcohol during treatment. IV infusion over 15–30 minutes. Stop and report numbness, tingling, unsteadiness, or seizures. Avoid unnecessary long courses.
c.preg: Limited human data; avoid in the first trimester and use later only if the benefit clearly outweighs the risk. Excreted into breast milk — avoid breastfeeding during treatment or pause it and resume after the course.
c.renal: Usually no adjustment in renal impairment; hemodialysis removes it, so give a dose after the session. In severe liver disease reduce the dose (or extend the interval) and monitor for neurologic side effects.

ind: Bacterial vaginosis and trichomoniasis in adults; also giardiasis and amoebiasis in some regions.
c.doc: Single-dose treatment of bacterial vaginosis and trichomoniasis
c.ci: Hypersensitivity to nitroimidazoles
c.sci: Alcohol; blood dyscrasias; CNS disease; hepatic impairment
ae: Vulvovaginal candidiasis, headache, nausea, dysgeusia, diarrhea
c.sae: Hypersensitivity / Disulfiram-like reaction (label advice: avoid alcohol)
c.info: Longest half-life of the group (~ 17 h) so one dose is enough. Sprinkle granules on applesauce, yogurt or pudding and eat within 30 minutes; do not crush or mix into liquid.
c.caution: Sprinkle the full contents of one sachet on applesauce, yogurt, or pudding and eat within 30 minutes without chewing; do not dissolve in liquid. Avoid alcohol as a precaution, as with other nitroimidazoles. Vulvovaginal yeast infection is a common side effect.
c.preg: Limited human data. Use only if clearly needed; metronidazole has more pregnancy experience and is generally preferred. Excreted into breast milk — consider pumping and discarding milk during treatment and for 96 hours after the dose.
c.renal: No adjustment in mild–moderate renal impairment; not studied in severe impairment or hemodialysis. Not studied in hepatic impairment.

c.sp:
Anaerobes: Bacteroides fragilis, Clostridium (including C. difficile), Fusobacterium, Peptostreptococcus
Protozoa: Entamoeba histolytica, Giardia lamblia, Trichomonas vaginalis
Other: Gardnerella (BV), Helicobacter pylori (in combination)
Not covered: aerobes, facultative bacteria, actinomyces
c.mn:
💊 Names: Metronidazole, Tinidazole, Ornidazole, Secnidazole (all -nidazole).
🦠 Kills: Anaerobes and protozoa: Trichomonas, Giardia, Entamoeba, BV.
🎯 Used for: Abscesses below the belt, amoebiasis, BV, C. diff, H. pylori.
💡 Tip: Metro + alcohol = flushing and vomiting; long neuropathy risk. Tini/Orni/Secni = longer acting.

ov.moa: Prodrugs activated by anaerobic nitroreductases to short-lived radicals that fragment DNA; bactericidal against anaerobic bacteria and protozoa; inactive against aerobes.
ov.ind: Anaerobic and mixed infections (intra-abdominal, pelvic, dental, brain abscess), amoebiasis, giardiasis, trichomoniasis, bacterial vaginosis, H. pylori regimens and C. difficile. Given with another agent when aerobic gram-negatives are also involved.
ov.ae: Metallic taste, nausea, dark urine, headache; disulfiram-like reaction with alcohol; peripheral neuropathy and CNS toxicity with prolonged or high-dose use; rarely seizures.
ov.ci: Avoid alcohol during therapy and for 48–72 hours after. Contraindicated with recent disulfiram. Caution in CNS disease, liver disease and Cockayne syndrome. Metronidazole raises warfarin effect.
ov.counsel: Avoid alcohol during and after treatment; take with food; urine may turn dark. Report numbness or tingling, confusion, seizures or severe rash.

ind: Serious gram-negative infections (Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Acinetobacter, carbapenem-resistant Enterobacterales); topical/ophthalmic use in combination products.
c.doc: Bloodstream and pulmonary MDR gram-negative infections (active drug given directly, better systemic exposure than CMS-based colistin)
c.ci: Hypersensitivity to polymyxins
c.sci: Renal impairment; myasthenia gravis; concurrent neurotoxic or nephrotoxic drugs; not for urinary infection (low urine levels)
ae: Nephrotoxicity, neurotoxicity (dizziness, paresthesia), neuromuscular blockade, injection-site pain, skin hyperpigmentation
c.sae: Nephrotoxicity / Neurotoxicity / Respiratory paralysis (boxed warning)
c.info: Same mechanism as colistin but given as the active drug (no prodrug conversion), so it reaches effective blood levels faster. It is mainly cleared non-renally, so it is not usually dose-reduced in kidney disease, and it does not reach the urine well.
c.caution: Reserve for infections without safer options. Monitor kidney function daily and watch for neurotoxicity (numbness, dizziness, weakness). Avoid concurrent nephrotoxic or neurotoxic drugs (aminoglycosides, vancomycin) and neuromuscular blockers (risk of respiratory paralysis). Intramuscular injection is very painful and is generally avoided. Dose is often written in units (10,000 units ≈ 1 mg), so check the label.
c.preg: Crosses the placenta; limited human data. Reserve for life-threatening infections with no alternative, given the nephrotoxic and neurotoxic risk. Excretion into breast milk is unknown, but oral absorption by the infant is poor — use with caution.
c.renal: Cleared mainly by non-renal routes, so many expert guidelines do not reduce the dose in renal impairment, although the product label advises reduction — follow local protocol. Nephrotoxic: monitor creatinine daily and avoid other nephrotoxins.

c.st: Inj colistimethate sodium 1 MIU, 2 MIU (about 80–160 mg)
c.dose: Inj colistimethate sodium 1 MIU, 2 MIU (about 80–160 mg)
ind: Multidrug-resistant gram-negative infections (Acinetobacter baumannii, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, carbapenem-resistant Enterobacterales) when other options fail; inhaled for cystic fibrosis.
c.doc: Carbapenem-resistant Acinetobacter and Pseudomonas as last-resort therapy (usually combined with another active drug)
c.ci: Hypersensitivity to colistin or polymyxins
c.sci: Renal impairment; myasthenia gravis; nephrotoxic or neuromuscular-blocking drugs
ae: Nephrotoxicity (dose-related), paresthesias, dizziness, neuromuscular weakness, rash
c.sae: Nephrotoxicity / Neurotoxicity / Neuromuscular blockade with apnea
c.info: A cationic polypeptide that binds lipid A of lipopolysaccharide, displacing calcium and magnesium and disrupting the outer membrane; concentration-dependent bactericidal. Given as the prodrug colistimethate sodium (CMS); dose is expressed in IU or mg colistin base activity, so check the units. A loading dose is needed. Resistance is plasmid-mediated (mcr-1).
c.caution: Check the label for the unit of dosing (mg CBA vs MIU vs mg CMS). Give a loading dose; adjust by renal function; monitor kidney function daily.
c.preg: Crosses the placenta; limited human data. Reserve for life-threatening multidrug-resistant infections when no alternative exists. Small amounts pass into breast milk and oral absorption by the infant is poor; use with caution and watch for diarrhea.
c.renal: Colistimethate is cleared largely by the kidneys — give the full loading dose, then reduce the maintenance dose by CrCl (and follow renal replacement therapy protocols). Nephrotoxic: monitor creatinine daily and avoid other nephrotoxins.

c.sp:
Gram-negative aerobes: Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Acinetobacter baumannii, Klebsiella, Escherichia coli, Enterobacter
Not covered (intrinsic resistance): Proteus, Providencia, Serratia, Morganella, Burkholderia; all gram-positives and anaerobes
c.mn:
💊 Names: Colistin (Polymyxin E), Polymyxin B.
🦠 Kills: Superbug gram-negatives (Acinetobacter, Pseudomonas, CRE).
🎯 Used for: Last resort when carbapenems fail.
💡 Tip: Poly-MYXIN: kidneys and nerves take the hit; loading dose first.

ov.moa: Cationic polypeptides that bind lipid A of gram-negative lipopolysaccharide, displace divalent cations and disrupt the outer membrane, causing cell leakage and death; concentration-dependent killing.
ov.ind: Last-resort therapy for multidrug-resistant gram-negative infections (Acinetobacter, Pseudomonas, carbapenem-resistant Enterobacterales); inhaled forms for cystic fibrosis; topical uses in combination products. Usually combined with a second active drug.
ov.ae: Nephrotoxicity (common, dose-related), neurotoxicity (paresthesias, dizziness), neuromuscular blockade with respiratory paralysis, rash.
ov.ci: Use with caution in renal impairment and avoid myasthenia gravis; avoid other nephrotoxic or neuromuscular-blocking drugs where possible. Not for gram-positives or Proteus/Serratia.
ov.counsel: Given by injection in hospital; report reduced urine, numbness or tingling around the mouth, weakness or breathing difficulty.

ind: Prophylaxis of recurrent urinary tract infection after the acute infection has been treated.
c.doc: Long-term prevention of recurrent UTI without promoting antibiotic resistance
c.ci: Severe renal or hepatic impairment; severe dehydration; concurrent sulfonamides
c.sci: Gout (uric acid crystals); alkalinizing agents (acetazolamide, sodium bicarbonate, thiazides)
ae: Nausea, rash, dysuria, GI upset, painful urination
c.sae: Crystalluria with sulfonamides / Hepatic dysfunction (formaldehyde/ammonia) / Rash
c.info: Hydrolyzed in acidic urine (pH below 6) to formaldehyde, which is bactericidal and causes no resistance. Needs an acidic urine, so avoid alkalinizing drugs. Not for treating an active infection or for upper tract infections.
c.caution: Works only in acidic urine — avoid antacids/alkalinizers. Never combine with sulfonamides (insoluble crystals).
c.preg: Limited data but no established teratogenic risk; may be used for preventing recurrent UTI when other options are unsuitable. Passes into breast milk in small amounts; generally acceptable while watching the infant for rash or GI upset.
c.renal: Contraindicated in severe renal impairment because it does not reach effective urine concentration and can crystallize, especially with sulfonamides. Also avoid in severe hepatic impairment (formaldehyde and ammonia load).

c.st: Cap 50, 100 mg (macrocrystals/monohydrate) · Tab 50, 100 mg · Susp 25 mg/5 mL
c.dose: Cap 50, 100 mg (macrocrystals/monohydrate) · Tab 50, 100 mg · Susp 25 mg/5 mL
ind: Treatment of uncomplicated lower urinary tract infection (cystitis) and long-term prophylaxis of recurrent UTI.
c.doc: First-line empirical therapy for uncomplicated cystitis in women (5 days); prophylaxis of recurrent UTI
c.ci: CrCl below 30 mL/min or anuria/oliguria; term pregnancy (38–42 weeks) and infants under 1 month; prior nitrofurantoin cholestatic jaundice or liver damage
c.sci: G6PD deficiency (hemolysis); lung disease; peripheral neuropathy risk (diabetes, anemia, B-vitamin deficiency)
ae: Nausea, headache, flatulence, brown-colored urine, rash
c.sae: Acute or chronic pulmonary reaction (fibrosis) / Hepatitis / Peripheral neuropathy / Hemolysis in G6PD deficiency
c.info: Reduced by bacterial flavoproteins to reactive intermediates that damage DNA, ribosomes and metabolic enzymes; bactericidal in urine. Reaches therapeutic levels only in the urine, so it is unsuitable for pyelonephritis, prostatitis or bacteremia. Covers E. coli and Enterococcus; Proteus, Pseudomonas and Serratia are intrinsically resistant. Avoid long courses because of pulmonary and liver toxicity.
c.caution: Take with food to improve absorption and reduce nausea. Not for treating kidney infections or when CrCl is low. Report cough, shortness of breath, fever or yellow skin.
c.preg: Acceptable in the first and second trimesters when no suitable alternative exists. Avoid at term (38–42 weeks), in labor and delivery, and in breastfed infants under 1 month or those with G6PD deficiency, because of the risk of hemolytic anemia in the newborn. Small amounts pass into breast milk; otherwise generally compatible with breastfeeding in healthy older infants.
c.renal: Contraindicated when CrCl is below 30 mL/min (or in anuria/oliguria): it fails to reach effective urine levels and toxicity (neuropathy, pulmonary and liver reactions) rises. Use caution in the elderly and in liver disease.

ind: Single-dose treatment of uncomplicated cystitis in women; intravenous formulations are used in some regions for multidrug-resistant infections.
c.doc: Single-dose therapy for uncomplicated cystitis, including ESBL-producing E. coli
c.ci: Hypersensitivity to fosfomycin
c.sci: Renal impairment (reduced urinary levels); meals delay absorption
ae: Diarrhea, headache, nausea, vaginitis, dizziness
c.sae: Diarrhea / Hypersensitivity
c.info: Inhibits MurA (enolpyruvyl transferase), blocking the first committed step of peptidoglycan synthesis; bactericidal in urine. Unusual structure means little cross-resistance. Covers E. coli (including ESBL), Enterococcus faecalis and many Klebsiella; single-dose regimen improves adherence.
c.caution: Dissolve the sachet in half a glass of water and drink immediately, on an empty stomach, ideally at bedtime after emptying the bladder.
c.preg: Crosses the placenta; single-dose treatment of cystitis and asymptomatic bacteriuria is acceptable in pregnancy, with no adverse fetal effects reported. Small amounts pass into breast milk; a single dose is generally compatible with breastfeeding, though watch for infant diarrhea.
c.renal: No adjustment for a single 3 g sachet in mild–moderate renal impairment, but urinary concentration falls as CrCl decreases, so it may be ineffective when CrCl is below about 30 mL/min. No adjustment in hepatic impairment.

c.sp:
Urinary pathogens: Escherichia coli (including ESBL producers), Enterococcus faecalis, Staphylococcus saprophyticus, Klebsiella (variable)
Not covered: Proteus, Pseudomonas, Serratia (nitrofurantoin); systemic or upper tract infections (levels only in urine)
c.mn:
💊 Names: Nitrofurantoin, Methenamine, Fosfomycin.
🦠 Kills: Bladder bugs, mainly E. coli (including ESBL); works in urine only.
🎯 Used for: Simple cystitis (nitrofurantoin 5 days, fosfomycin 1 dose); methenamine prevents recurrence.
💡 Tip: Nitrofurantoin = urine only, lungs and liver with long use, avoid in low CrCl. Methenamine needs acid urine.

ov.moa: Concentrated in urine, where nitrofurantoin damages bacterial DNA and enzymes after reduction, methenamine releases formaldehyde in acid urine, and fosfomycin blocks MurA to halt cell wall synthesis; none achieves therapeutic tissue or blood levels.
ov.ind: Uncomplicated cystitis (nitrofurantoin, fosfomycin) and prevention of recurrent UTI (nitrofurantoin, methenamine). Not for pyelonephritis, prostatitis, catheter-associated infection with systemic signs or bacteremia.
ov.ae: Nausea, headache, diarrhea, rash; nitrofurantoin pulmonary, hepatic and neuropathic reactions with long-term use; methenamine GI upset and dysuria.
ov.ci: Nitrofurantoin: avoid with CrCl below 30 mL/min, at term pregnancy and in infants under 1 month. Methenamine: avoid with sulfonamides and alkalinizing drugs, and in severe renal/hepatic failure.
ov.counsel: Take nitrofurantoin with food; fosfomycin as a single dose in water; methenamine with acidic urine (limit antacids). Report cough, breathlessness, jaundice or numbness in the feet.

meta.scope: No interaction entries have been added yet.
meta.source: None yet — curated, source-verified entries are added to interactions.json.

interactions.effect: Increased risk of nephrotoxicity when a cephalosporin (especially cefazolin/cefaloridine-type agents) is combined with an aminoglycoside.
interactions.mechanism: Both drug classes are independently nephrotoxic to renal tubular cells; the effects are additive rather than a pharmacokinetic interaction.
interactions.management: Avoid the combination if possible, especially in patients with pre-existing renal impairment. If unavoidable, monitor renal function (serum creatinine) and aminoglycoside levels closely.
interactions.source: Compiled interaction reference (SCTIMST Pharmacy Clinical Decision Support, gentamicin monograph); consistent with aminoglycoside nephrotoxicity literature (Moore RD et al., Ann Intern Med 1984;100:352-7)

interactions.effect: Reduced renal clearance of methotrexate, increasing the risk of methotrexate toxicity (myelosuppression, mucositis, hepatotoxicity), particularly with high-dose methotrexate or in renal impairment.
interactions.mechanism: Penicillins compete with methotrexate for active tubular secretion via renal organic anion transporters (OAT1/OAT3), reducing methotrexate elimination.
interactions.management: Use with caution, especially for penicillin courses longer than ~10 days. Monitor for signs of methotrexate toxicity (sore throat, mouth ulcers, unexplained bruising/bleeding); consider a short methotrexate hold if a course of antibiotics is needed.
interactions.source: NHS Specialist Pharmacy Service, "Managing interactions with methotrexate" (sps.nhs.uk)

interactions.effect: Significantly increased methotrexate toxicity, most often presenting as bone marrow suppression (pancytopenia) and mucosal toxicity; onset can be delayed and has occurred even after co-trimoxazole was started shortly after stopping methotrexate.
interactions.mechanism: Additive antifolate effect (trimethoprim also inhibits dihydrofolate reductase) plus sulfamethoxazole displacing methotrexate from plasma protein binding sites and reducing its renal tubular clearance.
interactions.management: Avoid co-trimoxazole/trimethoprim in patients on methotrexate where possible; consider an alternative antibiotic. If unavoidable, monitor full blood count closely and watch for mucositis, unexplained bleeding, or infection.
interactions.source: GPnotebook/Primary Care Notebook, "Methotrexate and co-trimoxazole and trimethoprim"; case reports: Thomas DR et al., J Am Acad Dermatol 1987;17:1055-6; Thomas MH & Gutterman LA, J Rheumatol 1986;13:440-1

interactions.effect: Increased phenytoin serum levels and prolonged phenytoin half-life, raising the risk of phenytoin toxicity (ataxia, nystagmus, sedation, confusion).
interactions.mechanism: Sulfamethoxazole and trimethoprim inhibit hepatic metabolism of phenytoin; a clinical dosage of co-trimoxazole has been shown to increase phenytoin half-life by ~39% and decrease its metabolic clearance by ~27%.
interactions.management: Monitor phenytoin levels and for signs of toxicity when starting or stopping co-trimoxazole in a patient on phenytoin; a phenytoin dose reduction may be needed.
interactions.source: FDA Sulfatrim (sulfamethoxazole/trimethoprim) Prescribing Information, Drug Interactions section

interactions.effect: Potentiated hypoglycemic effect of glyburide, with an increased risk of severe hypoglycemia requiring hospitalization, especially in elderly patients.
interactions.mechanism: Sulfamethoxazole inhibits CYP2C9-mediated metabolism of glyburide and may displace it from plasma protein binding, increasing free drug levels and prolonging its hypoglycemic effect.
interactions.management: Use an alternative antibiotic where possible in patients on sulfonylureas; if co-trimoxazole must be used, warn the patient about hypoglycemia symptoms and monitor blood glucose closely, particularly in the first few days.
interactions.source: Schelleman H et al., "Anti-infectives and the risk of severe hypoglycemia in users of glipizide or glyburide," Clin Pharmacol Ther 2010;88(2):214-22; ISMP Canada, "Drug-drug Interactions in the Geriatric Population"

interactions.effect: Reduced doxycycline absorption and lower serum levels, which can lead to treatment failure.
interactions.mechanism: Calcium forms a non-absorbable chelate complex with doxycycline in the gastrointestinal tract; oral bioavailability can fall by as much as ~90% depending on timing and dose.
interactions.management: Separate dosing by at least 2 hours before or 4-6 hours after calcium-containing products; avoid routine co-administration for the full course of treatment.
interactions.source: FDA Doxycycline Prescribing Information; PDR drug summary (Doxy 100); hellopharmacist.com interaction monograph ("Doxycycline with Calcium")

interactions.effect: Reduced absorption and serum levels of tetracycline, risking therapeutic failure.
interactions.mechanism: Aluminum ions chelate with tetracycline in the gut, forming an insoluble complex that is poorly absorbed.
interactions.management: Separate dosing by at least 1-2 hours; if concurrent use cannot be avoided, monitor for continued antibiotic efficacy.
interactions.source: FDA tetracycline product labeling; hellopharmacist.com interaction monograph ("Doxycycline with Calcium", chelation mechanism generalizes to the tetracycline class)

interactions.effect: Reduced doxycycline absorption; bioavailability can fall by up to ~80% depending on the magnesium dose and formulation.
interactions.mechanism: Magnesium, like calcium and aluminum, chelates doxycycline in the gastrointestinal tract, forming a poorly absorbed complex.
interactions.management: Take doxycycline at least 2-3 hours apart from magnesium-containing antacids or supplements.
interactions.source: J Pak Med Assoc (archive.jpma.org.pk), dissolution study of tetracyclines with magnesium-containing antacids; PDR doxycycline product labeling

interactions.effect: Elevated serum theophylline concentrations and prolonged elimination half-life, increasing the risk of theophylline toxicity (nausea, tremor, seizures, cardiac arrhythmia).
interactions.mechanism: Ciprofloxacin inhibits the hepatic CYP1A2 enzyme responsible for theophylline metabolism.
interactions.management: Avoid the combination if possible. If concurrent use is necessary, monitor serum theophylline levels and reduce the theophylline dose as needed.
interactions.source: FDA Ciprofloxacin Prescribing Information (DailyMed); Loi CM et al., "The effect of ciprofloxacin on theophylline pharmacokinetics in healthy subjects," PubMed 7619673

interactions.effect: Reduced oral bioavailability of ciprofloxacin, which can result in therapeutic failure.
interactions.mechanism: Polyvalent cations such as calcium form an insoluble chelate complex with the quinolone, reducing its absorption from the gastrointestinal tract.
interactions.management: Take ciprofloxacin at least 2 hours before or 6 hours after calcium-containing products, dairy, or other polyvalent-cation supplements.
interactions.source: FDA Ciprofloxacin Prescribing Information; Drugs.com interaction monograph ("Ciprofloxacin and Calcium")

interactions.effect: Increased risk of CNS stimulation and convulsive seizures, particularly in patients with a seizure predisposition.
interactions.mechanism: Fluoroquinolones inhibit GABA-A receptors; NSAIDs are thought to add to this GABA-antagonist effect, increasing CNS excitability.
interactions.management: Use the combination with caution, especially in patients with a history of seizures, renal impairment, or advanced age; consider an alternative analgesic (e.g. paracetamol) if there is a seizure risk factor.
interactions.source: hellopharmacist.com interaction monograph ("Ibuprofen with Norfloxacin"/quinolone-NSAID class effect); Seki Y et al., "In vitro and preclinical assessment of drug interactions between fluoroquinolones and a nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug predicting risk of seizure," Toxicological Sciences, 2026

interactions.effect: Reduced renal clearance of methotrexate, with a risk of increased methotrexate toxicity, especially at high-dose methotrexate regimens.
interactions.mechanism: Ciprofloxacin is thought to compete with methotrexate for renal tubular secretion, reducing its elimination.
interactions.management: Monitor for signs of methotrexate toxicity (mucositis, cytopenias) if ciprofloxacin is required during methotrexate therapy; consider an alternative antibiotic when feasible.
interactions.source: NHS Specialist Pharmacy Service, "Managing interactions with methotrexate"

interactions.effect: Potentiation of glyburide's hypoglycemic action, which can result in unexpected hypoglycemia.
interactions.mechanism: The mechanism is not fully established, but fluoroquinolones have been reported to affect ATP-sensitive potassium channels involved in insulin release and may act as P-glycoprotein inhibitors, raising sulfonylurea concentrations.
interactions.management: Monitor blood glucose closely when a fluoroquinolone is started in a patient on glyburide, particularly in elderly or renally impaired patients.
interactions.source: FDA Glyburide Prescribing Information, Drug Interactions section ("a possible interaction between glyburide and fluoroquinolone antibiotics")

interactions.effect: Markedly elevated tacrolimus blood concentrations, with case reports of resulting nephrotoxicity, neurotoxicity, hyperkalemia, and hyperglycemia.
interactions.mechanism: Clarithromycin is a potent inhibitor of intestinal and hepatic CYP3A4 and of the P-glycoprotein efflux transporter, both of which normally limit tacrolimus absorption and promote its clearance.
interactions.management: If concurrent use cannot be avoided, reduce the tacrolimus dose substantially (commonly 50-75%) before starting clarithromycin and monitor tacrolimus trough levels every 2-3 days; consider azithromycin as a lower-interaction alternative.
interactions.source: Tacrolimus toxicity in islet transplantation due to interaction with macrolides, Cardiovasc Diabetol Endocrinol Rep, 2016; Wen Y et al., Fundam Clin Pharmacol 2023;37(4):843-848

interactions.effect: Significantly increased sirolimus blood concentrations, raising the risk of sirolimus toxicity (myelosuppression, mucositis, impaired wound healing, nephrotoxicity).
interactions.mechanism: Clarithromycin is a strong CYP3A4 inhibitor; sirolimus is extensively metabolized by CYP3A4 and is also a P-glycoprotein substrate.
interactions.management: Avoid concurrent use where possible; if required, substantially reduce the sirolimus dose and monitor trough levels closely, resuming the usual dose only after clarithromycin is stopped and its effect has worn off.
interactions.source: Sirolimus (Rapamune) FDA Prescribing Information, Drug Interactions section (strong CYP3A4 inhibitors)

interactions.effect: Increased risk of QT-interval prolongation and life-threatening ventricular arrhythmia, including torsades de pointes; sudden deaths have been reported with this combination.
interactions.mechanism: Erythromycin inhibits CYP3A4-mediated metabolism of pimozide, raising pimozide blood levels; both drugs independently prolong the QT interval, so the effects are additive.
interactions.management: Concurrent use is contraindicated. Use an alternative antibiotic (e.g. azithromycin) in patients taking pimozide.
interactions.source: FDA Orap (pimozide) Prescribing Information, Contraindications section; DrugCentral Erythromycin label

interactions.effect: Increased risk of QT-interval prolongation, torsades de pointes, and sudden cardiac death; pimozide concentrations can rise 5-7 fold.
interactions.mechanism: Clarithromycin is a strong CYP3A4 inhibitor; pimozide is approximately 80% metabolized by CYP3A4.
interactions.management: Concurrent use is contraindicated. If clarithromycin is needed, hold pimozide for the course of treatment and resume only after clarithromycin is fully cleared (roughly 7 days after the last dose).
interactions.source: FDA Orap (pimozide) Prescribing Information, Section 4 Contraindications

interactions.effect: Increased carbamazepine (and active metabolite) plasma concentrations by roughly 50-100%, with a risk of carbamazepine toxicity (ataxia, diplopia, confusion, and in severe cases cardiac arrhythmia or coma).
interactions.mechanism: Clarithromycin is a potent, mechanism-based inhibitor of CYP3A4, the primary enzyme responsible for carbamazepine metabolism.
interactions.management: Monitor carbamazepine levels and for signs of toxicity if clarithromycin is started; consider an alternative antibiotic or a temporary carbamazepine dose reduction.
interactions.source: Clarithromycin (Biaxin) FDA Prescribing Information, Drug Interactions section

interactions.effect: Increased serum carbamazepine levels with development of signs of carbamazepine toxicity.
interactions.mechanism: Erythromycin inhibits hepatic CYP3A4-mediated metabolism of carbamazepine.
